items.title: AI in Classrooms
items.subtitle: policy · intermediate
items.body: Most teens now use chatbots for schoolwork, with or without permission. Should schools allow it, and teach students to use it well, or restrict it?

meta.title: AI in Classrooms
meta.resolution: Resolved: High schools should allow students to use generative artificial intelligence tools for schoolwork.
meta.summary: Most teens now use chatbots for schoolwork, with or without permission. Should schools allow it, and teach students to use it well, or restrict it?

background.p: Pew Research Center found the share of U.S. teens (13–17) who had used ChatGPT for schoolwork doubled from 13% in 2023 to 26% in 2024; teens were far more likely to call it acceptable for researching new topics (54%) than for writing essays (18%). A fall 2025 Pew survey found about 54% of teens used chatbots for schoolwork, and 59% said cheating with these tools had become a regular part of student life.

Early experiments point both ways. In a randomized trial in a Harvard introductory physics course (Kestin and colleagues, 2025), students learned more from a carefully designed tutoring tool than from an in-class active-learning lesson on the same topic. In a randomized trial with nearly 1,000 high school math students in Turkey (Bastani and colleagues, PNAS 2025), students with an unrestricted chatbot did better during practice but 17% worse on a later exam without it, while students using a version built to give hints rather than answers did about as well as students without the tool.

The difference between the two studies points to the real question: not only *whether* students use these tools, but *how*. Schools' policies range from bans to rules that allow specific uses (brainstorming, feedback, practice) while forbidding others (submitting generated work as one's own).

disputed.q: Do these tools help or hurt learning?
positions: Some controlled studies find well-designed tutoring tools raise learning, sometimes substantially.
Others find unrestricted use acts as a crutch: students do better while using the tool and worse without it.

terms.def: Software that produces text, images or other content in response to prompts, such as chatbots.
Design limits on a tool, such as giving hints instead of full answers.
Honesty in schoolwork: doing your own work and crediting sources.

aff.label: Affirmative
aff.stance: Schools should allow these tools and teach students to use them well, because students will use them anyway and can learn more with them.

args.claim: Well-designed tools can raise learning.
args.warrant: A tutor that explains step by step, answers questions instantly and adapts to each student offers help that a teacher with thirty students can't always give.
args.evidence: Kestin and colleagues (2025, Scientific Reports): students learned more with a structured tutoring tool than in an active-learning class session.
args.response: The negative answers that the same evidence shows design matters: unrestricted tools can harm learning, as Bastani and colleagues found.

args.claim: Students already use them; schools should teach responsible use.
args.warrant: Bans push use out of sight. Allowing use with clear rules lets teachers teach when it helps, when it doesn't, and how to check its errors.
args.evidence: Pew surveys showing most teens use chatbots for schoolwork; school district policies that permit specific uses.
args.response: The negative replies that widespread misuse is a reason to restrict, not to permit, and that rules for responsible use are hard to enforce.

args.claim: It helps students who lack other help.
args.warrant: Students whose families can't pay tutors or help with homework gain access to explanations at any hour, narrowing gaps.
args.evidence: Studies of tutoring's effects on achievement; reports on access to private tutoring by family income.
args.response: The negative argues that students with less support may also be most likely to lean on the tool as a crutch.

args.claim: Using these tools is a skill students will need.
args.warrant: Many jobs and colleges now expect people to use these tools; learning to use them critically is part of preparing for that.
args.evidence: Employer surveys; college policies allowing guided use.
args.response: The negative replies that students need strong basic skills first, and the tools change so fast that specific skills date quickly.

neg.label: Negative
neg.stance: Schools should restrict these tools for schoolwork, because they let students skip the thinking that learning requires.

args.claim: Unrestricted use can harm learning.
args.warrant: Learning comes from struggling through problems. If a tool supplies answers, students practice copying, not thinking.
args.evidence: Bastani and colleagues (PNAS 2025): students with an unrestricted chatbot scored 17% lower on a later exam without it.
args.response: The affirmative answers that the same study found a hint-based version didn't harm learning, so the answer is rules about design and use, not restriction.

args.claim: It makes cheating easy and hard to detect.
args.warrant: Generated essays and answers are hard to tell apart from student work, which undermines grades and trust.
args.evidence: Pew (2025): 59% of teens say cheating with these tools is a regular part of student life; research on the unreliability of detection software.
args.response: The affirmative replies that cheating happens under bans too; changing assignments (in-class writing, oral checks) works better than prohibition.

args.claim: The tools make mistakes students can't catch.
args.warrant: Chatbots can produce confident but wrong answers. Students who are still learning a subject are the least able to notice.
args.evidence: The Bastani study's finding that the unrestricted tool's answers were correct only about half the time; reports of fabricated citations.
args.response: The affirmative argues that teaching students to check answers is itself valuable, and newer tools with guardrails make fewer errors.

args.claim: Privacy and fairness concerns remain.
args.warrant: Students' questions and work are sent to private companies, and not every family can afford the best versions.
args.evidence: Student-privacy laws such as FERPA and COPPA; school district reviews of vendor contracts.
args.response: The affirmative replies that schools can choose approved tools with privacy protections and provide them free to all students.

strawmen.strawman: They want students to let a chatbot do all their homework.
strawmen.why: Supporters favor allowed uses with rules, not handing over the work.
strawmen.steelman: Students already use these tools; schools that permit specific uses can teach responsible habits and use well-designed tutors that research shows can raise learning.

strawmen.strawman: They're just afraid of new technology.
strawmen.why: Opponents point to controlled evidence that unrestricted use harms learning, plus cheating and accuracy problems.
strawmen.steelman: Learning requires doing the thinking; unrestricted tools let students skip it, as experiments show, and they make cheating easy and errors hard to catch.

weak.arg: Chatbots are always right.
weak.why: They make frequent errors; claiming otherwise is easily refuted.

weak.arg: Technology always makes students dumber.
weak.why: Overgeneralized; calculators, libraries and the internet have mixed and often positive effects.

aff: What happened in the Bastani study when students used an unrestricted chatbot?
How would a teacher know whether a student wrote an essay?
Which uses would you forbid?
neg: What did the Harvard physics study find?
If most students already use these tools, does a ban work?
Would you allow a hint-only tutoring tool?

items.title: The Alaska Purchase, 1867
items.subtitle: policy · intermediate
items.body: In March 1867, Secretary of State William Seward agreed to buy Russian America for $7.2 million. Critics called it a waste of money on a frozen land; supporters saw ports, furs, fish and a foothold in the Pacific. The Senate had to decide.

meta.title: The Alaska Purchase, 1867
meta.resolution: Historical question (1867): Should the United States buy Alaska from Russia?
meta.summary: In March 1867, Secretary of State William Seward agreed to buy Russian America for $7.2 million. Critics called it a waste of money on a frozen land; supporters saw ports, furs, fish and a foothold in the Pacific. The Senate had to decide.

background.p: Russia had held Alaska since the 1700s, but it never had more than about 400 permanent Russian settlers there and lacked the money to defend it. After losing the Crimean War, it offered in 1859 to sell the territory to the United States, partly to keep it from Great Britain, its rival in the Pacific. The Civil War delayed talks. On March 30, 1867, Seward and the Russian minister, Edouard de Stoeckl, agreed on a treaty: the United States would pay $7.2 million in gold for nearly 600,000 square miles, less than 2 cents an acre.

Senator Charles Sumner of Massachusetts, chairman of the Foreign Relations Committee, was doubtful at first. He studied the territory and on April 8 spoke for about three hours in favor of the treaty, describing its climate, minerals, forests and fisheries. The next day, April 9, 1867, the Senate approved the treaty 37 to 2. Russia formally handed over the territory at Sitka on October 18, 1867. The House delayed the money for more than a year and approved it on July 14, 1868, by 113 to 43.

Critics mocked the purchase as "Seward's Folly" and "Seward's Icebox." Some historians argue the opposition was smaller than the legend suggests, since many newspapers supported the treaty. By the Russian estimates Seward cited, about 60,000 people lived in the territory, most of them Alaska Native peoples living outside Russian control; the treaty was made between the two governments. Gold strikes in the Yukon and Alaska in the 1890s later changed many minds. Alaska became a state in 1959.

disputed.q: How unpopular was the purchase in 1867?
positions: The traditional story says most Americans thought it was a foolish waste, as the nicknames suggest.
Some historians, citing newspaper studies and the lopsided Senate vote, argue that most papers and lawmakers supported it and the "folly" story is largely a myth.

terms.def: The name used for Alaska before the purchase. Sumner urged the name "Alaska," from a Native word.
The formal handing over of territory from one country to another by treaty.
Under the Constitution, a treaty takes effect only if two-thirds of the senators present approve it.
A law that sets aside public money for a purpose. The House had to vote the $7.2 million even after the Senate approved the treaty.
Sharing a border. Alaska was not contiguous with the rest of the United States, since British territory lay between.

aff.label: For the purchase
aff.stance: Alaska is a bargain that gives the nation Pacific ports, valuable resources and a stronger place in the world.

args.claim: Alaska opens the way to Pacific trade.
args.warrant: Seward and many others expected Asia to become a great market. Ports and coastline in the north Pacific would help American ships and merchants reach it.
args.evidence: Seward's speeches and letters on Pacific commerce; Sumner's April 1867 speech on the territory's harbors and its place on the route to Asia.
args.response: Opponents answered that the country already had Pacific ports in California, Oregon and Washington Territory, far closer to settled land.

args.claim: The land holds real wealth.
args.warrant: Furs, fisheries, forests and likely minerals could repay the price many times over, even if the land is cold.
args.evidence: Sumner's speech, which surveyed the climate, soil, minerals, timber and fisheries using more than 100 books and reports he studied.
args.response: Opponents answered that little was known for certain about the interior, and hoped-for minerals were only guesses.

args.claim: The price is very low.
args.warrant: Nearly 600,000 square miles for $7.2 million is less than 2 cents an acre. Few chances like it come along, and if the United States refuses, another power might buy it.
args.evidence: The treaty's terms; comparisons with the prices of earlier land purchases.
args.response: Opponents answered that a low price per acre means little if the acres can't be used, and $7.2 million was a large sum for a nation in debt.

args.claim: It strengthens friendship with Russia and the nation's position against Britain.
args.warrant: Russia was friendly to the Union during the Civil War. Buying Alaska rewards that friendship and leaves British Columbia surrounded by American territory, which some hoped would lead it to join the United States.
args.evidence: Newspaper editorials of 1867, many of which cited friendship with Russia and the chance of gaining British Columbia.
args.response: Opponents answered that a treaty shouldn't be bought to flatter a foreign government, and that hopes of taking British Columbia were speculation.

neg.label: Against the purchase
neg.stance: The nation is deep in debt from the Civil War and shouldn't spend millions on a distant, frozen land it can't use or defend.

args.claim: The country can't afford it now.
args.warrant: The Civil War left a huge national debt and heavy taxes. Money spent on Alaska could instead pay down debt or cut taxes.
args.evidence: Horace Greeley's New York Tribune, which argued the money would be better spent reducing the income tax; Treasury debt figures of the 1860s.
args.response: Supporters answered that $7.2 million was small next to the debt, and a land with valuable resources would pay for itself.

args.claim: Alaska is too far away to govern or defend.
args.warrant: It doesn't border any state; British territory lies between. Holding a distant colony would cost money for soldiers and officials and could pull the nation into conflicts.
args.evidence: Speeches and editorials of 1867–68 calling it a colony not contiguous to the national domain.
args.response: Supporters answered that the sea joins Alaska to the Pacific coast, and that leaving it to Britain would be worse for defense.

args.claim: We don't know what we're buying.
args.warrant: Few Americans had seen the territory. Critics described it as a frozen wilderness of ice, snow and rock, with few settlers and no proven gold.
args.evidence: Critics' descriptions collected on the Senate history page; the New York World's line that Russia had sold "a sucked orange."
args.response: Supporters answered that Sumner's research showed rich fisheries, forests and furs, and that the coast was milder than critics claimed.

args.claim: The deal was made in secret and in haste.
args.warrant: Seward negotiated the treaty quietly and finished it overnight, leaving the public and the House, which must vote the money, little say.
args.evidence: Accounts of the March 1867 negotiation; criticism of Seward's secrecy; the House's long delay in voting the money.
args.response: Supporters answered that the Senate studied the treaty in committee and approved it 37 to 2, which is the process the Constitution sets for treaties.

strawmen.strawman: Seward just wanted more land on the map, whatever it cost.
strawmen.why: Supporters gave specific reasons: Pacific trade, furs and fisheries, a very low price, and relations with Russia and Britain.
strawmen.steelman: For less than 2 cents an acre, the nation could gain Pacific ports, valuable resources and a stronger position against Britain, while rewarding a friendly Russia.

strawmen.strawman: The critics were just short-sighted people who couldn't imagine the future.
strawmen.why: Critics made real arguments about war debt, the cost of governing a distant territory, and how little was known about the land.
strawmen.steelman: A nation burdened by war debt shouldn't spend millions on a distant, little-known land it would have to govern and defend, especially on a treaty made in secret.

weak.arg: Buy it, because gold will be found there.
weak.why: In 1867 no one knew about the gold strikes of the 1890s; using later events to argue an 1867 debate isn't fair to the people deciding.

weak.arg: It's just ice and polar bears.
weak.why: That joke ignores what was known in 1867 about the coast's furs, fish and timber, which supporters could easily point to.

aff: What do we know for certain about the land's value today, in 1867?
Who will pay for governing and defending a territory so far away?
Why must the treaty be decided so quickly?
neg: If we refuse, who might buy Alaska instead?
Is $7.2 million large compared with the national debt?
Why are Pacific ports in the north worth less than ports in the south?

items.title: Animals in Medical Research
items.subtitle: value · advanced
items.body: Animal research has contributed to many medical advances, and new methods are beginning to replace some of it. Is using animals to protect human health morally justified?

meta.title: Animals in Medical Research
meta.resolution: Resolved: The use of animals in medical research is morally justified.
meta.summary: Animal research has contributed to many medical advances, and new methods are beginning to replace some of it. Is using animals to protect human health morally justified?

background.p: Animals such as mice, rats, fish and, less often, dogs and primates are used in research on diseases and in testing whether new drugs are safe. U.S. law regulates the care of many research animals, and scientists are expected to follow the "3Rs": **replace** animals where possible, **reduce** the number used and **refine** methods to lessen suffering.

Policy is shifting. The FDA Modernization Act 2.0 (2022) removed the legal requirement that new drugs be tested on animals before human trials, allowing alternatives. In April 2025, the FDA announced it would phase out animal-testing requirements for monoclonal antibodies and other drugs where human-relevant methods, such as organoids (tiny lab-grown organ models) and computer models, can be used, while noting the change would be gradual. Scientists note that animal models have both strengths (controlled conditions, whole living systems) and limits (animals process some chemicals differently from people).

disputed.q: Can alternatives replace animal research?
positions: Supporters of alternatives point to organoids, computer models and human data that can be more relevant to people.
Many researchers say alternatives can't yet capture a whole living body, so some animal research is still needed for safety and basic science.

terms.def: Replace, reduce and refine: principles for using fewer animals and causing less suffering.
A tiny three-dimensional cluster of cells grown in a lab that mimics part of an organ.
Research done before a drug is tested in people.
Whether, and how much, a being's interests count morally.

aff.label: Affirmative
aff.stance: Carefully regulated animal research is justified because it saves human and animal lives.

args.claim: Animal research has contributed to major medical advances.
args.warrant: Studying whole living bodies reveals how diseases progress and how treatments work in ways cells in a dish can't.
args.evidence: Histories of vaccines, insulin and surgical techniques; Nobel Prize research involving animal models.
args.response: The negative answers that past use doesn't prove animals are still needed, now that better methods exist.

args.claim: Safety testing protects people.
args.warrant: Testing new drugs in animals first can reveal dangerous effects before humans are exposed.
args.evidence: Regulatory history of drug safety testing; cases where animal tests flagged toxicity.
args.response: The negative replies that many drugs that pass animal tests still fail in humans, showing the tests' limits.

args.claim: Human welfare can outweigh animal suffering when suffering is minimized.
args.warrant: If research can save many human lives and is done under rules that minimize pain, the benefits can justify the costs.
args.evidence: Ethical frameworks weighing benefits and harms; the 3Rs and animal-welfare laws.
args.response: The negative argues that animals' suffering counts morally, and benefits to us don't justify harming beings who can't consent.

args.claim: Animal research also helps animals.
args.warrant: Veterinary medicines and vaccines for pets, livestock and wildlife come from the same research.
args.evidence: Veterinary vaccine development records.
args.response: The negative replies that this justifies research for animals' own benefit, not the much larger use for human medicine.

neg.label: Negative
neg.stance: Animals' suffering counts, and better methods make most animal research unjustified.

args.claim: Animals can suffer, and they can't consent.
args.warrant: If a being can feel pain and fear, causing it pain needs a very strong justification, especially when it can't agree to the risk.
args.evidence: Scientific research on animal sentience; philosophical arguments on moral status.
args.response: The affirmative answers that the rules require minimizing pain, and some human benefit is strong enough to justify it.

args.claim: Animal models often fail to predict human results.
args.warrant: Species differ in how they process drugs, so results don't always transfer; tests can miss harms or wrongly flag safe drugs.
args.evidence: Dr. Paul Locke's comments in coverage of the FDA's 2025 announcement; drug failure rates in human trials.
args.response: The affirmative replies that animal tests still catch many problems, and imperfect isn't useless.

args.claim: Better alternatives are emerging.
args.warrant: Organoids, computer models and human data may be more relevant to people, so continued animal use is harder to justify.
args.evidence: The FDA Modernization Act 2.0 (2022) and the FDA's April 2025 plan.
args.response: The affirmative argues the FDA itself says the change will be gradual because alternatives can't yet do everything.

args.claim: The benefits are not shared fairly.
args.warrant: Animals bear all the costs and receive little of the benefit, which treats them merely as tools.
args.evidence: Philosophical arguments drawing on Kant's and utilitarian ideas about moral consideration.
args.response: The affirmative replies that people and animals both benefit from veterinary advances, and moral status may differ between species.

strawmen.strawman: Researchers don't care if animals suffer.
strawmen.why: Research is governed by welfare rules and the 3Rs, and many researchers work to reduce animal use.
strawmen.steelman: Regulated animal research has contributed to major advances and protects people from unsafe drugs; when suffering is minimized, the lifesaving benefits justify it.

strawmen.strawman: Opponents care more about mice than about sick children.
strawmen.why: Opponents argue that animal suffering counts and that better human-relevant methods exist.
strawmen.steelman: Animals can suffer and can't consent, animal models often fail to predict human results, and emerging alternatives make most animal research hard to justify.

weak.arg: Every medical advance in history came from animal testing.
weak.why: Many advances came from other methods; overclaiming invites easy rebuttal.

weak.arg: Animal testing has never helped anyone.
weak.why: Contradicted by medical history; it costs credibility.

aff: What did the FDA announce in 2025, and why?
How often do drugs that pass animal tests fail in humans?
Which research would you still allow if alternatives existed?
neg: Can an organoid show how a drug affects a whole body?
Did the FDA say alternatives could replace all animal tests now?
Would you allow research that helps animals themselves?

items.title: A Carbon Tax
items.subtitle: policy · advanced
items.body: Thousands of economists have endorsed taxing carbon emissions and returning the money to households. Others question whether it's the right tool. Should the U.S. adopt one?

meta.title: A Carbon Tax
meta.resolution: Resolved: The United States federal government should enact a carbon tax with the revenue returned to citizens.
meta.summary: Thousands of economists have endorsed taxing carbon emissions and returning the money to households. Others question whether it's the right tool. Should the U.S. adopt one?

background.p: A **carbon tax** charges fuel producers or importers for the carbon dioxide their fuels release when burned, so the price of fossil fuels reflects some of the cost of the emissions. In January 2019, the Wall Street Journal published the "Economists' Statement on Carbon Dividends," signed by 45 prominent economists, including former Federal Reserve chairs from both parties and Nobel laureates, and later by more than 3,500 economists. It proposed a carbon tax rising each year, with all revenue returned to Americans as equal payments, a border adjustment on imports, and the replacement of some regulations.

British Columbia has taxed carbon since 2008. Studies summarized by the CBC found it reduced emissions roughly 5 to 15% below what they would otherwise have been, with no clear harm to the province's economy, though total emissions stayed roughly flat as the population and economy grew. Canada's national consumer carbon charge, built on a similar idea, was ended in 2025.

disputed.q: How much does a carbon tax cut emissions?
positions: Studies of British Columbia find meaningful reductions compared with what would have happened without the tax.
Critics note total emissions there stayed roughly flat, and that fuel demand responds slowly to price.

terms.def: A cost (or benefit) of an activity that falls on people outside the transaction, like pollution.
Returning carbon tax revenue to households as equal payments.
A fee on imports from countries without a similar carbon price, and a rebate for exports.
Taking a larger share of income from lower-income households.

aff.label: Affirmative
aff.stance: Putting a price on carbon is the cheapest way to cut emissions, and dividends protect families.

args.claim: A price on carbon cuts emissions at the lowest cost.
args.warrant: When fossil fuels cost more, millions of people and businesses find the cheapest ways to use less, rather than the government choosing the method for each industry.
args.evidence: The Economists' Statement on Carbon Dividends (2019); economic research on carbon pricing.
args.response: The negative answers that demand for fuel responds slowly, so a tax low enough to be politically possible cuts emissions only modestly.

args.claim: Dividends make most families whole.
args.warrant: If revenue is returned equally, households that use less energy than average (often lower-income households) can get back more than they pay.
args.evidence: Analyses of carbon-dividend proposals by income group; the statement's proposal for equal lump-sum payments.
args.response: The negative replies that rural drivers and people in cold climates may pay more than they get back, and dividends may not survive future budgets.

args.claim: It can replace a tangle of regulations.
args.warrant: One clear price can do the work of many rules, giving businesses certainty and lowering compliance costs.
args.evidence: The statement's proposal to replace less efficient regulations; studies of regulatory costs.
args.response: The negative argues regulations would likely stay, so businesses face both.

args.claim: A border adjustment protects American industry.
args.warrant: Charging imports from countries without a carbon price keeps U.S. producers competitive and encourages other countries to act.
args.evidence: Proposals for border carbon adjustments; the European Union's border carbon mechanism.
args.response: The negative replies that border adjustments are complex, may break trade rules and invite retaliation.

neg.label: Negative
neg.stance: A carbon tax raises energy costs, hits some families and regions hardest, and is a weak tool in practice.

args.claim: It raises the cost of energy and everything made with it.
args.warrant: Fuel and electricity feed into nearly every product, so a carbon tax raises prices across the economy.
args.evidence: Energy price studies; EIA data on fuel's share of household budgets.
args.response: The affirmative answers that dividends return the money, so most households come out even or ahead.

args.claim: The burden falls unevenly.
args.warrant: Rural families who drive long distances and people in cold or energy-producing regions pay more, while equal dividends don't match their costs.
args.evidence: Studies of carbon tax burdens by region and income; Canada's experience with public opposition.
args.response: The affirmative replies that dividends can be adjusted, and doing nothing about climate also has uneven costs.

args.claim: Real-world results are modest.
args.warrant: If emissions stayed roughly flat even where the tax has run longest, a carbon tax alone may not deliver large reductions.
args.evidence: British Columbia's total emissions (roughly flat 2005–2017); studies summarized by the CBC estimating reductions of about 5 to 15% below what emissions would otherwise have been.
args.response: The affirmative argues that emissions were lower than they would have been, which is the right comparison.

args.claim: The U.S. acting alone may shift emissions abroad.
args.warrant: If energy-intensive production moves to countries without carbon prices, global emissions may barely change while U.S. jobs leave.
args.evidence: Research on "carbon leakage"; trade data on energy-intensive goods.
args.response: The affirmative replies that a border adjustment is designed to stop exactly this.

strawmen.strawman: They want to make gas so expensive nobody can drive.
strawmen.why: Proposals return revenue to households and phase in gradually.
strawmen.steelman: A rising carbon price with dividends cuts emissions at the lowest cost, protects most families, and can replace less efficient rules.

strawmen.strawman: Opponents don't believe in climate change.
strawmen.why: Many opponents accept climate change but doubt the tax's fairness, politics or effectiveness.
strawmen.steelman: A carbon tax raises costs across the economy, falls hardest on rural and cold-climate families, and has delivered modest results where tried.

weak.arg: A carbon tax will solve climate change by itself.
weak.why: No single policy can; overclaiming invites an easy answer.

weak.arg: Carbon dioxide is plant food, so it isn't pollution.
weak.why: This ignores the warming effect that is the basis of the debate; it won't persuade a judge.

aff: How much would gasoline prices rise per gallon at your starting price?
Would rural households get back what they pay?
Would existing regulations be repealed?
neg: What did studies find about British Columbia's emissions compared with no tax?
Who gets more back than they pay under equal dividends?
What policy would you use instead to cut emissions?

items.title: Civil Disobedience
items.subtitle: value · advanced
items.body: Is it right to break a law openly and peacefully to protest an injustice, even in a democracy where citizens can vote and petition? A classic Lincoln-Douglas question with roots in Socrates, Thoreau and King.

meta.title: Civil Disobedience
meta.resolution: Resolved: In a democracy, civil disobedience is a morally justified response to injustice.
meta.summary: Is it right to break a law openly and peacefully to protest an injustice, even in a democracy where citizens can vote and petition? A classic Lincoln-Douglas question with roots in Socrates, Thoreau and King.

background.p: **Civil disobedience** usually means breaking a law publicly, without violence, to protest a law or policy and to persuade others, often while accepting the legal penalty. Philosophers disagree about the exact definition and about when, if ever, it is justified, especially in a democracy that offers legal ways to change laws.

The question is ancient. In Plato's *Crito*, Socrates refuses to escape from prison before his execution, arguing that a citizen who has accepted a city's laws should not break them, even when treated unjustly. Henry David Thoreau's essay "Resistance to Civil Government" (1849), later known as "Civil Disobedience," defended refusing to pay a tax that supported slavery and an unjust war. Martin Luther King Jr.'s "Letter from Birmingham Jail" (1963) argued that one has a moral responsibility to disobey unjust laws, openly, lovingly and with a willingness to accept the penalty. Today, debaters must decide how these arguments apply to modern democracies.

terms.def: Public, nonviolent lawbreaking meant to protest and change a law or policy, usually with acceptance of the penalty.
The principle that everyone, including officials, is bound by publicly known laws applied equally.
The rightful authority of a government or law, often tied to consent and fair procedures.
Refusing to obey a law, usually privately, because it violates one's conscience, without aiming to change it.

aff.label: Affirmative
aff.stance: When legal channels fail to correct serious injustice, open, peaceful lawbreaking can be right.

args.claim: Democracies can still enact unjust laws.
args.warrant: Majorities can vote to harm minorities, and people denied a vote can't use legal channels; disobedience can be the only way to be heard.
args.evidence: The civil rights movement and segregation laws passed through democratic procedures; King's Letter from Birmingham Jail.
args.response: The negative answers that the civil rights era included denial of voting rights, so it was not a full democracy for those protesters.

args.claim: Civil disobedience respects the law even while breaking it.
args.warrant: By acting openly, peacefully and accepting the penalty, protesters show respect for the legal system while appealing to the community's sense of justice.
args.evidence: King's argument that one must break unjust laws "openly, lovingly" and accept the penalty; philosophers' accounts summarized by the Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy.
args.response: The negative replies that accepting the penalty doesn't undo the harm of encouraging others to choose which laws to obey.

args.claim: It has corrected injustices that legal means did not.
args.warrant: When petitions and lawsuits move slowly or fail, visible protest can change public opinion and lead to reform.
args.evidence: Historical cases such as lunch-counter sit-ins and their role in desegregation.
args.response: The negative argues that legal action (court cases, elections) also drove these changes, and it's hard to separate causes.

args.claim: Individuals have a duty of conscience.
args.warrant: A person shouldn't take part in serious wrongdoing just because a law demands it; moral responsibility can't be handed to the state.
args.evidence: Thoreau's "Resistance to Civil Government"; moral philosophy on individual responsibility.
args.response: The negative replies that conscience varies by person, and if everyone follows their own, law can't function.

neg.label: Negative
neg.stance: In a working democracy, citizens should change unjust laws through legal means, not by breaking them.

args.claim: Democracy provides legal ways to change laws.
args.warrant: Where citizens can vote, speak, petition, sue and protest lawfully, breaking the law bypasses the fair process everyone shares.
args.evidence: First Amendment protections for speech, assembly and petition; history of legal reform movements.
args.response: The affirmative answers that legal channels can be closed or too slow for people facing serious injustice now.

args.claim: Lawbreaking weakens the rule of law.
args.warrant: If each person may break laws they judge unjust, people with opposing views will do the same, and law loses its authority.
args.evidence: Socrates' argument in Plato's Crito; arguments about the rule of law in political philosophy.
args.response: The affirmative replies that accepting the penalty and acting openly distinguishes civil disobedience from ordinary lawbreaking.

args.claim: Who decides what's unjust?
args.warrant: People sincerely disagree about justice; a principle justifying disobedience for one cause also justifies it for causes we reject.
args.evidence: Examples of civil disobedience across the political spectrum; the SEP's discussion of disagreement.
args.response: The affirmative argues that limits (nonviolence, publicity, serious injustice, exhausting legal means) prevent the principle from justifying anything.

args.claim: Disobedience can harm innocent people.
args.warrant: Blocking roads, for example, can delay ambulances or workers who had nothing to do with the injustice.
args.evidence: Reports of protests disrupting emergency services; debates about protest tactics.
args.response: The affirmative replies that well-chosen civil disobedience targets the unjust law itself and avoids harming bystanders.

strawmen.strawman: They think anyone can break any law they don't like.
strawmen.why: Defenders set conditions: serious injustice, nonviolence, openness, and acceptance of the penalty.
strawmen.steelman: Democracies can still enact serious injustices; open, peaceful disobedience that accepts the penalty can be the only effective way to correct them.

strawmen.strawman: They think the civil rights protesters were wrong.
strawmen.why: Many on the negative argue that era lacked full democracy for the protesters, and focus on working democracies today.
strawmen.steelman: Where citizens have real legal means of change, breaking the law undermines the fair process and the rule of law, and invites everyone to disobey laws they dislike.

weak.arg: Laws are just opinions anyway.
weak.why: Dismisses the rule of law entirely; it undermines the distinction you need between just and unjust laws.

weak.arg: Breaking the law is always wrong, period.
weak.why: Hard to defend against the strongest historical examples; argue about working democracies instead.

aff: What conditions must civil disobedience meet?
Would your principle justify disobedience for causes you oppose?
Have legal channels been tried first?
neg: Were Black citizens in 1963 Alabama able to vote freely?
Is accepting the penalty a form of respect for law?
Should someone obey a law requiring them to do something gravely wrong?

items.title: College Athletes as Employees
items.subtitle: policy · intermediate
items.body: College athletes can now earn money from endorsements, and schools can share revenue with them. Should they go further and be treated as employees, with wages and the right to bargain?

meta.title: College Athletes as Employees
meta.resolution: Resolved: College athletes should be classified as employees of their universities.
meta.summary: College athletes can now earn money from endorsements, and schools can share revenue with them. Should they go further and be treated as employees, with wages and the right to bargain?

background.p: For decades the NCAA barred college athletes from being paid beyond scholarships. Since 2021, athletes have been allowed to earn money from their name, image and likeness (NIL) through endorsements and sponsorships. In June 2025 a federal judge approved the settlement in *House v. NCAA*, which provides about $2.8 billion in back damages to former athletes and lets schools share athletic revenue directly with players, up to a cap of $20.5 million per school in 2025–26, rising each year. It also replaced scholarship limits with roster limits, which cost some walk-on and partial-scholarship athletes their spots.

The settlement did not decide whether athletes are employees, which would bring wages, workplace protections, taxes and possibly union bargaining. Supporters of employee status say athletes work long hours generating billions; opponents worry it would end the student-athlete model, force cuts to sports that don't earn money, and create problems under Title IX, the law requiring equal opportunity for women in school sports.

disputed.q: Would employee status force schools to cut sports?
positions: Opponents expect schools to cut sports that don't earn money if they must pay wages and benefits to all athletes.
Supporters say most money flows in football and basketball, and schools have choices about coaches' salaries and facilities.

terms.def: Name, image and likeness: athletes' right to earn money from endorsements and appearances.
Schools paying part of their athletic revenue directly to athletes, as allowed under the House settlement.
The 1972 federal law banning sex discrimination in education programs, including athletics.
Negotiation between employers and a union representing employees.

aff.label: Affirmative
aff.stance: Athletes who do the work that brings in billions should have the rights and pay of employees.

args.claim: Athletes perform work that generates large revenue.
args.warrant: Long practice hours, travel and games produce media and ticket revenue for schools; people doing that work should be treated as workers.
args.evidence: Athletic department revenue data; time-demand surveys of athletes; the size of the House settlement.
args.response: The negative answers that most college sports lose money, and athletes are students first.

args.claim: Employee status brings protections.
args.warrant: Employees get workplace safety rules, injury coverage and the right to bargain; athletes with serious injuries can be left with little support.
args.evidence: Labor law protections; cases of athletes' long-term injuries and medical costs.
args.response: The negative replies that schools can provide health coverage and protections without employee status.

args.claim: Revenue sharing alone leaves athletes without a voice.
args.warrant: Schools and conferences set the terms of revenue sharing; only collective bargaining gives athletes a say in rules, pay and schedules.
args.evidence: Terms of the House settlement set without an athletes' union; examples from professional leagues.
args.response: The negative argues that bargaining across hundreds of schools would be unworkable and costly.

args.claim: The old amateur model treated athletes unfairly.
args.warrant: Coaches and administrators earned millions while athletes couldn't be paid, which courts found violated antitrust law.
args.evidence: O'Bannon v. NCAA (Ninth Circuit, 2015), which found the NCAA's ban on paying athletes for the use of their names and images violated antitrust law; the House settlement's back damages.
args.response: The negative answers that NIL and revenue sharing already fix this without turning students into employees.

neg.label: Negative
neg.stance: Athletes should be paid fairly, but as student-athletes, not employees.

args.claim: Employee status could lead schools to cut sports.
args.warrant: Most college teams don't make money; adding wages, benefits and taxes may push schools to cut sports such as swimming, wrestling and track.
args.evidence: Athletic department budgets; roster cuts that followed the House settlement.
args.response: The affirmative answers that schools could reduce spending on coaches' salaries and facilities instead.

args.claim: It creates conflicts with Title IX.
args.warrant: If most pay goes to football and men's basketball players, schools may face claims that they're failing to provide equal opportunity to women athletes.
args.evidence: Title IX challenges filed against the House settlement by women athletes.
args.response: The affirmative replies that Title IX can be applied to pay just as it is to scholarships.

args.claim: Athletes are students first.
args.warrant: College sports exist within education; making athletes employees could subordinate classes to work demands.
args.evidence: Graduation data for athletes; NCAA academic requirements.
args.response: The affirmative argues that work demands already dominate for many athletes, so recognizing reality is more honest.

args.claim: New pay systems already address fairness.
args.warrant: NIL deals and revenue sharing put money in athletes' hands without the legal complications of employment.
args.evidence: The House settlement's revenue-sharing cap; NIL earnings data.
args.response: The affirmative replies that these leave athletes without protections or bargaining rights.

strawmen.strawman: They want to turn college sports into the NFL.
strawmen.why: Supporters want rights and protections for athletes, not necessarily professional leagues.
strawmen.steelman: Athletes do work that generates billions; employee status would give them pay, injury protections and a voice through bargaining.

strawmen.strawman: They don't think athletes deserve anything.
strawmen.why: Most opponents support NIL and revenue sharing.
strawmen.steelman: Athletes should be paid through NIL and revenue sharing, but employee status could cut sports, create Title IX conflicts and undermine the student part of student-athlete.

weak.arg: Every college athlete brings in millions.
weak.why: Most programs and athletes don't generate large revenue.

weak.arg: A scholarship is payment enough.
weak.why: Courts and the House settlement have already moved past this; argue about employment specifically.

aff: How many college sports earn more than they cost?
What happens to women's sports under your plan?
Would athletes pay income tax on scholarships?
neg: Who decided the terms of revenue sharing?
Who pays for a career-ending injury now?
What did the courts decide in O'Bannon v. NCAA?

items.title: Tuition-Free Community College
items.subtitle: policy · intermediate
items.body: Tennessee and other states cover community college tuition for recent high school graduates. Should every state do it?

meta.title: Tuition-Free Community College
meta.resolution: Resolved: States should make community college tuition-free.
meta.summary: Tennessee and other states cover community college tuition for recent high school graduates. Should every state do it?

background.p: Since 2015, Tennessee Promise has covered community college tuition and fees left after other grants for students who enroll right after high school, keep at least a 2.0 GPA, work with a mentor and do community service. More than 200 "promise" programs now exist across the U.S., with varying rules.

A 2025 working paper by economists Celeste Carruthers and Paige Schoonover, reported by Higher Ed Dive, found Tennessee Promise raised college enrollment among 19-year-olds by 5.4 percentage points and associate degrees among 21-year-olds by 2.9 points, increased transfers to four-year colleges, and raised early-career earnings by 6 to 8%. Because most students already qualify for Pell Grants or state aid, the program cost under $1,000 per participating student a year; one author said it pays for itself through higher earnings. Results of other promise programs vary.

disputed.q: Does free tuition raise graduation, or mostly enrollment?
positions: Tennessee's results show gains in both enrollment and degrees.
Critics note completion rates at community colleges remain low and that tuition is often not the main barrier; results differ across programs.

terms.def: Covers whatever tuition remains after other grants, like Pell Grants, are applied.
Covers tuition before other aid, so grants can go to living costs.
Federal grant aid for students from lower-income families.
The share of students who finish a degree or certificate within a set time.

aff.label: Affirmative
aff.stance: Tuition-free community college opens doors to degrees and better jobs at a modest cost.

args.claim: Free tuition gets more students into college.
args.warrant: A clear promise of "free" is easier to understand than aid forms, and it reaches students who assume college isn't for them.
args.evidence: Carruthers and Schoonover: a 5.4-point rise in enrollment among 19-year-olds in Tennessee.
args.response: The negative answers that getting students in the door isn't enough if many don't finish.

args.claim: It raises degrees and earnings.
args.warrant: More students who enroll and finish credentials earn more, which helps them and the state's economy.
args.evidence: Tennessee Promise: associate degrees up 2.9 points; earnings 6 to 8% higher in early adulthood; more transfers to four-year colleges.
args.response: The negative replies that one state's results may not carry over, and other programs show smaller effects.

args.claim: The cost is modest.
args.warrant: Because federal and state grants already cover much tuition, a last-dollar promise costs relatively little per student.
args.evidence: Under $1,000 per participating student per year in Tennessee, as reported by Higher Ed Dive.
args.response: The negative argues last-dollar designs give little to the poorest students, whose tuition is already covered, while first-dollar designs cost much more.

args.claim: Workforce needs call for more trained workers.
args.warrant: Many growing jobs need a certificate or associate degree, and community colleges train nurses, technicians and tradespeople.
args.evidence: Bureau of Labor Statistics projections by education level; state workforce reports.
args.response: The negative replies that apprenticeships and employer-paid training may meet those needs more directly.

neg.label: Negative
neg.stance: Free tuition spends money on the wrong barrier; aid should target need and completion.

args.claim: Tuition isn't the main barrier for low-income students.
args.warrant: Pell Grants already cover community college tuition for many low-income students; their bigger obstacles are living costs, work hours and child care.
args.evidence: Data on Pell Grant amounts and community college tuition; surveys of why students leave college.
args.response: The affirmative answers that the simple message of "free" still raises enrollment, as Tennessee shows.

args.claim: Benefits flow to families who could pay.
args.warrant: Last-dollar programs give the most money to students who don't qualify for need-based aid, often from middle- and higher-income families.
args.evidence: Analyses of who receives promise-program dollars by income.
args.response: The affirmative replies that middle-income families also struggle with costs, and universal programs win broad support.

args.claim: Completion matters more than enrollment.
args.warrant: Students who enroll and leave without a credential may end up with lost time and no payoff; money for advising and support may do more.
args.evidence: Community college completion data; studies of advising programs such as CUNY ASAP.
args.response: The affirmative replies that Tennessee's program includes mentoring and raised degrees, not just enrollment.

args.claim: States have competing needs.
args.warrant: Dollars for free tuition can't go to K–12 schools, need-based aid or apprenticeships, which may help more students per dollar.
args.evidence: State budget data; evaluations of alternative workforce programs.
args.response: The affirmative argues the program's low cost and higher earnings mean it may pay for itself.

strawmen.strawman: They think everyone should get a free ride for everything.
strawmen.why: Most proposals cover only community college tuition, with requirements like GPA and mentoring.
strawmen.steelman: A clear promise of free community college raises enrollment, degrees and earnings at modest cost, as Tennessee shows.

strawmen.strawman: They don't want poor kids to go to college.
strawmen.why: Opponents favor aid targeted to need and to completion.
strawmen.steelman: Tuition isn't the main barrier for most low-income students; money should target living costs, advising and completion instead of tuition for families who can pay.

weak.arg: Free college means no one will have student debt.
weak.why: Living costs and four-year degrees still create debt; overclaiming invites an easy answer.

weak.arg: Nothing free is ever valued.
weak.why: A slogan, not evidence; Tennessee's results contradict it.

aff: Does your plan cover tuition before or after Pell Grants?
What happens to students who enroll but don't finish?
Do other promise programs show the same results as Tennessee?
neg: What did the Tennessee study find about degrees and earnings?
How much did it cost per student?
What would you fund instead, and what evidence supports it?

items.title: Compulsory Voting
items.subtitle: value · intermediate
items.body: Australia has required citizens to vote for a century, and turnout is about 90%. Is compulsory voting a duty a democracy may require, or an intrusion on liberty?

meta.title: Compulsory Voting
meta.resolution: Resolved: In a democracy, voting ought to be compulsory.
meta.summary: Australia has required citizens to vote for a century, and turnout is about 90%. Is compulsory voting a duty a democracy may require, or an intrusion on liberty?

background.p: Australia made voting compulsory in federal elections in 1924. Turnout had been 59.4% at the 1922 election and has been above 90% at nearly every election since; it was 89.8% for the House of Representatives in 2022. People who don't vote without a valid reason face a small fine. Voters may return a blank or spoiled ballot, so in practice the requirement is to show up (or vote by mail), not to choose a candidate. About 70% of Australians support the system, according to a 2024 lecture published by the Australian Parliament.

A number of other democracies, including Belgium, Brazil and Argentina, have some form of compulsory voting, with differing enforcement. In the United States, no state requires voting. This is a classic Lincoln-Douglas value resolution: the debate is about what a democracy owes and may ask of its citizens.

disputed.q: Does compulsory voting change election results or policies?
positions: Supporters say it makes the electorate more representative and rewards moderate, broad-based campaigns.
Skeptics say evidence on policy effects is mixed and mostly comes from a few countries with different histories.

terms.def: A legal duty to vote (or at least to attend the polls), usually enforced by a small fine.
The share of eligible people who vote.
A ballot cast without a valid vote; it lets people meet the duty without choosing.
The public's acceptance that a government has the right to rule.

aff.label: Affirmative
aff.stance: A democracy is strongest when all citizens take part, and a small civic duty is a fair way to ensure it.

args.claim: Universal turnout makes government more representative.
args.warrant: When turnout is low, those who vote differ from those who don't by age, income and education; a democracy should hear from all its citizens.
args.evidence: Australian turnout before and after 1924; U.S. data on turnout gaps by age and income.
args.response: The negative answers that representation means representing those who choose to participate, and non-voters can still be heard in other ways.

args.claim: It strengthens legitimacy and reduces polarization.
args.warrant: When nearly everyone votes, winners must appeal to the broad middle, not just energize their most motivated supporters.
args.evidence: Paul Strangio's 2024 Australian Senate lecture on centrism and legitimacy; comparative studies of compulsory voting.
args.response: The negative replies that other factors drive polarization, and the evidence comes mostly from a few countries.

args.claim: Voting is a civic duty like jury service.
args.warrant: Democracies already require small duties for the common good (jury service, taxes, school attendance); voting a few times a year is a modest addition.
args.evidence: Comparisons with jury duty laws; Australia's small fines.
args.response: The negative replies that jury service is needed for trials to happen at all; elections work without universal turnout.

args.claim: The burden is small and choice is preserved.
args.warrant: Because voters may cast a blank ballot, no one is forced to support a candidate; the only requirement is showing up.
args.evidence: Australian Electoral Commission rules; Australians' roughly 70% support for the system.
args.response: The negative answers that being forced to attend is still compulsion, and fines fall hardest on those with least time and money.

neg.label: Negative
neg.stance: In a free society, the choice not to vote must be respected.

args.claim: Freedom includes the freedom not to participate.
args.warrant: Abstaining can be a deliberate statement (protest, conscience, or lack of a good choice); compelling attendance overrides personal autonomy.
args.evidence: Liberal political philosophy on autonomy; critics such as former Australian Senator Nick Minchin, who called it "an affront to democracy."
args.response: The affirmative answers that blank ballots preserve that statement while still recording participation.

args.claim: Forced votes can be uninformed or random.
args.warrant: People who don't follow politics may vote carelessly; adding their votes may add noise rather than wisdom.
args.evidence: Research on "donkey votes" and random ballot choices in Australia; studies of voter information.
args.response: The affirmative replies that a duty to vote also gives people a reason to pay attention.

args.claim: Better ways exist to raise turnout.
args.warrant: Automatic registration, mail voting and early voting raise participation without penalties.
args.evidence: Studies of automatic voter registration and vote-by-mail effects on turnout.
args.response: The affirmative argues these help modestly but leave large gaps that compulsory voting closes.

args.claim: Penalties fall hardest on the vulnerable.
args.warrant: People who miss elections are often those with unstable housing, inflexible jobs or health problems; fining them adds to their burdens.
args.evidence: Data on non-voters' demographics; enforcement records where compulsory voting is used.
args.response: The affirmative replies that valid excuses are accepted and fines are small.

strawmen.strawman: They want to force people to vote for candidates they hate.
strawmen.why: Blank ballots are allowed; the duty is to participate.
strawmen.steelman: A democracy is more representative and legitimate when all citizens take part, and a small duty that allows a blank ballot respects choice.

strawmen.strawman: They don't care whether people vote.
strawmen.why: Many opponents favor making voting easier; they object to compulsion.
strawmen.steelman: Freedom includes the choice not to vote; turnout can be raised by making voting easier, without fines that fall on the vulnerable.

weak.arg: Everyone has to vote in Australia, and it's great, so it would work here.
weak.why: One country's success doesn't prove it fits another; argue the principle and the evidence.

weak.arg: Compulsory voting is tyranny.
weak.why: Overstated; Australia is a free democracy. Argue autonomy instead.

aff: Is choosing not to vote ever a form of expression?
What happens to someone who can't pay the fine?
Would automatic registration raise turnout enough?
neg: What was Australia's turnout before 1924, and after?
Can Australians cast a blank ballot?
Is jury duty a fair requirement?

items.title: 18-Year Terms for Supreme Court Justices
items.subtitle: policy · advanced
items.body: Justices serve "during good Behaviour," which in practice means for life. A common proposal would give each justice 18 years of active service, so each president would fill one seat every two years. Would it help the Court or hurt it?

meta.title: 18-Year Terms for Supreme Court Justices
meta.resolution: Resolved: The United States should limit Supreme Court justices to fixed 18-year terms.
meta.summary: Justices serve "during good Behaviour," which in practice means for life. A common proposal would give each justice 18 years of active service, so each president would fill one seat every two years. Would it help the Court or hurt it?

background.p: Article III of the Constitution says federal judges "shall hold their Offices during good Behaviour." Justices may be removed only by impeachment, so they serve until they retire or die. The Presidential Commission on the Supreme Court reported in December 2021 that average service was about fifteen years until the late 1960s and has risen to roughly twenty-six years. The commission studied term limits in detail but took no position on whether to adopt them, and its members disagreed.

The most common proposal is a staggered 18-year term: with nine justices, one seat would open every two years, so each four-year presidential term would bring two appointments. Former justices would usually keep their salary and might serve on lower federal courts. A central question is whether this needs a constitutional amendment, which requires two-thirds of both houses of Congress and three-fourths of the states, or could be done by ordinary law. A Congressional Research Service report notes that many commentators believe an amendment is required, while some scholars argue a carefully written statute would be constitutional; no court has ruled on the question.

The idea has drawn support across the political spectrum at different times. In a July 2022 AP-NORC poll, 67 percent of U.S. adults favored a set term for justices. Nearly every state uses a term of years or a mandatory retirement age for its own high court.

disputed.q: Can Congress set 18-year terms by ordinary law?
positions: Many scholars, including some who favor term limits, say the Good Behaviour Clause guarantees life tenure, so a constitutional amendment is required.
Others argue that if justices keep their office and salary as judges and move to other federal courts after 18 years, a statute could satisfy the clause.

disputed.q: Would regular appointments make confirmation fights calmer or more frequent?
positions: Supporters say predictable openings would lower the stakes of each one, because no single seat could tip the Court for decades.
Critics say a seat on the ballot in every presidential and midterm cycle would make the Court a constant campaign issue.

terms.def: Article III's rule that federal judges hold office "during good Behaviour," generally read as life tenure unless impeached and removed.
Terms that start and end at different times, so members leave one by one instead of all at once.
A form of semi-retirement for federal judges, who keep their office and salary but take a lighter caseload.
The part of the Constitution describing how it can be amended.
The idea that judges should decide cases on the law without pressure from elected officials, voters or concern for their own careers.

aff.label: Affirmative
aff.stance: Fixed 18-year terms would make appointments regular and fair, keep the Court connected to the country over time, and lower the stakes of each vacancy.

args.claim: Appointments now depend on chance.
args.warrant: Under life tenure, vacancies come whenever a justice dies or retires. Some presidents appoint several justices in one term and others none, so the Court's makeup turns on luck and timing more than on elections.
args.evidence: Records of appointments by president; the CRS report's discussion of irregular vacancies; the presidential commission's report.
args.response: The negative answers that under the plan vacancies could still come early through death or resignation, and the Senate could still refuse to confirm, so regularity isn't guaranteed.

args.claim: Tenures have grown much longer.
args.warrant: Average service has risen from about 15 years to roughly 26, and recent nominees have been in their late 40s and early 50s. One appointment can now shape the law for a generation, which raises the stakes of every vacancy.
args.evidence: The presidential commission's tenure figures; Brennan Center analysis of nominees' ages and service lengths.
args.response: The negative replies that long service brings experience and stability, and longer lives are a reason to value judges' wisdom, not to cut it short.

args.claim: It ends strategic retirements and service in poor health.
args.warrant: Justices sometimes time their retirement so a president of their choosing can replace them, or stay on while ill. A fixed term removes both incentives.
args.evidence: The CRS report's list of criticisms of life tenure, including declining health and strategic retirements; historical examples discussed by legal scholars.
args.response: The negative replies that a fixed term creates its own strategies, such as justices thinking about their next job as the term nears its end.

args.claim: Nearly every other high court has limits.
args.warrant: Almost every state supreme court and the top courts of other constitutional democracies use terms or retirement ages and still protect judicial independence. Their experience shows limits can work.
args.evidence: State constitutions on judicial terms; Brennan Center surveys of state and foreign high courts.
args.response: The negative answers that many states elect their judges, which is a different system, and that the U.S. Supreme Court's national role makes comparisons imperfect.

neg.label: Negative
neg.stance: Life tenure protects judicial independence and stability, and term limits would bring new problems and a serious constitutional risk.

args.claim: Life tenure protects independence.
args.warrant: The framers gave judges tenure during good behavior so they could rule against popular opinion and powerful officials without fear for their jobs. A judge who must plan a next career may not be as free.
args.evidence: Federalist No. 78 on permanent tenure; the R Street Institute's 2018 analysis of conflicts of interest from post-Court careers.
args.response: The affirmative answers that 18 years with a guaranteed lifetime salary still protects independence, and most proposals let former justices keep serving as judges.

args.claim: It would make the Court a constant campaign issue.
args.warrant: If every presidential term brings exactly two seats, every election becomes a fight over the Court, and justices may come to be seen as partisan appointees.
args.evidence: Critics' arguments summarized in the presidential commission's report; the 2018 R Street analysis.
args.response: The affirmative replies that the Court is already a campaign issue, and predictable openings lower the stakes of each one.

args.claim: Doing it by statute may be unconstitutional.
args.warrant: The Good Behaviour Clause is widely read to guarantee life tenure. A law forcing justices off the Court could be struck down and would invite a crisis; an amendment is very hard to pass.
args.evidence: The CRS report stating that many commentators believe an amendment is required; National Constitution Center summary of the debate.
args.response: The affirmative answers that the resolution can be met by an amendment, and that some scholars argue a careful statute keeping justices in office as judges would be valid.

args.claim: The details create new problems.
args.warrant: Moving to the new system means deciding what happens to sitting justices, how to fill seats that open early, and what to do if the Senate refuses to confirm. Each fix could add new disputes.
args.evidence: The presidential commission's chapter on design questions; the CRS discussion of a Court with more or fewer than nine justices during the transition.
args.response: The affirmative replies that these design questions have workable answers, such as phasing in the system with new appointees only.

strawmen.strawman: They want to pack the Court with judges who'll rule their way.
strawmen.why: Supporters across the political spectrum back 18-year terms as a neutral rule that gives every president the same number of appointments.
strawmen.steelman: Regular, staggered terms would give each president two appointments, end the role of chance and strategic retirements, and keep the Court connected to the country over time while preserving independence.

strawmen.strawman: They just like the current justices and want to keep them.
strawmen.why: Opponents argue from the Constitution's text, judicial independence and practical problems, and many proposals wouldn't affect sitting justices anyway.
strawmen.steelman: Life tenure protects judges from political and career pressure; term limits risk making every election about the Court and may require an amendment, which is very hard to pass.

weak.arg: The justices are too old to do the job.
weak.why: It's an attack on people rather than the system, and age alone says little about a judge's ability.

weak.arg: The framers chose life tenure, so it must be right forever.
weak.why: The framers also created Article V so the Constitution could be changed; argue about why life tenure still works.

Would your plan need a constitutional amendment, and if so, how would it get three-fourths of the states?
Would former justices be able to take jobs with law firms or run for office?

items.title: Teaching Cursive
items.subtitle: policy · beginner
items.body: About half the states now require cursive instruction, and more are considering it. Is cursive worth class time in a typing world?

meta.title: Teaching Cursive
meta.resolution: Resolved: Elementary schools should be required to teach cursive handwriting.
meta.summary: About half the states now require cursive instruction, and more are considering it. Is cursive worth class time in a typing world?

background.p: The Common Core standards adopted by many states around 2010 did not require cursive, and many schools stopped teaching it. Since then, states have added requirements back; by early 2026, Pennsylvania and New Jersey had joined about two dozen other states with cursive mandates, according to Education Next.

Research distinguishes handwriting in general from cursive in particular. A 2023 review by Hewitt and Sachdeva, described in Education Next, found that handwriting (especially for young children) supports letter recognition, spelling and memory better than typing, but found no evidence that cursive offers advantages over printing. Cursive remains useful for reading historical documents and letters written by hand.

disputed.q: Does cursive help children learn more than printing does?
positions: Supporters cite brain and learning research showing benefits of handwriting and argue connected letters add fluency.
A 2023 review found handwriting beats typing for early literacy but no evidence that cursive beats printing.

terms.def: Handwriting in which letters are joined.
Printed handwriting with separate letters.
Typing skills, taught in many schools in place of or alongside handwriting.

aff.label: Affirmative
aff.stance: Cursive is a lasting skill that connects students to history and builds fluent handwriting.

args.claim: Cursive lets students read handwritten history.
args.warrant: Letters, diaries, family records and many historical documents are in cursive. A student who can't read it is cut off from primary sources and family history.
args.evidence: National Archives and Library of Congress collections of handwritten documents; Education Next's note that cursive matters for archival research.
args.response: The negative answers that the founding documents are widely available in print, and reading cursive can be taught in a short unit without a full writing requirement.

args.claim: Handwriting supports early learning.
args.warrant: Forming letters by hand engages memory and attention in ways typing doesn't, helping children recognize letters and spell.
args.evidence: Hewitt and Sachdeva's 2023 review of handwriting versus typing; studies of letter recognition in young children.
args.response: The negative replies that the same review found no advantage for cursive over printing, so the handwriting benefits don't require cursive.

args.claim: Cursive can be faster and more fluent for some writers.
args.warrant: Connected letters let some students write without lifting the pencil, which can help with note-taking and timed writing.
args.evidence: Occupational therapists' and teachers' reports; studies of handwriting speed.
args.response: The negative points out that research found no consistent speed advantage for cursive.

args.claim: A requirement ensures every child gets the chance.
args.warrant: Without a mandate, some schools teach cursive and others don't, so students' skills depend on which school they attend.
args.evidence: State-by-state differences in cursive instruction; parent demand reported in states that passed mandates.
args.response: The negative answers that local schools should decide how to use limited time, and a mandate takes time from other subjects.

neg.label: Negative
neg.stance: Class time is limited; handwriting matters, but cursive in particular doesn't need a state mandate.

args.claim: Cursive's special benefits aren't supported by evidence.
args.warrant: The research supports handwriting over typing, but printing gives the same benefits.
args.evidence: Hewitt and Sachdeva (2023), as described in Education Next: "unlikely that cursive offers more cognitive benefits than printing."
args.response: The affirmative answers that cursive is still handwriting, so it shares those benefits, and it adds the ability to read historical documents.

args.claim: Mandates take time from other subjects.
args.warrant: Every hour spent on cursive practice is an hour not spent on reading, science or history content.
args.evidence: Education Next's opportunity-cost argument; data on elementary instructional time.
args.response: The affirmative replies that a few minutes a day over a year or two is enough, and handwriting practice can be combined with spelling and writing.

args.claim: Signatures and daily life no longer require cursive.
args.warrant: Most signing is electronic, and printed signatures are legally accepted, so cursive isn't needed for adult life.
args.evidence: Laws on electronic signatures; Education Next on signatures.
args.response: The affirmative answers that reading cursive, not just signing, is the main skill at stake.

args.claim: Reading cursive can be taught without a writing mandate.
args.warrant: A short unit can teach students to read cursive for history class, which captures the main benefit at a fraction of the time.
args.evidence: Examples of history and archival programs that teach cursive reading.
args.response: The affirmative replies that learning to write cursive is the most reliable way to learn to read it.

strawmen.strawman: Cursive fans are just nostalgic for the old days.
strawmen.why: Supporters cite reading primary sources and research on handwriting.
strawmen.steelman: Cursive lets students read handwritten history and family records, shares handwriting's learning benefits, and a requirement gives every child the chance to learn it.

strawmen.strawman: Opponents think handwriting doesn't matter at all.
strawmen.why: Many opponents support handwriting; they question cursive specifically.
strawmen.steelman: Handwriting helps early learning, but printing gives the same benefits, so a cursive mandate takes time from other subjects without added gains.

weak.arg: Without cursive, students can't read the Constitution.
weak.why: The Constitution is widely printed in modern type; the stronger point is about handwritten sources generally.

weak.arg: Nobody writes by hand anymore.
weak.why: Students write by hand often, and research shows handwriting matters; argue about cursive specifically.

aff: What does research say about cursive compared with printing?
How many minutes a week would your requirement take?
Could a short unit teach students to read cursive?
neg: How would a student read a great-grandparent's letters?
Does handwriting help young children learn letters?
Should a skill depend on which school a child attends?
