items.title: Permanent Daylight Saving Time
items.subtitle: policy · beginner
items.body: Many Americans want to stop changing the clocks twice a year. If we pick one time all year, should it be daylight saving time or standard time?

meta.title: Permanent Daylight Saving Time
meta.resolution: Resolved: The United States should adopt permanent daylight saving time.
meta.summary: Many Americans want to stop changing the clocks twice a year. If we pick one time all year, should it be daylight saving time or standard time?

background.p: Most of the United States moves clocks forward an hour in spring (daylight saving time) and back in fall (standard time). In March 2022 the U.S. Senate passed the Sunshine Protection Act by unanimous consent, which would have made daylight saving time permanent, but the House did not pass it; the bill has been reintroduced since. Federal law currently lets states choose permanent *standard* time (as Hawaii and most of Arizona do) but not permanent daylight saving time.

The country tried year-round daylight saving time once before, starting in January 1974 during an energy crisis. Public support fell sharply during that dark winter, and Congress restored standard time for the winter months later that year. Today, sleep scientists, including the American Academy of Sleep Medicine, support ending clock changes but favor permanent standard time, saying it better matches the body's clock; supporters of permanent daylight saving time point to more evening daylight.

disputed.q: Which permanent time is better for health and safety?
positions: Sleep-medicine groups say standard time fits the body's clock better and avoids very dark winter mornings.
Supporters of daylight saving time cite studies linking evening light to fewer evening crashes and crimes and more outdoor activity.

terms.def: Clock time set by the time zone, used in winter; noon is close to when the sun is highest.
Clocks set one hour ahead of standard time, moving daylight from morning to evening.
The body's roughly 24-hour internal clock, set mainly by light.
The mismatch between the body's clock and the clock on the wall.

aff.label: Affirmative
aff.stance: End the clock switching and keep the extra hour of evening light all year.

args.claim: Ending the twice-yearly switch prevents its harms.
args.warrant: The spring change cuts an hour of sleep, and studies link the weeks after clock changes to more heart attacks and crashes. One permanent time ends that.
args.evidence: Studies linking the days after clock changes to more heart attacks and accidents; studies of the spring transition.
args.response: The negative answers that permanent standard time also ends the switch, so this argument doesn't favor daylight saving time.

args.claim: Evening light helps people be active and safe.
args.warrant: More daylight after school and work means more time outdoors, and darkness during the evening commute is linked to more pedestrian crashes and some crimes.
args.evidence: Studies of evening light and crime and traffic safety; research on physical activity and daylight.
args.response: The negative replies that the same hour is taken from the morning, putting children at bus stops in the dark.

args.claim: People like long summer evenings.
args.warrant: Polls show many Americans prefer daylight saving time's later sunsets, and the Senate passed the bill unanimously, reflecting broad support.
args.evidence: Senate passage of the Sunshine Protection Act (March 2022); public opinion polls on time preferences.
args.response: The negative points out that in 1974 public support collapsed once people lived through dark winter mornings.

args.claim: Businesses and recreation benefit from later light.
args.warrant: Shops, parks, sports leagues and outdoor businesses do better when daylight lasts into the evening.
args.evidence: Industry studies of retail and recreation during daylight saving time; testimony from business groups.
args.response: The negative replies that economic gains are uncertain and don't outweigh health concerns.

neg.label: Negative
neg.stance: Ending clock changes is good, but standard time, not daylight saving time, should be permanent.

args.claim: Standard time better matches the body's clock.
args.warrant: Morning light sets the body's internal clock. Permanent daylight saving time would leave many people waking and starting work or school in the dark for months, causing chronic "social jet lag."
args.evidence: American Academy of Sleep Medicine position statements; circadian research.
args.response: The affirmative answers that people adapt, and evening light offers its own health benefits through activity.

args.claim: Winter mornings would be very dark.
args.warrant: Under permanent daylight saving time, winter sunrise would come after 8 a.m. in much of the country and after 9 a.m. in some northern places, so children would wait for buses and walk to school in the dark.
args.evidence: AASM analysis of winter sunrise times; sunrise tables for northern cities.
args.response: The affirmative replies that schools can adjust start times, and evening darkness is also dangerous.

args.claim: The country tried it and reversed course.
args.warrant: In 1974, year-round daylight saving time was popular until people lived through a dark winter; support fell and Congress changed the law within the year.
args.evidence: History of the Emergency Daylight Saving Time Energy Conservation Act of 1973 and its repeal.
args.response: The affirmative argues that was a sudden emergency change, and today's debate is more informed.

args.claim: Health and safety groups favor standard time.
args.warrant: When sleep doctors, the National Safety Council and the National PTA agree, their combined expertise on health and children's safety deserves weight.
args.evidence: AASM statement supported by more than a dozen organizations, as reported in 2022.
args.response: The affirmative replies that expert groups disagree on how to weigh evening safety and activity, and voters also deserve a say.

strawmen.strawman: They just want more time to play outside in summer.
strawmen.why: Supporters also cite the harms of clock changes and evening safety.
strawmen.steelman: Ending the switch prevents its harms, and keeping evening light all year supports activity, safety and the economy, which is why the Senate passed it unanimously.

strawmen.strawman: They want to keep changing the clocks forever.
strawmen.why: Most opponents of permanent DST want to end the switch too, but on standard time.
strawmen.steelman: End the switch, but on standard time, which matches the body's clock and avoids dark winter mornings, as sleep experts recommend and as 1974 showed.

weak.arg: Daylight saving time gives us more daylight.
weak.why: It moves daylight from morning to evening; the total is the same.

weak.arg: Farmers need daylight saving time.
weak.why: A common myth; farmers generally opposed it. It also argues against your own side.

aff: When would the sun rise in December in your city under your plan?
What happened in 1974?
Does permanent standard time also end the switch?
neg: Do most Americans prefer later sunsets?
Are evening commutes in the dark dangerous too?
Why did the Senate pass the bill unanimously?

items.title: Election Day as a National Holiday
items.subtitle: policy · beginner
items.body: Federal elections fall on a Tuesday in November, a regular workday. Would a national holiday help more people vote?

meta.title: Election Day as a National Holiday
meta.resolution: Resolved: The United States should make Election Day a federal holiday.
meta.summary: Federal elections fall on a Tuesday in November, a regular workday. Would a national holiday help more people vote?

background.p: Federal law has set Election Day as the Tuesday after the first Monday in November since 1845 for presidential elections, and later for congressional elections. Some states give state workers the day off or require employers to allow time to vote, and many states now offer early voting or voting by mail, so many voters no longer vote on Election Day itself.

Evidence on holidays is limited. A 2009 Princeton study by economist Henry Farber compared state employees in states that give them an Election Day holiday with other workers and found no significant increase in turnout, concluding that a holiday by itself isn't an effective way to raise turnout. Supporters respond that a national holiday would reach far more people than state workers and would signal the importance of voting.

disputed.q: Would a holiday raise turnout?
positions: Supporters expect higher turnout and point to countries that vote on weekends or holidays.
Farber's study of state holidays found no significant effect, and many voters already vote early or by mail.

terms.def: A day off for federal workers; many private employers and schools follow it, but they aren't required to.
Voting in person before Election Day.
A person who helps run a polling place, often a volunteer or temporary worker.

aff.label: Affirmative
aff.stance: A national holiday would make voting easier and show that democracy matters.

args.claim: Work schedules keep people from voting.
args.warrant: Long lines and long workdays make it hard for some workers to vote on a Tuesday; a day off removes that barrier.
args.evidence: Census surveys in which non-voters cite being too busy or schedule conflicts.
args.response: The negative answers that many workers in retail, health care and transportation would still work, and early voting already addresses schedules.

args.claim: A holiday could ease the shortage of poll workers.
args.warrant: With schools and offices closed, more people could staff polling places, shortening lines.
args.evidence: Reports from election officials on poll-worker shortages; use of schools as polling places.
args.response: The negative replies that recruiting and paying poll workers addresses this more directly.

args.claim: It signals that voting is a shared civic duty.
args.warrant: Holidays mark what a nation values; making Election Day one would encourage civic celebration and participation.
args.evidence: Arguments in legal scholarship, such as "The Case for Making Election Day a Federal Holiday" (Cornell Journal of Law and Public Policy).
args.response: The negative replies that symbols don't change behavior much, as Farber's results suggest.

args.claim: Election Day still matters despite early voting.
args.warrant: Many voters still prefer to vote on Election Day, and some states offer little early voting.
args.evidence: Election data on the share of votes cast on Election Day by state.
args.response: The negative argues that expanding early voting in those states would help more than one day off.

neg.label: Negative
neg.stance: A holiday is costly and unlikely to raise turnout; better tools exist.

args.claim: Evidence shows holidays alone don't raise turnout.
args.warrant: If state workers who get the day off don't vote more, a national holiday may not either.
args.evidence: Farber (Princeton, 2009) on state Election Day holidays.
args.response: The affirmative answers that a national holiday reaches many more people and could have different effects.

args.claim: Many workers wouldn't get the day off.
args.warrant: Stores, hospitals and transit stay open on federal holidays; hourly workers who most need time may still work, and some parents would need child care.
args.evidence: Data on private-sector holiday practices.
args.response: The affirmative replies that a holiday plus a requirement for paid time to vote would reach those workers.

args.claim: A federal holiday is expensive.
args.warrant: Closing federal offices costs paid leave and lost work, money that could fund election administration.
args.evidence: Estimates of the cost of a federal holiday.
args.response: The affirmative argues the cost is small for strengthening democracy.

args.claim: Early and mail voting work better.
args.warrant: Giving voters many days and ways to vote fits more schedules than a single day off.
args.evidence: Research on turnout effects of early voting and vote-by-mail.
args.response: The affirmative answers that the two approaches can work together.

strawmen.strawman: They just want another day off.
strawmen.why: Supporters argue about barriers to voting and poll-worker shortages.
strawmen.steelman: A holiday removes work barriers to voting, helps staff polling places and signals that voting is a shared civic duty.

strawmen.strawman: They don't want more people to vote.
strawmen.why: Many opponents favor early and mail voting instead.
strawmen.steelman: Evidence suggests holidays alone don't raise turnout, many workers wouldn't get the day off, and early and mail voting do more.

weak.arg: A holiday will double turnout.
weak.why: No evidence supports such a large effect.

weak.arg: People will just go to the beach.
weak.why: A guess without evidence; use Farber's study instead.

aff: What did Farber find about state Election Day holidays?
Would grocery and hospital workers get the day off?
How many votes are already cast before Election Day?
neg: Do non-voters say schedules kept them from voting?
How do poll-worker shortages affect lines?
Would you support a holiday combined with paid time off to vote?

items.title: The Electoral College
items.subtitle: policy · intermediate
items.body: Presidents are chosen by 538 electors allotted to the states. Twice in recent decades the popular-vote loser won. Should the country switch to a national popular vote?

meta.title: The Electoral College
meta.resolution: Resolved: The United States should elect its president by national popular vote.
meta.summary: Presidents are chosen by 538 electors allotted to the states. Twice in recent decades the popular-vote loser won. Should the country switch to a national popular vote?

background.p: Under Article II and the 12th Amendment, each state gets electors equal to its number of representatives plus its two senators (and the District of Columbia gets three), for 538 in all; a candidate needs 270 to win. Nearly every state gives all its electors to the statewide winner; Maine and Nebraska split theirs by congressional district. Five times in U.S. history, including 2000 and 2016, the winner of the electoral vote lost the national popular vote.

Replacing the Electoral College directly would require a constitutional amendment. A different approach, the National Popular Vote Interstate Compact, asks states to give their electors to the national popular-vote winner once states totaling 270 electoral votes have joined. With Virginia's entry in April 2026, 18 states plus D.C., with 222 electoral votes, had joined. Supporters say every vote should count equally; critics say the compact bypasses the amendment process the Constitution requires, and a court challenge is expected if it reaches 270.

disputed.q: Would a national popular vote change where candidates campaign?
positions: Supporters say candidates would seek votes everywhere instead of focusing on a handful of battleground states.
Opponents say candidates would focus on large cities and populous regions, neglecting rural and small-state voters.

terms.def: A person chosen to cast one of a state's electoral votes for president.
Giving all of a state's electors to the candidate who wins the state's popular vote.
A state where either major party could win, so campaigns focus there.
A binding agreement among states.
The division of power between the national government and the states.

aff.label: Affirmative
aff.stance: Every citizen's vote for president should count the same, wherever they live.

args.claim: A national popular vote treats every vote equally.
args.warrant: Under winner-take-all, a vote in a close state can decide the election while a vote in a safe state barely matters; a national count gives each vote equal weight.
args.evidence: Analyses of campaign visits and spending concentrated in battleground states; National Popular Vote advocates' data.
args.response: The negative answers that the president leads a union of states, and the system is designed to require broad support across states, not just raw numbers.

args.claim: The winner should be the candidate most people chose.
args.warrant: When the candidate with fewer votes wins, it weakens confidence that the government reflects the people's choice.
args.evidence: The 2000 and 2016 elections; Pew polling showing a majority of Americans prefer a popular vote.
args.response: The negative replies that campaigns run to win the Electoral College, so we can't know how a popular-vote campaign would have turned out.

args.claim: Campaigns would reach more of the country.
args.warrant: If every vote counted equally, candidates would campaign in safe states too, including in rural parts of states that are reliably blue or red.
args.evidence: Campaign-event data by state; studies of turnout in battleground versus safe states.
args.response: The negative argues candidates would focus on the biggest population centers, where votes are cheapest to reach.

args.claim: It would raise turnout in non-competitive states.
args.warrant: Voters in safe states have less reason to vote for president when the outcome is known; a national count gives every voter a reason.
args.evidence: Research comparing turnout in battleground and safe states.
args.response: The negative replies that turnout differences are modest, and down-ballot races already bring voters out.

neg.label: Negative
neg.stance: The Electoral College protects the federal design, requires broad support and contains election disputes.

args.claim: It requires winners to build broad coalitions across states.
args.warrant: Because candidates must win states, they can't rely on running up huge margins in a few regions; they need support across a diverse country.
args.evidence: Writings defending the Electoral College on federalism grounds; election maps of winning coalitions.
args.response: The affirmative answers that in practice campaigns ignore most states, focusing on a few battlegrounds.

args.claim: It contains disputes and recounts.
args.warrant: A close national popular vote could force recounts in every state at once; the Electoral College usually confines disputes to one or a few states.
args.evidence: The 2000 Florida recount; analyses of how close national margins could trigger nationwide recounts.
args.response: The affirmative replies that national margins are usually large in raw votes, making nationwide recounts rare.

args.claim: It reflects the country's federal design.
args.warrant: The United States is a union of states, with states running elections; the Electoral College gives them a role, protecting smaller states' voices.
args.evidence: The Constitutional Convention's debates; Federalist No. 68 on the method of choosing the president.
args.response: The affirmative argues the framers also expected electors to deliberate, which no longer happens, so the original design has already changed.

args.claim: The compact would sidestep the Constitution.
args.warrant: A change this basic should go through the amendment process, which requires broad agreement, not a compact among some states.
args.evidence: Legal scholars quoted by NPR, such as Iowa's deputy solicitor general Patrick Valencia; amendment procedures in Article V.
args.response: The affirmative replies that the Constitution lets each state choose how to appoint its electors, and courts have upheld that power.

strawmen.strawman: They want big cities to rule the country.
strawmen.why: Supporters argue for equal weight for each voter, including rural voters in safe states.
strawmen.steelman: Every vote should count equally, the candidate with the most votes should win, and campaigns would have reason to reach voters in every state.

strawmen.strawman: They just want their party to win.
strawmen.why: Defenders argue from federalism, coalition-building and dispute containment, principles that don't depend on which party benefits in a given year.
strawmen.steelman: The Electoral College requires broad support across states, confines disputes, and reflects the federal design; changing it should go through an amendment.

weak.arg: The Electoral College was created only to protect slavery.
weak.why: Historians debate the role of slavery among several motives; claiming it was the only reason is contested and invites a fight you may lose.

weak.arg: We're a republic, not a democracy, so the popular vote doesn't matter.
weak.why: The U.S. is both a republic and a representative democracy; this is a slogan, not an argument.

aff: How would a close national recount work?
Would you need a constitutional amendment, or the compact?
Where would candidates campaign under a national vote?
neg: How many states did the last campaigns focus on?
How many times has the popular-vote loser won?
Do the electors still deliberate as the framers expected?

items.title: Police Use of Facial Recognition
items.subtitle: policy · advanced
items.body: Facial recognition can help police identify suspects and find missing people, but errors and privacy concerns have led some cities to ban it. Where should the line be?

meta.title: Police Use of Facial Recognition
meta.resolution: Resolved: Police in the United States should be prohibited from using facial recognition technology.
meta.summary: Facial recognition can help police identify suspects and find missing people, but errors and privacy concerns have led some cities to ban it. Where should the line be?

background.p: Facial recognition software compares a face in a photo or video with a database of images, such as mugshots or driver's license photos, and suggests possible matches. Police use it to generate leads in investigations. Several U.S. cities, including San Francisco (2019) and Boston (2020), banned city agencies, including police, from using it, while other places have adopted rules on how it may be used.

In 2019, the National Institute of Standards and Technology (NIST) tested many algorithms on about 18 million government photos of 8.5 million people. It found demographic differences in most algorithms: in one-to-one matching, false positives for African American, Asian and Native American faces were often 10 to 100 times more frequent than for white faces, and women had more false matches than men. Results varied greatly by algorithm; some performed much better than others, and NIST said the findings weren't definitive proof of systemic bias. Wrongful arrests after faulty matches have been reported in several cities.

disputed.q: Are today's best systems accurate enough for police use?
positions: Supporters say top algorithms are highly accurate and that a match is only a lead, checked by investigators.
Critics point to demographic differences in error rates and to wrongful arrests where matches were treated as proof.

terms.def: Checking whether two images show the same person, as when unlocking a phone.
Searching a database for anyone who matches a face, as in an investigation.
The system wrongly says two different people match.
A possible match that police must confirm with other evidence before acting.

aff.label: Affirmative
aff.stance: The risks of misidentification and mass surveillance are too great; police shouldn't use it.

args.claim: Errors fall unevenly and can lead to wrongful arrests.
args.warrant: If a tool is more likely to misidentify some groups, those people face a higher risk of being questioned or arrested for crimes they didn't commit.
args.evidence: NIST's 2019 study of demographic differences; reported cases of wrongful arrests after faulty matches.
args.response: The negative answers that the best algorithms show much smaller differences, and rules can require confirming evidence before any arrest.

args.claim: It enables mass surveillance.
args.warrant: Cameras plus facial recognition could track where anyone goes, chilling free movement, protest and association.
args.evidence: Civil-liberties reports on surveillance networks; examples of the technology used to monitor crowds abroad.
args.response: The negative replies that rules can limit use to specific investigations and forbid tracking crowds.

args.claim: Rules have proved hard to enforce.
args.warrant: Police departments have sometimes used the technology without clear policies or public knowledge, so a ban is the only reliable safeguard.
args.evidence: Reports of undisclosed police use; city council hearings before bans in San Francisco and Boston.
args.response: The negative argues that transparency laws and audits can enforce rules without banning a useful tool.

args.claim: Communities have chosen bans.
args.warrant: Cities that weighed the costs and benefits decided the risks outweighed the help, showing a ban is a reasonable policy.
args.evidence: San Francisco's 2019 and Boston's 2020 bans.
args.response: The negative replies that other cities chose regulation, and some later loosened their bans.

neg.label: Negative
neg.stance: Used with strict rules, facial recognition helps solve crimes and find people, and shouldn't be banned outright.

args.claim: It helps solve serious crimes and find missing people.
args.warrant: When investigators have only an image of a suspect or a missing child, a database search can produce leads that would otherwise take weeks or never come.
args.evidence: Police reports of cases solved with facial recognition leads; use in identifying trafficking victims.
args.response: The affirmative answers that the same leads have led to wrongful arrests.

args.claim: Accuracy varies, and the best systems are very accurate.
args.warrant: NIST found results differ greatly by algorithm; requiring only top-performing systems reduces errors and demographic gaps.
args.evidence: NIST's 2019 findings that algorithms vary widely and that its results weren't definitive proof of systemic bias.
args.response: The affirmative replies that police don't always use the best systems, and image quality in real cases is often poor.

args.claim: Rules can prevent misuse.
args.warrant: Requiring a warrant or serious-crime limits, human review, and confirming evidence before arrest keeps the benefits while limiting harm.
args.evidence: State and local laws regulating police facial recognition; department policies.
args.response: The affirmative argues that rules are hard to enforce and have been broken.

args.claim: Human eyewitnesses also make mistakes.
args.warrant: Eyewitness identification is a leading factor in wrongful convictions; a carefully used algorithm can be one more check.
args.evidence: Research on eyewitness error and exonerations.
args.response: The affirmative replies that adding a confident-seeming computer match may make investigators trust a wrong identification more.

strawmen.strawman: Ban supporters want criminals to go free.
strawmen.why: Supporters worry about wrongful arrests and surveillance, which also harm innocent people.
strawmen.steelman: Uneven error rates, wrongful arrests and the risk of mass surveillance are too great, and rules have proved hard to enforce, so a ban is the reliable safeguard.

strawmen.strawman: Opponents of a ban want a surveillance state.
strawmen.why: Most support strict rules limiting use to investigations.
strawmen.steelman: With strict rules and top-performing systems, facial recognition helps solve serious crimes and find missing people; a ban throws that away.

weak.arg: Facial recognition never works.
weak.why: Contradicted by testing; argue about error rates and misuse instead.

weak.arg: If you have nothing to hide, you have nothing to fear.
weak.why: A slogan that ignores wrongful arrests of innocent people, which is the other side's main point.

Would you allow use to find a missing child?
How do eyewitness errors compare?
neg: How many wrongful arrests after faulty matches have been reported?
Who checks that police use only the best algorithms?
What stops use on crowds at protests?

items.title: Fast Fashion
items.subtitle: value · beginner
items.body: Cheap, quickly changing clothing has made fashion affordable for many people and created millions of factory jobs, but it also creates waste and pollution. Do the harms outweigh the benefits?

meta.title: Fast Fashion
meta.resolution: Resolved: The harms of fast fashion outweigh its benefits.
meta.summary: Cheap, quickly changing clothing has made fashion affordable for many people and created millions of factory jobs, but it also creates waste and pollution. Do the harms outweigh the benefits?

background.p: **Fast fashion** is clothing designed, made and sold quickly and cheaply to follow trends, often worn only a few times. The EPA estimated that Americans generated about 17 million tons of textile waste in 2018; about 2.5 million tons (14.7%) were recycled, 3.2 million tons burned for energy, and 11.3 million tons landfilled.

Garment manufacturing employs millions of workers, many of them women, in countries such as Bangladesh, Vietnam and Cambodia. Supporters of the industry, such as Johan Norberg of the Cato Institute, argue that garment exports have been a major path out of poverty, citing World Bank figures on falling extreme poverty in Bangladesh and Cambodia. Critics point to unsafe conditions (the 2013 Rana Plaza factory collapse in Bangladesh killed more than 1,100 workers), low wages, water and chemical pollution, and waste exported to poorer countries. A 2018 article in *Environmental Health* (Bick, Halsey and Ekenga) described these burdens as a global environmental injustice.

disputed.q: Are garment factory jobs good for workers in poor countries?
positions: Many economists say export factory jobs pay more than the realistic alternatives and have helped reduce poverty.
Critics say wages and safety remain poor, and that progress came despite, not because of, pressure for ever-cheaper clothing.

terms.def: Trend-driven clothing produced quickly and cheaply in large volumes.
All the steps and companies involved in making and delivering a product.
Discarded clothing and fabric.
Pay high enough to meet a worker's basic needs where they live.

aff.label: Affirmative
aff.stance: Fast fashion's waste, pollution and worker harms outweigh the savings on cheap clothes.

args.claim: Fast fashion creates enormous waste.
args.warrant: Clothes made to be worn a few times are thrown away quickly; most end up in landfills, where synthetic fabrics break down very slowly.
args.evidence: EPA (2018): 11.3 million tons of textiles landfilled in the U.S.; research on clothing utilization.
args.response: The negative answers that waste comes from consumer habits, and recycling and resale are growing.

args.claim: Production pollutes water and air.
args.warrant: Dyeing and finishing fabrics use large amounts of water and chemicals, and much manufacturing relies on fossil fuels.
args.evidence: Bick, Halsey and Ekenga (2018) on environmental and health burdens; reports on textile dyeing pollution.
args.response: The negative replies that these harms come from manufacturing generally, and cleaner production is possible within the industry.

args.claim: Workers face unsafe conditions and low pay.
args.warrant: Pressure for speed and low prices pushes factories to cut costs, including on safety.
args.evidence: The 2013 Rana Plaza collapse; labor-rights reports on garment factories.
args.response: The negative answers that safety reforms since Rana Plaza have improved conditions, and the jobs pay more than alternatives.

args.claim: The burdens fall on poorer countries.
args.warrant: Rich countries get cheap clothes while producing countries bear the pollution, and used clothing is often shipped back to them as waste.
args.evidence: Bick and colleagues (2018) describing a global environmental injustice; reports on used-clothing exports.
args.response: The negative argues producing countries choose these industries because they bring jobs and growth.

neg.label: Negative
neg.stance: Affordable clothing and millions of jobs are real benefits; the harms can be reduced without ending the industry.

args.claim: Garment jobs have helped lift millions out of poverty.
args.warrant: Export factories often pay more than farming or informal work, giving workers, especially women, income and independence.
args.evidence: Norberg (Cato, 2015) citing World Bank figures on poverty in Bangladesh and Cambodia; development economics research.
args.response: The affirmative answers that jobs could exist with better wages and safety; cheapness isn't required for jobs.

args.claim: Affordable clothing helps low-income families.
args.warrant: Cheap clothing lets families with tight budgets dress children for school and adults for work.
args.evidence: Consumer price data on clothing; household spending surveys.
args.response: The affirmative replies that higher-quality clothing lasts longer and can cost less over time.

args.claim: The harms can be addressed directly.
args.warrant: Safety laws, recycling programs and cleaner dyeing target the harms without ending affordable clothing.
args.evidence: Factory safety agreements after Rana Plaza; textile recycling programs.
args.response: The affirmative argues reforms have been slow, and the business model depends on volume.

args.claim: Ending fast fashion could hurt the workers critics want to help.
args.warrant: If demand falls sharply, factories close, and workers lose jobs with few better alternatives.
args.evidence: Economic studies of garment-sector employment; reports on effects of boycotts.
args.response: The affirmative replies that a gradual shift toward better production can protect jobs.

strawmen.strawman: Critics just think cheap clothes are tacky.
strawmen.why: Critics focus on waste, pollution and worker safety.
strawmen.steelman: Fast fashion's waste, pollution and unsafe conditions fall heavily on poorer countries, outweighing the savings on cheap clothes.

strawmen.strawman: Defenders don't care about factory workers.
strawmen.why: Defenders argue the jobs help workers escape poverty.
strawmen.steelman: Garment jobs have helped millions escape poverty, cheap clothing helps low-income families, and the harms can be fixed directly.

weak.arg: Everyone should just buy expensive clothes.
weak.why: Ignores families on tight budgets; it hands the other side its best argument.

weak.arg: Factories are fine now; Rana Plaza was a one-time accident.
weak.why: Dismissive and contested; argue about reforms with evidence.

aff: What jobs would garment workers have without these factories?
How would low-income families afford clothing?
Which harms could be fixed with regulation?
neg: How many tons of textiles are landfilled in the U.S. each year?
What happened at Rana Plaza?
Who bears the pollution from dyeing?

items.title: The Four-Day School Week
items.subtitle: policy · beginner
items.body: Hundreds of mostly rural districts now hold school four days a week with longer days. Is the trade worth it?

meta.title: The Four-Day School Week
meta.resolution: Resolved: Public school districts should adopt a four-day school week.
meta.summary: Hundreds of mostly rural districts now hold school four days a week with longer days. Is the trade worth it?

background.p: About 1,600 schools in 24 states had four-day weeks by spring 2019, up from about 250 in 1999, and more switched during and after the pandemic, according to reporting by The Hechinger Report. Most are rural. Schools usually lengthen the remaining four days to keep instructional hours close to state minimums.

Districts first adopted the schedule mainly to save money, but studies found savings of only about 1 to 2% of budgets, since teacher salaries don't change. Many districts now cite recruiting and keeping teachers. A RAND survey (2021) found 85% of parents and 95% of students in four-day districts wanted to keep the schedule.

Research on achievement is mixed. An early Colorado study found gains; most newer studies, including one in Oregon, found small to moderate negative effects, while a study of rural Oklahoma found no penalty. A multi-state study (Morton and colleagues, 2022) found slightly slower growth overall, with no significant penalty for rural students.

disputed.q: Do four-day weeks hurt learning?
positions: Several recent studies find small to moderate losses, especially outside rural areas and in reading.
Others find no penalty in rural districts, where many students already missed Fridays for sports and travel.

terms.def: The time students spend in class, which states often require at a minimum.
The day off, often used for sports, appointments, optional tutoring, or teacher training.

aff.label: Affirmative
aff.stance: For many districts, a four-day week helps keep good teachers and is popular with families, at little academic cost.

args.claim: It helps districts hire and keep teachers.
args.warrant: Rural districts often can't match city salaries. A three-day weekend is a benefit that costs little and can attract and retain teachers.
args.evidence: District reports and surveys of teachers in four-day schools; research on rural teacher shortages; Hechinger reporting on recruitment as a main reason for switching.
args.response: The negative replies that the evidence on recruitment is mostly anecdotal, and if many districts switch, the advantage disappears.

args.claim: Families and students strongly prefer it.
args.warrant: When parents and students who've lived with a policy overwhelmingly want to keep it, that's evidence it works for them.
args.evidence: RAND (2021): 85% of parents and 95% of students in four-day districts would keep it.
args.response: The negative answers that popularity isn't the same as learning; students would also prefer less homework.

args.claim: In rural areas, the academic cost may be near zero.
args.warrant: Where students already miss Fridays for long trips to games, moving those absences to a day off can protect class time.
args.evidence: Morton's research finding no significant penalty for rural students and no penalty in rural Oklahoma.
args.response: The negative points out that other studies (such as Oregon's) found real losses, and the resolution covers all districts, not only rural ones.

args.claim: The fifth day can be put to good use.
args.warrant: Districts can offer optional tutoring, enrichment or teacher training on the day off, and families can schedule appointments without missing class.
args.evidence: Descriptions of fifth-day programs in four-day districts; attendance data on medical appointments.
args.response: The negative replies that optional programs reach few students and cost money the schedule was supposed to save.

neg.label: Negative
neg.stance: Shorter weeks tend to cost learning and shift burdens to families, without the promised savings.

args.claim: Most recent studies find learning losses.
args.warrant: Longer days don't fully make up for a lost day; young students tire, and less frequent instruction weakens practice.
args.evidence: The Oregon study (losses equal to several weeks of fifth-grade math growth); Morton and colleagues' multi-state study; summaries by Hechinger and NCSL.
args.response: The affirmative answers that effects vary, are near zero in rural districts, and some studies found gains.

args.claim: Savings are small.
args.warrant: Salaries, the biggest cost, don't change, so cutting a day saves only on buses, utilities and some hourly staff.
args.evidence: Studies finding savings of about 1 to 2% of district budgets.
args.response: The affirmative replies that districts now choose it for teacher recruitment, not savings, so small savings don't matter.

args.claim: The day off can burden working families.
args.warrant: Parents who work five days need child care for the fifth day, and children who rely on school meals miss a day of them.
args.evidence: Parent surveys in four-day districts; school meal participation data.
args.response: The affirmative points out that most parents in four-day districts support the schedule, and many districts offer care or meals on the fifth day.

args.claim: Longer days are hard on young children.
args.warrant: Adding time to each day can push young students past the point where they can pay attention, so the extra minutes teach less.
args.evidence: Research on attention spans and the length of the school day; teacher reports from four-day schools.
args.response: The affirmative replies that schedules can add breaks and recess, and the extra minutes are often only 30 to 60 a day.

strawmen.strawman: Supporters just want a three-day weekend.
strawmen.why: Supporters cite teacher recruitment, family support and evidence of little harm in rural districts.
strawmen.steelman: For districts struggling to keep teachers, a four-day week is a low-cost benefit that families strongly support, with little academic cost in rural areas.

strawmen.strawman: Opponents don't care what teachers want.
strawmen.why: Opponents focus on learning losses and family burdens, not on teachers' wishes.
strawmen.steelman: Most recent studies find learning losses, savings are small, and the fifth day burdens working families, so the costs outweigh the benefits.

weak.arg: It saves a lot of money.
weak.why: Studies find savings of only 1 to 2%; this argument is easy to refute.

weak.arg: Students will just play video games all Friday.
weak.why: It's an assumption without evidence and ignores how districts use the fifth day.

aff: What do the most recent studies find about achievement?
How much money does the schedule save?
Would your plan apply to suburban districts too?
neg: Why do so many parents in four-day districts want to keep it?
What is the effect in rural districts?
How should a rural district without enough teachers recruit them?

items.title: Genetically Modified Crops
items.subtitle: value · advanced
items.body: Most U.S. corn, soybeans and cotton are genetically engineered. A major scientific review found them safe to eat, but debates continue over farming practices, weeds, seed ownership and promised benefits.

meta.title: Genetically Modified Crops
meta.resolution: Resolved: The benefits of genetically modified crops outweigh their harms.
meta.summary: Most U.S. corn, soybeans and cotton are genetically engineered. A major scientific review found them safe to eat, but debates continue over farming practices, weeds, seed ownership and promised benefits.

background.p: Genetically modified (genetically engineered) crops have had genes added or changed to give them traits such as resistance to insects or tolerance of herbicides. They have been grown widely in the United States since the late 1990s, especially corn, soybeans and cotton.

In 2016, a committee of the National Academies of Sciences, Engineering, and Medicine, chaired by entomologist Fred Gould (who had earlier criticized some GM crops), reviewed hundreds of studies. It found no evidence that genetically engineered crops on the market were riskier to eat than conventional crops, and no evidence that they had reduced plant and insect diversity on farms. It also found no evidence they had sped up the long-term rise in crop yields, said insect-resistant crops had let some farmers spray less insecticide while insects could evolve resistance, and recommended that new crops be reviewed based on their novelty and risk rather than how they were made. Some critics questioned panel members' industry ties.

disputed.q: Have GM crops increased yields?
positions: Supporters point to farm-level studies showing higher yields and less crop loss to pests, especially in developing countries.
The 2016 National Academies review found no evidence that GM traits had sped up the overall rise in U.S. yields.

terms.def: Crops whose DNA has been changed using modern molecular techniques.
Crops that make a protein from the bacterium *Bacillus thuringiensis* that kills certain insect pests.
Crops engineered to survive a weed killer, so farmers can spray fields without killing the crop.
Newer methods (such as CRISPR) that make precise changes to a plant's own genes.

aff.label: Affirmative
aff.stance: GM crops are safe to eat and have brought real benefits to farmers and the environment.

args.claim: GM foods on the market are as safe to eat as conventional foods.
args.warrant: After decades of study and widespread eating, large scientific reviews have found no added risk, so fears about eating them aren't supported.
args.evidence: National Academies (2016) review; statements by scientific bodies.
args.response: The negative answers that eating safety isn't the main dispute; the harms are in farming practices, weeds and economics.

args.claim: Insect-resistant crops have cut insecticide spraying.
args.warrant: When the plant itself resists certain pests, farmers can spray less, which reduces costs and exposure for workers and wildlife.
args.evidence: National Academies findings on reduced insecticide use for some crops; farm studies of Bt cotton and corn.
args.response: The negative replies that pests are evolving resistance, and herbicide use rose with herbicide-tolerant crops.

args.claim: Genetic engineering can solve problems breeding can't.
args.warrant: Engineering can add traits like virus resistance or extra nutrients faster than conventional breeding, helping farmers facing diseases or nutritional gaps.
args.evidence: Cases such as virus-resistant papaya in Hawaii and nutrient-enhanced crops; reports on gene-edited crops.
args.response: The negative argues that several promised nutritional crops have reached few farmers, and conventional breeding has also improved yields.

args.claim: Farmers choose them because they work.
args.warrant: Farmers pay more for GM seed only if it saves them labor, pesticide or losses; their widespread choice reflects real benefits on the farm.
args.evidence: USDA data on adoption rates; farmer surveys on time and cost savings.
args.response: The negative replies that seed choices narrowed as a few companies came to dominate seed markets, so adoption may reflect limited options.

neg.label: Negative
neg.stance: Even if GM foods are safe to eat, the way these crops are used has brought harms that outweigh the benefits.

args.claim: Herbicide-tolerant crops have helped breed resistant weeds.
args.warrant: Spraying the same weed killer over huge areas year after year selects for weeds that survive it, pushing farmers to stronger chemicals.
args.evidence: Research on glyphosate-resistant weeds; National Academies discussion of resistance; weed-science surveys.
args.response: The affirmative answers that resistance comes from how herbicides are used, not genetic engineering itself, and better rotation fixes it.

args.claim: The promised benefits have been oversold.
args.warrant: If GM crops haven't raised yields faster, the case that they're needed to feed the world is weaker.
args.evidence: National Academies (2016) finding no evidence of faster yield growth in the U.S.
args.response: The affirmative replies that reduced losses to pests and lower spraying are benefits even without faster yield growth.

args.claim: Patents and seed concentration hurt farmers.
args.warrant: Patented seeds can't be saved and replanted, and a few companies control much of the market, raising seed prices and limiting choice.
args.evidence: USDA and antitrust research on seed-industry concentration; seed price data.
args.response: The affirmative answers that hybrid conventional seeds also aren't saved, and patents fund the research that creates new varieties.

args.claim: Unwanted spread can hurt other farmers.
args.warrant: Pollen and seed can drift into organic or non-GM fields, costing those farmers their markets.
args.evidence: Cases of GM traits found in non-GM crops; organic certification rules.
args.response: The affirmative replies that buffer zones and coexistence rules reduce this, and cases are rare.

strawmen.strawman: GMO supporters are just paid by big chemical companies.
strawmen.why: Many independent scientists and reviews support the safety findings; attacking motives skips the evidence.
strawmen.steelman: Large independent reviews find GM foods safe to eat, insect-resistant crops have cut spraying, and engineering can deliver traits breeding can't.

strawmen.strawman: GMO critics think genetically modified food is poison.
strawmen.why: Many critics accept the safety findings and focus on farming practices, weeds and seed markets.
strawmen.steelman: Even if safe to eat, GM crops have encouraged herbicide-resistant weeds, delivered less than promised on yields, and concentrated seed markets.

weak.arg: Without GMOs, the world would starve.
weak.why: The yield evidence doesn't support this; it invites an easy answer.

weak.arg: GMOs cause cancer.
weak.why: Major scientific reviews found no evidence of added health risk from eating approved GM foods. It will cost you the round.

aff: What did the National Academies find about yields?
Why did herbicide-resistant weeds spread?
Can farmers save patented seed?
neg: Did the National Academies find GM foods riskier to eat?
Have Bt crops reduced insecticide spraying?
Is herbicide resistance caused by engineering or by how herbicides are used?

items.title: Letter Grades vs Standards-Based Grading
items.subtitle: policy · intermediate
items.body: Standards-based grading reports how well a student has mastered each skill, often allowing retakes and keeping homework and behavior separate. Should it replace A–F grades?

meta.title: Letter Grades vs Standards-Based Grading
meta.resolution: Resolved: Schools should replace traditional letter grades with standards-based grading.
meta.summary: Standards-based grading reports how well a student has mastered each skill, often allowing retakes and keeping homework and behavior separate. Should it replace A–F grades?

background.p: In traditional grading, teachers average points from tests, homework, participation and other work into one letter grade. **Standards-based grading** (also called competency- or proficiency-based grading) reports a student's level on each learning standard, usually on a scale such as 1 to 4, often lets students reassess after more practice, and reports work habits like homework and punctuality separately.

A 2023 research brief from the University of Rochester found limited but encouraging evidence on achievement and lower test anxiety, along with real challenges: uneven implementation, confusion for some parents and students, teacher workload, and lower homework completion when homework stopped counting. The brief's main conclusion was that "no grading system by itself improves student learning."

disputed.q: Does standards-based grading raise achievement?
positions: Some studies find better alignment between grades and test results and modest gains.
The research is young, mostly from elementary and middle schools, and results depend heavily on how well schools carry it out.

terms.def: A specific skill or piece of knowledge students should master, such as "add fractions with unlike denominators."
A chance to show mastery again after more learning, replacing the earlier score.
Levels such as 1 (beginning) to 4 (exceeds) used instead of percentages.

aff.label: Affirmative
aff.stance: Grades should tell students and parents what a student knows and can do.

args.claim: Standards-based grades give clearer information.
args.warrant: A B in math hides which skills a student has mastered and which they haven't. A report by standard tells families exactly where to help.
args.evidence: University of Rochester brief (2023) on clearer feedback reported by students, parents and teachers; district report-card examples.
args.response: The negative answers that many parents find standards-based reports confusing, and a single grade is easier to understand.

args.claim: Separating behavior from achievement makes grades more accurate.
args.warrant: When homework completion and neatness are mixed into grades, a student who knows the material can get a low grade and one who complies can get a high one.
args.evidence: Research comparing grades to test performance; the Rochester brief's discussion of reporting behaviors separately.
args.response: The negative replies that work habits matter for success, and when they don't count, students do less of the work that builds learning.

args.claim: Reassessment rewards learning, not speed.
args.warrant: Students learn at different paces. Letting them show mastery later encourages them to keep learning instead of giving up after a bad test.
args.evidence: Studies linking reassessment to lower test anxiety and greater persistence, summarized in the Rochester brief.
args.response: The negative argues retakes are hard to manage and may teach students that deadlines don't matter.

args.claim: It shifts classrooms toward learning instead of point-chasing.
args.warrant: When grades reflect mastery rather than accumulated points, students ask "what don't I understand?" instead of "how many points is this worth?"
args.evidence: Teacher and student surveys in standards-based schools reported in the research literature.
args.response: The negative replies that motivation often dips during the change, and some students do less work when points disappear.

neg.label: Negative
neg.stance: Letter grades are familiar, useful and can be improved without replacing the whole system.

args.claim: Families and colleges understand letter grades.
args.warrant: A grade everyone understands is useful information. New scales confuse parents and create worries about college applications and scholarships.
args.evidence: The Rochester brief's discussion of parent concerns and confusing report cards; parent surveys in districts adopting standards-based grading.
args.response: The affirmative answers that the same brief found colleges treat standards-based transcripts on par with traditional ones, and confusion fades with time.

args.claim: When homework doesn't count, students do less of it.
args.warrant: Practice builds skill. If it carries no grade, many students skip it, and the ones who skip it are often those who need it most.
args.evidence: Huey and colleagues (2022), summarized in the Rochester brief: homework completion dropped and students who saw practice as optional did worse on math assessments.
args.response: The affirmative replies that the same study found gains on some standards, and teachers can require practice before reassessment.

args.claim: Implementation is hard, and inconsistency feels unfair.
args.warrant: Standards-based grading needs training and consistency across teachers. When teachers apply it differently, students see it as unfair.
args.evidence: The Rochester brief on uneven implementation, teacher workload and an "implementation dip."
args.response: The affirmative argues that any grading system is applied unevenly, and training and gradual rollout solve this.

args.claim: Traditional grades can be fixed without replacing them.
args.warrant: Schools can weight tests more, allow some retakes, and report behavior separately within the A–F system, getting many benefits without a disruptive change.
args.evidence: Examples of "grading reform" within letter-grade systems; the Rochester brief's point that no grading system alone improves learning.
args.response: The affirmative replies that half-measures keep the main problem: one averaged letter hides what students know.

strawmen.strawman: They want to get rid of grades so everyone gets a trophy.
strawmen.why: Standards-based grading still rates students, often more specifically; it doesn't remove standards.
strawmen.steelman: Grades should report mastery of each skill, separate from behavior, so students and parents know exactly what has been learned.

strawmen.strawman: They just don't want to change anything.
strawmen.why: Many defenders of letter grades support reforms like retakes or reporting behavior separately.
strawmen.steelman: Letter grades are understood by families and colleges and keep students doing practice; schools can fix their flaws without a confusing overhaul.

weak.arg: Standards-based grading is proven to raise test scores.
weak.why: The evidence is limited; overclaiming invites an easy answer.

weak.arg: Colleges won't accept standards-based transcripts.
weak.why: Research summarized by the Rochester brief suggests colleges evaluate them on par with traditional ones.

aff: What happens to homework completion when homework stops counting?
How would a college compare your scale to an A–F transcript?
How many reassessments would a student get?
neg: What does a B in math tell a parent about which skills to practice?
Should a student who knows the material get a low grade for late homework?
Can letter grades be reformed to fix that?

items.title: Homeschoolers on School Teams
items.subtitle: policy · beginner
items.body: Some states let homeschooled students try out for public school teams, some leave it to each district, and some don't allow it. Should every homeschooled student get the chance to play?

meta.title: Homeschoolers on School Teams
meta.resolution: Resolved: Homeschooled students should be allowed to play on their local public school's sports teams.
meta.summary: Some states let homeschooled students try out for public school teams, some leave it to each district, and some don't allow it. Should every homeschooled student get the chance to play?

background.p: The National Center for Education Statistics estimated that 3.4 percent of students ages 5 to 17 were homeschooled in 2012, and a somewhat lower share in 2019. Parents' most common reasons included concern about the school environment (80 percent), a wish to give moral instruction (75 percent) and dissatisfaction with academic instruction (73 percent).

State rules differ a great deal, and they change often. A 2015 count by the Coalition for Responsible Home Education, which supports access, found about 20 states giving homeschoolers full access to public school sports, about 10 allowing it with district approval or part-time enrollment, and about 20 barring it. Bills of this kind are often called "Tebow bills," after quarterback Tim Tebow, who was homeschooled in Florida and played football for a public high school there. Counts since then vary by source, partly because sources define "access" differently.

Texas shows how the rules can work. A 2021 law let each district choose to open University Interscholastic League (UIL) activities to homeschooled students. A 2025 law reversed the default: districts now allow homeschool participation unless the school board votes to opt out. Homeschooled players must meet the same rules as enrolled students and must show grade-level skills on a nationally recognized test in the first six weeks of the school year.

disputed.q: Can schools hold homeschooled players to the same academic standards?
positions: Supporters say tests, parent reports and portfolios can confirm a homeschooled student is keeping up, as states like Texas require.
Opponents say enrolled players must pass every class each grading period under a teacher's grading, and a parent's report or a once-a-year test isn't the same check.

terms.def: Educating a child at home, usually by a parent, instead of enrolling the child in a public or private school. Each state sets its own rules.
Rules a student must meet to play school sports, such as passing grades, attendance, age limits and living in the school's attendance zone.
The organization in each state that runs high school sports and sets eligibility rules, such as the UIL in Texas.
Whether a district must vote to allow something (opt in) or must vote to refuse it (opt out).

aff.label: Affirmative
aff.stance: Homeschooled children are part of the community their local school serves, and they should have the same chance to play.

args.claim: Homeschooling families pay for the schools too.
args.warrant: Public schools are funded mostly by local and state taxes that homeschooling families pay. Shutting their children out of a program those taxes support treats them as outsiders in their own district.
args.evidence: State school-funding formulas; testimony in state legislatures, such as the arguments supporters made for the 2021 Texas bill.
args.response: The negative answers that taxes pay for a whole school system that families are free to use or not; paying for roads doesn't entitle you to one lane.

args.claim: Sports teach lessons every child should get.
args.warrant: Teamwork, discipline, losing well and keeping fit are good for any child. In many towns, especially rural ones, the public school team is the only team there is.
args.evidence: Research on youth sports and health and character; reports on rural areas with no club or league teams.
args.response: The negative replies that homeschool leagues, club teams and community sports exist in many places, so the choice isn't school sports or nothing.

args.claim: Many states already do it without serious trouble.
args.warrant: If the policy caused the harms opponents predict, the states that have allowed it for decades would show them. Their experience is the best test.
args.evidence: State laws and athletic association rules (see the reading list); reports from states that have allowed access for many years.
args.response: The negative argues that "no serious trouble" is hard to measure, and complaints about eligibility and roster spots do come up in those states.

args.claim: Fair rules can answer the fairness worries.
args.warrant: States can require homeschoolers to meet the same age, residency, fee and conduct rules as everyone else, plus proof of academic progress. That keeps the playing field level.
args.evidence: The Texas rules, which require a norm-referenced test in the first six weeks and the same eligibility forms as enrolled students.
args.response: The negative replies that a test once a year is a lighter check than passing every class every six weeks, so the field still isn't level.

neg.label: Negative
neg.stance: School teams belong to the students who attend the school, and families who choose another path accept its trade-offs.

args.claim: School sports are part of school, not a separate service.
args.warrant: A school team represents a community of students who attend classes together. The rule that players must be enrolled students keeps sports tied to the school's mission.
args.evidence: State activities association rules that require enrolled or full-time students; statements from school administrators, such as those quoted in Education Week's 2013 reporting.
args.response: The affirmative answers that the school serves the whole district's children, and the team still represents that community.

args.claim: Eligibility rules can't be applied the same way.
args.warrant: Enrolled players must pass their classes under teachers who grade them, and they can lose eligibility mid-season. A parent who is also the teacher can't be checked the same way.
args.evidence: State no-pass, no-play rules; the critics' arguments in the Texas House Research Organization analysis of the 2021 bill.
args.response: The affirmative replies that states can require outside tests, portfolios or evaluations to confirm progress.

args.claim: Roster spots are limited.
args.warrant: Teams have a fixed number of places. Each spot that goes to a non-enrolled student is one that an enrolled student, who follows all the school's rules, doesn't get.
args.evidence: Team size limits in popular sports; reports from coaches and parents in states that allow access.
args.response: The affirmative answers that spots go to whoever earns them at tryouts, and a homeschooled student who lives in the district is a local student too.

args.claim: It adds costs that school funding doesn't cover.
args.warrant: Districts usually get state money per enrolled student. A student who joins only for sports adds coaching, travel and insurance costs without bringing that funding.
args.evidence: Testimony from school boards associations, such as the Wyoming School Boards Association in 2026; state funding formulas.
args.response: The affirmative replies that states can count these students for activity funding or charge them the same fees enrolled students pay.

strawmen.strawman: They want all the perks of public school without any of the rules.
strawmen.why: Most supporters accept the same eligibility, conduct and fee rules as enrolled students, and many bills add academic checks.
strawmen.steelman: Homeschooled children live in the district and their families help pay for its schools, so with the same eligibility rules and proof of progress they should get the same chance to try out.

strawmen.strawman: They just don't like homeschoolers.
strawmen.why: Opponents argue about enrollment, fair eligibility checks, roster spots and funding, not about families' choices.
strawmen.steelman: A school team belongs to the students who attend the school; eligibility can't be checked the same way for students the school doesn't teach, and roster spots and funding are limited.

weak.arg: Homeschoolers are better students, so of course they should play.
weak.why: It doesn't answer the question of who teams are for, and claims about which group does better are disputed and depend on who is studied.

weak.arg: If you want school sports, just go to school.
weak.why: It skips the real arguments about enrollment, fairness and funding, and families choose homeschooling for many reasons that have nothing to do with sports.

aff: How would a school check a homeschooled player's grades during the season?
Should a homeschooled student also be allowed in the band, the play and the robotics team?
What should happen to an enrolled student who loses a roster spot?
neg: Where should a homeschooled student in a small rural town play, if not on the school team?
Do private school students in your district get any access to public programs?
If a homeschooler meets every eligibility rule, what harm does playing cause?

items.title: Homework
items.subtitle: policy · beginner
items.body: Research links homework to achievement much more strongly in the upper grades than in elementary school. Should elementary schools stop assigning graded homework?

meta.title: Homework
meta.resolution: Resolved: Elementary schools should eliminate graded homework.
meta.summary: Research links homework to achievement much more strongly in the upper grades than in elementary school. Should elementary schools stop assigning graded homework?

background.p: A review of more than 60 studies led by Duke psychologist Harris Cooper (2006) found that homework has a positive link to achievement, and that the link is stronger in grades 7–12 than in elementary school. Many teachers follow a "10-minute rule": about ten minutes a night per grade level, so about 40 minutes in fourth grade. Cooper also found that very large amounts were not linked to higher achievement, even in high school.

For younger students, Cooper suggested homework may mainly build study habits and time management rather than raise grades, and recommended short assignments that students can complete successfully. A 2014 Stanford study of students at ten high-performing high schools (Pope and colleagues) found they averaged about three hours of homework a night and many named it as a main source of stress. That study was of high schoolers, not elementary students.

disputed.q: Does homework help elementary students learn?
positions: Reviews find only a small link between homework and achievement in elementary grades.
Supporters reply that small amounts of practice and the habits it builds pay off later, and that the research measures mostly test scores, not habits.

terms.def: Work done at home that counts toward a student's grade. The resolution covers graded homework only; optional practice and reading at home could continue.
The idea that spaced, repeated practice helps learning last.
A common guideline of about ten minutes of homework per night per grade level.

aff.label: Affirmative
aff.stance: In elementary school, graded homework costs family time and causes stress without clear learning gains.

args.claim: Graded homework does little for young students' achievement.
args.warrant: If a policy takes time every night, it should have clear benefits. Reviews find the homework-achievement link is weak in the elementary grades, so the time costs more than it returns.
args.evidence: Cooper's 2006 review (Duke) finding a stronger link in grades 7–12 than in elementary school; later reviews of the homework literature.
args.response: The negative replies that a weak link in test scores doesn't measure the habits homework builds, which the same researcher stresses.

args.claim: Grading homework measures home help, not learning.
args.warrant: Some children have a parent who can help every night; others have parents working evenings or who don't speak English. Grading the result rewards the home, not the child.
args.evidence: Research on homework and family resources; teacher surveys on unequal home support.
args.response: The negative argues that teachers can design homework children can do alone, and grading it lightly keeps students accountable.

args.claim: Evenings are better used for reading, play, sleep and family.
args.warrant: Young children learn through free reading, conversation and play, and they need sleep; time on worksheets crowds these out.
args.evidence: Pediatric guidance on sleep and play; research on reading for pleasure and vocabulary growth.
args.response: The negative replies that ten or twenty minutes is a small part of an evening, and many families value the routine.

args.claim: Removing grades doesn't remove practice.
args.warrant: Teachers can still send home optional practice and reading logs. Removing grades ends the penalty for children whose homes can't support homework, without ending learning at home.
args.evidence: Districts that have adopted no-graded-homework or reading-only policies, and their reports.
args.response: The negative argues that optional work is often skipped by the students who need practice most, as studies of ungraded practice have found.

neg.label: Negative
neg.stance: Short, purposeful homework builds skills and habits that pay off for years.

args.claim: Practice helps learning stick.
args.warrant: Spelling, math facts and reading fluency improve with spaced practice; school hours alone may not give enough repetitions.
args.evidence: Cognitive science research on spaced practice and retrieval; Cooper's finding of a positive (if smaller) link in younger grades.
args.response: The affirmative answers that practice can happen in school or at home without being graded, so the resolution doesn't stop it.

args.claim: Homework builds study habits before the stakes rise.
args.warrant: Students who learn to manage small assignments in elementary school are ready for heavier loads in middle and high school, where homework matters more.
args.evidence: Cooper's observation that elementary homework may mainly build time management and study skills; teacher reports on the middle-school transition.
args.response: The affirmative replies that habits can be taught through school routines and optional work; grades aren't what build them.

args.claim: Grades keep homework meaningful and fair.
args.warrant: When homework doesn't count, many students skip it, often those who need practice most, and teachers lose a picture of who needs help.
args.evidence: Research on ungraded practice (for example, Huey et al., 2022, summarized by the University of Rochester, finding completion fell when homework didn't count); teacher surveys.
args.response: The affirmative argues that the same research found some gains when homework was removed from grades, and teachers can check work without grading it.

args.claim: Homework connects parents to what children are learning.
args.warrant: Seeing assignments lets parents follow progress and spot problems early.
args.evidence: Studies of parent involvement in school; Cooper's recommendation that some elementary homework involve parents.
args.response: The affirmative answers that newsletters, conferences and ungraded work do this without the stress of grades.

strawmen.strawman: They think kids should never have to work hard.
strawmen.why: Supporters of the resolution object to graded homework for young children, not to effort or practice.
strawmen.steelman: Research finds little achievement benefit from elementary homework, and grading it rewards home support more than learning, so practice should be optional and evenings left for reading, play and sleep.

strawmen.strawman: They just want to keep kids busy every night.
strawmen.why: Defenders of homework point to practice effects and study habits, and most support small amounts.
strawmen.steelman: Short, purposeful homework gives practice that helps skills last and builds habits students need later; grading keeps it meaningful.

weak.arg: Homework is pointless.
weak.why: Research finds a positive link in the upper grades and small benefits in younger ones; calling it pointless is easy to refute.

weak.arg: If we don't grade homework, kids will stop learning.
weak.why: Students learn mostly in class; this exaggerates what homework does.

aff: Would your plan still allow optional practice?
How would teachers know who needs extra help?
Does the research measure study habits, or only test scores?
neg: How many minutes a night do you think is right for a second grader?
What should happen to a student whose parents can't help?
Would ungraded practice give the same benefits?
