items.title: Joining the League of Nations, 1919
items.subtitle: policy · advanced
items.body: After World War I, President Woodrow Wilson championed a League of Nations to keep the peace. Senator Henry Cabot Lodge led the fight for reservations. The Senate's rejection shaped American foreign policy for a generation.

meta.title: Joining the League of Nations, 1919
meta.resolution: Historical question (1919): Should the United States Senate ratify the Treaty of Versailles and join the League of Nations?
meta.summary: After World War I, President Woodrow Wilson championed a League of Nations to keep the peace. Senator Henry Cabot Lodge led the fight for reservations. The Senate's rejection shaped American foreign policy for a generation.

background.p: The Treaty of Versailles, signed in June 1919, ended World War I with Germany and included the Covenant of the League of Nations, an organization of countries meant to settle disputes and prevent war. President Woodrow Wilson had made the League the center of his peace plan. Under the Constitution, a treaty needs the approval of two-thirds of the Senate.

Republicans controlled the Senate after the 1918 elections, and Henry Cabot Lodge chaired the Foreign Relations Committee. His committee attached reservations to the treaty, most importantly limiting Article X, which committed members to preserve one another's territory against aggression. A smaller group of "irreconcilables" opposed the treaty in any form. Wilson refused to accept the reservations and urged his supporters to vote against the treaty with them; on November 19, 1919, the Senate rejected a peace treaty for the first time in its history, and a final attempt failed in March 1920. The United States never joined the League.

terms.def: An international organization founded in 1920 to promote peace; the forerunner of the United Nations.
The League Covenant's pledge that members would respect and preserve each other's territory and independence against external aggression.
A condition the Senate attaches to its approval of a treaty.
The idea that nations agree to treat an attack on one as a concern of all.
Senators who opposed the treaty in any form.

aff.label: Wilson's position (ratify)
aff.stance: Joining the League gives the world a way to prevent another catastrophic war, and America must lead it.

args.claim: Collective security can prevent future wars.
args.warrant: If nations pledge together to resist aggression, would-be aggressors will be deterred, as no country could act against all.
args.evidence: Wilson's speeches during his 1919 tour; the League Covenant.
args.response: Lodge's side answered that Article X could drag the U.S. into foreign conflicts without Congress's consent.

args.claim: Without America, the League will be weak.
args.warrant: The United States was the world's leading economic power; a League without it would lack the strength to act.
args.evidence: The relative economic and military strength of the major powers after 1918.
args.response: Opponents replied that America could cooperate with other nations case by case without binding commitments.

args.claim: The war's sacrifices demand a lasting peace.
args.warrant: After millions of deaths, nations have a duty to build institutions that make such a war less likely.
args.evidence: Casualty figures from World War I; Wilson's appeals to the war's purpose.
args.response: Opponents answered that a flawed treaty might sow future conflict rather than prevent it.

args.claim: Reservations would weaken the League's promise.
args.warrant: If the U.S. joined only with exceptions to its core pledge, other nations might add their own, and collective security would mean little.
args.evidence: Wilson's statements opposing the Lodge reservations.
args.response: Lodge's side replied that the reservations protected the Constitution's war powers and that other allies could accept them.

neg.label: Lodge's position (reservations or reject)
neg.stance: The treaty as written would commit America to wars without Congress's consent and limit its independence.

args.claim: Article X could commit the U.S. to war without Congress.
args.warrant: The Constitution gives Congress the power to declare war; an open-ended pledge to defend other nations' borders could override that.
args.evidence: Lodge's reservations, especially on Article X; Senate debates of 1919.
args.response: Wilson's side argued that Article X was a moral obligation, not an automatic legal command, and Congress would still decide.

args.claim: America should keep its independence in foreign affairs.
args.warrant: From Washington's Farewell Address on, American policy had avoided permanent alliances; the League would bind the country to others' disputes.
args.evidence: Washington's Farewell Address (1796); the Monroe Doctrine.
args.response: Wilson's side replied that the world had changed, and isolation hadn't kept America out of World War I.

args.claim: The treaty's terms were flawed.
args.warrant: A peace that imposed harsh terms and redrew borders by the victors' choices might cause future conflicts the League would then require America to fight.
args.evidence: Contemporary criticism of the treaty's terms.
args.response: Wilson's side argued that the League itself was the means to correct the treaty's flaws over time.

args.claim: Reservations were a reasonable compromise.
args.warrant: Approving the treaty with conditions that protect the Constitution would let America join while keeping its war powers; refusing compromise was the real cause of failure.
args.evidence: The Senate Historical Office's account of the 1919 votes and Wilson's refusal to negotiate.
args.response: Wilson's side held that the reservations gutted the treaty's central promise.

strawmen.strawman: Wilson wanted foreign countries to run America.
strawmen.why: Wilson argued for collective security among sovereign nations, with America leading.
strawmen.steelman: Collective security can deter aggression; the League needs American strength, and the war's sacrifices demand an institution to keep the peace.

strawmen.strawman: Lodge just hated Wilson and wanted to sabotage peace.
strawmen.why: Lodge and the reservationists offered to approve the treaty with conditions protecting Congress's war powers.
strawmen.steelman: Article X could commit America to war without Congress; reservations would protect the Constitution and American independence while allowing participation.

weak.arg: If the U.S. had joined, World War II would never have happened.
weak.why: A speculative counterfactual; historians debate the League's weaknesses beyond American absence.

weak.arg: America never needs allies.
weak.why: An overstatement; even many reservationists supported cooperation with other nations.

aff: Would Article X require the U.S. to send troops without a vote of Congress?
Why not accept the reservations to get the treaty approved?
How would the League enforce its decisions?
neg: How would America prevent another world war without the League?
Did staying out of alliances keep the U.S. out of World War I?
Would other nations accept American reservations?

items.title: Lincoln and Douglas, 1858
items.subtitle: policy · advanced
items.body: The seven debates between Abraham Lincoln and Stephen Douglas, the most famous political debates in American history, turned on whether slavery should be allowed to spread into the territories. Study how each man made his case.

meta.title: Lincoln and Douglas, 1858
meta.resolution: Historical question (1858): Should the federal government keep slavery out of the western territories, or should the people of each territory decide?
meta.summary: The seven debates between Abraham Lincoln and Stephen Douglas, the most famous political debates in American history, turned on whether slavery should be allowed to spread into the territories. Study how each man made his case.

background.p: **A note before you read.** Slavery was a grave moral wrong; it was abolished in the United States by the Thirteenth Amendment in 1865. This page is history: it shows how two candidates argued in 1858, so you can study the reasoning, the rhetoric and why the debates mattered. Both men also said things about race that were wrong and are offensive by today's standards; historians record them, and you'll meet them if you read the full texts. Treat this page as a case study for analysis, not as a resolution for a practice round.

In 1858, Illinois voters chose a state legislature that would elect a U.S. senator. The Democratic incumbent, Stephen A. Douglas, was one of the country's best-known politicians; the Republican challenger, Abraham Lincoln, was a lawyer who had served one term in Congress. They held seven debates across Illinois between August 21 and October 15. In each, one spoke for an hour, the other for an hour and a half, and the first then answered for half an hour. Lincoln-Douglas debate, the high school format, is named for them.

The central question was whether slavery should be allowed to expand into the western territories. Douglas championed **popular sovereignty**: let the residents of each territory decide. Lincoln and the Republicans held that slavery was a moral wrong that federal policy should keep from spreading, placing it, as Lincoln put it, on a course of "ultimate extinction." The Supreme Court's 1857 *Dred Scott* decision had declared that Congress could not ban slavery in the territories, which sharpened the clash. Democrats won the legislature, 46 seats to 41, so Douglas kept his seat; but the debates made Lincoln nationally known and helped lead to his presidential nomination in 1860.

terms.def: Douglas's principle that the settlers of each territory should decide for themselves whether to allow slavery.
The Republican position that slavery should not expand into the territories.
A Supreme Court decision holding that Congress could not ban slavery in the territories and that Black Americans could not be citizens; overturned by the Thirteenth and Fourteenth Amendments.
Douglas's answer at Freeport that settlers could still keep slavery out in practice by refusing to pass local laws to protect it.
Lincoln's June 1858 speech arguing the nation could not endure permanently half slave and half free.

aff.label: Lincoln's position
aff.stance: Slavery is a moral wrong; the nation should stop its spread and put it on the road to ultimate extinction.

args.claim: Slavery is wrong, and policy should treat it as wrong.
args.warrant: A policy of indifference, letting each territory vote slavery "up or down," treats a moral wrong as a matter of local taste. A nation must decide whether something is right or wrong.
args.evidence: Lincoln's debate speeches criticizing Douglas's "don't care" stance; Republican platform statements.
args.response: Douglas answered that the people of each territory, not Congress, had the right to make that decision, and that forcing one view risked tearing the Union apart.

args.claim: The Declaration of Independence applies to all people.
args.warrant: "All men are created equal" with rights to life, liberty and the pursuit of happiness is the nation's founding principle; slavery contradicts it.
args.evidence: Lincoln's appeals to the Declaration throughout the debates and his earlier speeches.
args.response: Douglas argued that the signers had not meant to include enslaved people and that the government was made for the existing political community.

args.claim: The founders meant to limit slavery's spread.
args.warrant: The founders banned slavery in the Northwest Territory and ended the foreign slave trade, showing they expected slavery to die out; Lincoln wanted to return to that course.
args.evidence: The Northwest Ordinance (1787); the 1808 ban on the international slave trade.
args.response: Douglas replied that the founders left each state free to decide its own institutions, the principle he defended.

args.claim: A house divided against itself cannot stand.
args.warrant: The nation was drifting toward making slavery lawful everywhere; only by stopping its spread could the country become all free over time.
args.evidence: The "House Divided" speech (June 1858); the Dred Scott decision as evidence of the drift.
args.response: Douglas called this a doctrine of sectional conflict, insisting the nation had existed half slave and half free since its founding and could continue to.

neg.label: Douglas's position
neg.stance: The people of each territory should decide for themselves; Congress should not impose one answer.

args.claim: Self-government means local decision.
args.warrant: Americans had fought for the right to govern themselves; settlers of a territory, like citizens of a state, should make their own laws.
args.evidence: Douglas's speeches on popular sovereignty; the Kansas-Nebraska Act (1854), which he wrote.
args.response: Lincoln answered that no one has a right to do wrong, and that self-government could not include the right to govern other people without their consent.

args.claim: Pressing the issue nationally threatened the Union.
args.warrant: Forcing one section's view on the other risked secession and war; leaving the question local kept the country together.
args.evidence: Douglas's warnings that Lincoln's "House Divided" doctrine meant conflict between the sections.
args.response: Lincoln replied that the division already existed and would not end until the nation set slavery on the path to extinction.

args.claim: The courts had settled the law.
args.warrant: The Supreme Court had ruled in Dred Scott; respecting the Court's decisions was part of the rule of law.
args.evidence: The Dred Scott decision (1857); Douglas's criticism of Lincoln for opposing the Court.
args.response: Lincoln argued the decision was wrong, that the Court could reverse itself, and that citizens could oppose a decision by lawful political means.

args.claim: In practice, settlers could keep slavery out.
args.warrant: Slavery needed local laws to protect it; if settlers refused to pass them, it could not take root, so popular sovereignty was workable even after Dred Scott.
args.evidence: The Freeport Doctrine (August 27, 1858).
args.response: Lincoln pressed that this contradicted Dred Scott, which Douglas also endorsed, and the answer cost Douglas support in the South.

strawmen.strawman: Lincoln just wanted to start a war with the South.
strawmen.why: In 1858 Lincoln said he did not seek to interfere with slavery where it already existed; his aim was to stop its spread.
strawmen.steelman: Slavery is a moral wrong contrary to the Declaration; the founders limited its spread, and the nation should do so again to place it on the course of ultimate extinction.

strawmen.strawman: Douglas wanted to spread slavery to every state.
strawmen.why: Douglas said he did not care whether slavery was voted up or down; his principle was local decision, and he opposed the pro-slavery Lecompton Constitution in Kansas.
strawmen.steelman: Each territory's people should govern themselves, the courts had spoken, and treating the issue as national risked breaking the Union.

weak.arg: Lincoln in 1858 called for full equality and immediate emancipation.
weak.why: Historically inaccurate; Lincoln ran on stopping slavery's spread and made statements about race that historians record as reflecting the prejudices of his time.

weak.arg: Douglas's position was neutral and harmed no one.
weak.why: Indifference to slavery's spread left enslaved people's fate to others' votes; that was exactly Lincoln's objection, and it can't be waved away.

aff: (Questions Douglas pressed) If the founders allowed slavery in some states, why can't a territory choose it?
Wouldn't your doctrine set the sections against each other?
Will you obey the Supreme Court's decision in Dred Scott?
neg: (Questions Lincoln pressed) Can the people of a territory lawfully exclude slavery before forming a state constitution?
Is slavery right or wrong?
Does anyone have a right to do a wrong?

items.body: The federal minimum wage has been $7.25 since 2009, though many states and cities set higher ones. Should the national floor rise to $15?

meta.title: Raising the Minimum Wage
meta.resolution: Resolved: The United States federal government should raise the federal minimum wage to $15 an hour.
meta.summary: The federal minimum wage has been $7.25 since 2009, though many states and cities set higher ones. Should the national floor rise to $15?

background.p: The federal minimum wage has been $7.25 an hour since July 2009. Many states and cities have set higher minimums, some above $15, so the federal floor mainly matters in states that haven't raised their own.

In 2021 the Congressional Budget Office estimated the effects of raising the federal minimum to $15 by 2025. Its average estimate: about 17 million workers would get raises directly (and many above $15 would also be affected), about 900,000 fewer people would be in poverty, and employment would be about 1.4 million lower (0.9%) in 2025, with a wide range of uncertainty. Economists disagree about how much higher minimums reduce jobs; the answer likely depends on how high the minimum is compared with local wages.

disputed.q: How much do higher minimum wages reduce employment?
positions: Many studies of past increases find small or no job losses, especially for moderate increases.
Other studies, and CBO's estimates, find meaningful job losses for large increases, falling most on the least experienced workers; effects may differ in low-wage regions.

terms.def: The lowest hourly pay employers may legally pay most workers.
Tying the minimum wage to inflation or median wages so it rises automatically.
A labor market where employers have power to set wages below what a competitive market would pay.
A federal tax credit that adds to the income of low-wage working families.

aff.label: Affirmative
aff.stance: A $15 floor raises pay for millions of low-wage workers and reduces poverty.

args.claim: Millions of workers would get raises.
args.warrant: A higher floor directly lifts the pay of workers below it and pushes up pay just above it, putting money in the hands of families who most need it.
args.evidence: CBO (2021): about 17 million workers directly affected and many more indirectly.
args.response: The negative answers that the same report estimates about 1.4 million fewer jobs, and those who lose work are hurt badly.

args.claim: It would lift hundreds of thousands out of poverty.
args.warrant: Full-time work at $7.25 leaves a family below the poverty line; higher pay reduces the need for public assistance.
args.evidence: CBO's estimate of about 900,000 fewer people in poverty; data on full-time minimum-wage earnings versus poverty thresholds.
args.response: The negative replies that many minimum-wage earners aren't in poor households, so the EITC targets poverty more precisely.

args.claim: Job losses from past increases have often been small.
args.warrant: Employers can absorb higher wages through lower turnover, small price increases and higher productivity, and some labor markets give employers wage-setting power.
args.evidence: Studies of state and city increases comparing neighboring areas; research on monopsony in labor markets.
args.response: The negative argues that $15 nationwide is much higher, relative to wages in low-cost regions, than most increases studied.

args.claim: The federal minimum has lost value to inflation.
args.warrant: Since 2009, prices have risen while $7.25 hasn't changed, so the real wage floor has fallen year after year.
args.evidence: Bureau of Labor Statistics inflation data; history of federal minimum-wage changes.
args.response: The negative answers that most states have already raised their own minimums, and a uniform federal number ignores cost-of-living differences.

neg.label: Negative
neg.stance: A $15 national floor risks jobs and hours for the least experienced workers, especially in low-wage regions.

args.claim: It would cost jobs.
args.warrant: When labor costs rise sharply, some employers hire fewer workers, cut hours or automate, and those who lose out are often young and less-skilled workers.
args.evidence: CBO (2021): employment about 1.4 million lower in 2025 under its average estimate; studies finding job losses from large increases.
args.response: The affirmative answers that many studies of past increases find small effects, and CBO's estimate has a wide range.

args.claim: One national number ignores regional differences.
args.warrant: $15 is close to typical wages in some low-cost areas, where its effects would be much larger than in high-cost cities.
args.evidence: Bureau of Labor Statistics wage data by state and metro area; research on the minimum wage relative to the local median wage.
args.response: The affirmative replies that the increase can be phased in, and low-cost areas have the most workers living in poverty.

args.claim: Other tools target poverty better.
args.warrant: Many minimum-wage workers are teenagers or second earners in households above the poverty line, while the EITC goes to low-income working families specifically and doesn't raise employers' costs.
args.evidence: Census data on the household incomes of minimum-wage workers; research on the EITC's effects on work and poverty.
args.response: The affirmative argues the two work together, and the EITC is paid by taxpayers rather than by employers.

args.claim: Prices may rise and small businesses may struggle.
args.warrant: Restaurants and small shops with thin margins may raise prices or close, and higher prices fall partly on low-income customers.
args.evidence: Studies of price effects of minimum-wage increases, especially in restaurants; small-business surveys.
args.response: The affirmative replies that measured price increases have been small, and higher pay also boosts customer spending.

strawmen.strawman: They don't understand that businesses have costs.
strawmen.why: Supporters argue, with evidence, that past increases caused small job effects and businesses adjusted.
strawmen.steelman: A higher floor raises pay for millions and lifts many out of poverty, and studies of past increases often find small job effects.

strawmen.strawman: They want workers to stay poor.
strawmen.why: Opponents argue a high national floor would cost some low-wage workers their jobs and favor tools like the EITC.
strawmen.steelman: A $15 national floor could cost jobs and hours for the least experienced workers, especially in low-wage regions, while the EITC targets poverty more directly.

weak.arg: Raising the minimum wage never costs any jobs.
weak.why: Even supportive research finds some effects for large increases; overclaiming invites an easy answer.

weak.arg: Everyone earning minimum wage is a teenager.
weak.why: Many minimum-wage workers are adults, and some support families. Inaccurate claims hurt credibility.

aff: What does CBO estimate for job losses at $15?
How would $15 compare to typical wages in the lowest-wage states?
Would you index the minimum to inflation or to local wages?
neg: What does CBO estimate for the number of workers who'd get raises?
Has the real value of $7.25 fallen since 2009?
Should there be any increase? How much?

items.title: Moon First or Mars First?
items.subtitle: policy · intermediate
items.body: NASA plans to return astronauts to the Moon's surface and use what it learns to prepare for Mars. Some argue the Moon is a needed proving ground; others say it's a costly detour from the bigger goal. Which should come first?

meta.title: Moon First or Mars First?
meta.resolution: Resolved: NASA should land astronauts on the Moon again before sending astronauts to Mars.
meta.summary: NASA plans to return astronauts to the Moon's surface and use what it learns to prepare for Mars. Some argue the Moon is a needed proving ground; others say it's a costly detour from the bigger goal. Which should come first?

background.p: No one has walked on the Moon since Apollo 17 in December 1972. NASA's Artemis program aims to go back. On Artemis II, four astronauts (Reid Wiseman, Victor Glover and Christina Koch of NASA and Jeremy Hansen of the Canadian Space Agency) flew around the Moon, launching April 1, 2026, and splashing down in the Pacific on April 10, 2026.

In February 2026, NASA changed its plan. Artemis III, set for 2027, became a test flight in low Earth orbit, where astronauts will practice docking with commercial Moon landers from SpaceX and Blue Origin and test new spacesuits. Artemis IV, planned for 2028, is to be the first landing, and NASA said it aims for at least one landing a year after that. NASA restated this timeline in October 2026.

NASA's Moon to Mars objectives (September 2022) call for missions on and around the Moon "followed by missions to Mars," using the Moon partly to test systems for Mars. Mars is much harder: a NASA workshop paper describes an example round trip of about 850 days, a one-way radio delay of up to about 22 minutes, and notes that lessons from lunar mission aborts will have limited direct use for Mars, since an early return from Mars could take hundreds of days. The Moon program is expensive: NASA's Inspector General projected in 2021 that the agency would spend about $93 billion on the Artemis effort through fiscal year 2025.

disputed.q: How much does practice on the Moon help with Mars?
positions: NASA's plans hold that landing, living and working on the Moon tests the systems, suits and operations Mars will need, close enough to Earth to come home if something fails.
Critics say the Moon's lack of air, its weaker gravity and its short distance from Earth make it a poor stand-in, so Moon hardware and practice may not carry over well to Mars.

terms.def: NASA's program to return astronauts to the Moon, using the Space Launch System rocket, the Orion capsule and commercial landers.
Orbit a few hundred miles above Earth, where the International Space Station flies.
A place to test equipment and skills before using them where failure would be more dangerous.
A period when a launch can reach its target efficiently. Good windows to Mars come about every 26 months.

aff.label: Affirmative (Moon first)
aff.stance: The Moon is close, reachable and a safe place to learn the skills and test the machines a Mars mission will depend on.

args.claim: The Moon is a safer place to learn.
args.warrant: The Moon is about three days from Earth. If something goes wrong, a crew can come home in days. At Mars, help is months away, so mistakes must be found and fixed first.
args.evidence: NASA's Moon to Mars objectives, which call for using the Moon to shorten testing before Mars; NASA's Mars challenges paper on long abort times.
args.response: The negative answers that the Moon tests the wrong things: NASA's own paper says lessons from lunar aborts will have limited direct use at Mars.

args.claim: We need to test life support and suits on another world.
args.warrant: Astronauts will need to live for long periods away from Earth, wear suits in harsh dust and work outside daily. The Moon lets NASA test all of this on a real surface.
args.evidence: Artemis plans for surface stays and new spacesuits; NASA's architecture documents on Mars-forward tests at the Moon.
args.response: The negative replies that the space station and Earth-based tests can do much of this without the cost of landings.

args.claim: The program is already moving.
args.warrant: Artemis II has flown, landers are being built and a 2028 landing is planned. Changing direction now would waste years of work and money and could leave the nation with neither goal.
args.evidence: NASA's 2026 Artemis updates; history of programs canceled midstream, such as Constellation in 2010.
args.response: The negative answers that money already spent is gone either way (the sunk cost fallacy), and the question is what's best from here.

args.claim: The Moon has science and resources of its own.
args.warrant: The Moon's craters hold clues to the early solar system, and ice near the south pole might one day supply water and fuel. These are worth exploring for their own sake.
args.evidence: NASA lunar science goals; studies of water ice at the lunar south pole.
args.response: The negative replies that robots can study the Moon cheaply, and that Mars may hold the bigger scientific prize: signs of past life.

neg.label: Negative (Mars first)
neg.stance: Mars is the goal that matters most, and spending decades and billions on the Moon delays it without preparing for it well.

args.claim: Mars holds the biggest questions.
args.warrant: Mars once had liquid water and may have had life. Astronauts there could search in ways robots can't, so the most important science is on Mars, not the Moon.
args.evidence: NASA Mars science goals; findings from Mars rovers about ancient water.
args.response: The affirmative answers that the science will still be there in a decade, and getting astronauts home safely matters more than getting there first.

args.claim: The Moon is a poor practice ground for Mars.
args.warrant: Mars has an atmosphere, stronger gravity, long communication delays and trips measured in years. Landing on the Moon teaches different skills, so Moon hardware may not carry over.
args.evidence: NASA's 2024 Mars challenges workshop paper, noting an 850-day example mission, 22-minute one-way delays and limited lessons from lunar aborts.
args.response: The affirmative replies that life support, suits, surface operations and long missions far from Earth all carry over, even if landing does not.

args.claim: Money and time are limited.
args.warrant: NASA's budget is a small, fairly flat share of federal spending. Every dollar and year spent on lunar landings is a dollar and year not spent on Mars.
args.evidence: NASA Inspector General (2021): about $93 billion on Artemis through fiscal year 2025 and about $4.1 billion for each launch of the rocket and capsule through Artemis IV; NASA's small, flat share of federal spending.
args.response: The affirmative answers that Mars systems, such as landers and life support, can be built while the Moon program runs, and Congress decides the budget.

args.claim: We've already been to the Moon.
args.warrant: Apollo landed twelve astronauts on the Moon. A bold new goal can inspire students and the public and draw support in a way a return trip may not.
args.evidence: Apollo history; surveys of public interest in space goals.
args.response: The affirmative replies that Apollo made short visits, and learning to stay and work on the Moon is a new and harder goal.

strawmen.strawman: They just want to redo Apollo because it's familiar.
strawmen.why: Supporters argue for long stays, new technology and safety testing close to home, which Apollo never did.
strawmen.steelman: The Moon is days from Earth, so it's the safest place to test the life support, suits and surface work Mars will require before risking a crew months from help.

strawmen.strawman: They want to rush astronauts to Mars no matter the danger.
strawmen.why: Mars-first supporters usually want careful testing too, but through other means than lunar landings.
strawmen.steelman: Mars holds the biggest scientific questions, and the Moon differs from Mars so much that landing there may delay Mars without preparing for it well.

weak.arg: We have to beat other countries to the Moon.
weak.why: Competition may matter, but it doesn't show that the Moon must come before Mars; tie your case to preparation and safety.

weak.arg: The Moon is boring.
weak.why: It's a feeling, not an argument, and it ignores the Moon's science and its use as a test site.

aff: Which Mars skills can only be practiced on the Moon?
How many years would Moon landings delay the first Mars mission?
If the money ran short, which would you cut first?
neg: Where would you test a Mars lander and life support before sending a crew?
How would a crew get home if something failed on the way to Mars?
Should NASA stop the Artemis landings already being built?

items.title: Hamilton vs Jefferson on a National Bank, 1791
items.subtitle: fact · advanced
items.body: In February 1791, President Washington asked his cabinet whether the bank bill Congress had passed was constitutional. Jefferson said no; Hamilton said yes. Their opinions still frame debates about federal power.

meta.title: Hamilton vs Jefferson on a National Bank, 1791
meta.resolution: Historical question (1791): Does the Constitution give Congress the power to charter a national bank?
meta.summary: In February 1791, President Washington asked his cabinet whether the bank bill Congress had passed was constitutional. Jefferson said no; Hamilton said yes. Their opinions still frame debates about federal power.

background.p: Treasury Secretary Alexander Hamilton proposed a Bank of the United States to hold government funds, make loans, issue a sound currency and help manage the national debt. Congress passed the bill in early 1791. Before signing it, President George Washington asked members of his cabinet for written opinions on whether it was constitutional, since the Constitution doesn't mention banks or corporations.

Secretary of State Thomas Jefferson (February 15, 1791) argued that Congress has only the powers the Constitution lists, that a bank is not among them, and that the "necessary and proper" clause allows only means that are truly necessary, not merely convenient. Hamilton (February 23, 1791) argued that the government's listed powers carry implied powers to use suitable means, and that "necessary" in the clause means "needful, requisite, incidental, useful, or conducive to." Washington signed the bill. In McCulloch v. Maryland (1819), the Supreme Court upheld a later national bank, adopting reasoning close to Hamilton's.

terms.def: The powers the Constitution lists for Congress, mainly in Article I, Section 8.
Powers not listed but understood to follow from listed ones.
Article I, Section 8's final clause, letting Congress make laws "necessary and proper" for carrying out its powers.
Reading the Constitution's grants of power narrowly (strict) or generously (broad).
Powers not delegated to the federal government are reserved to the states or the people.

aff.label: Hamilton's position (constitutional)
aff.stance: A bank is a reasonable means to carry out Congress's listed powers, so the Constitution allows it.

args.claim: Every power granted includes the means to carry it out.
args.warrant: A government given ends (taxing, borrowing, regulating commerce) must be able to choose suitable means, or the grants are empty.
args.evidence: Hamilton's opinion: "every power vested in a Government is in its nature sovereign" within its objects.
args.response: Jefferson's answer: if any convenient means is allowed, the list of powers no longer limits anything.

args.claim: "Necessary" means useful or conducive, not indispensable.
args.warrant: In ordinary speech, "necessary" often means needful or useful; a strict reading would leave Congress unable to act.
args.evidence: Hamilton's analysis of the word, and the clause's purpose to give flexibility.
args.response: Jefferson's answer: the word means what it says, and treating it as "convenient" swallows the limits.

args.claim: The bank relates directly to listed powers.
args.warrant: A bank helps collect taxes, borrow money and manage the currency, all federal responsibilities.
args.evidence: Hamilton's link of the bank to taxation, borrowing and trade; the Treasury's needs.
args.response: Jefferson's answer: these tasks could be done without a bank, through existing state banks and Treasury orders.

args.claim: The test is relation to a legitimate end, not degree of need.
args.warrant: Courts and Congress can ask whether a measure has a natural relation to a federal purpose; how badly it's needed is a policy question.
args.evidence: Hamilton: "the criterion of constitutionality" is not "the more or less of necessity or utility"; later echoed in McCulloch v. Maryland.
args.response: Jefferson's answer: such a test gives no real boundary, so federal power would grow without limit.

neg.label: Jefferson's position (unconstitutional)
neg.stance: The Constitution gives Congress only listed powers, and chartering a bank isn't one of them.

args.claim: Federal powers are limited to those delegated.
args.warrant: The Constitution's foundation is that powers not given to the federal government stay with the states or the people.
args.evidence: Jefferson's opinion citing what became the Tenth Amendment.
args.response: Hamilton's answer: implied powers are delegated as fully as express ones, so the Tenth Amendment doesn't bar them.

args.claim: The bank fits none of Congress's listed powers.
args.warrant: Chartering a bank isn't laying taxes, borrowing money or regulating commerce; creating something to be bought and sold isn't regulating trade.
args.evidence: Jefferson's line-by-line review of the enumerated powers.
args.response: Hamilton's answer: the bank isn't a new end but a means toward several listed ends.

args.claim: "Necessary" must mean necessary.
args.warrant: If merely convenient means are allowed, nearly anything can be justified, and the careful list of powers means nothing.
args.evidence: Jefferson's reading of the Necessary and Proper Clause.
args.response: Hamilton's answer: the strict reading would make the government unable to function.

args.claim: The bank would override state laws.
args.warrant: A federal corporation would displace long-standing state laws on property, inheritance and monopolies, a serious step that only true necessity could justify.
args.evidence: Jefferson's list of state laws the charter would affect.
args.response: Hamilton's answer: the bank abridges no existing state or individual right, which supports its constitutionality.

strawmen.strawman: Hamilton wanted the federal government to do anything it pleased.
strawmen.why: Hamilton tied the bank to specific listed powers and proposed a test of relation to legitimate ends.
strawmen.steelman: A government given ends must have the means to reach them; a bank relates naturally to taxing, borrowing and managing currency, so the Constitution allows it.

strawmen.strawman: Jefferson was simply against banks and modern finance.
strawmen.why: His opinion was a constitutional argument about limited, listed powers.
strawmen.steelman: Federal powers are limited to those delegated; a bank fits none, and reading "necessary" as "convenient" would erase the Constitution's limits.

weak.arg: The Constitution says nothing against banks, so they're allowed.
weak.why: That ignores the principle of enumerated powers, which both sides accepted.

weak.arg: The bank was a bad idea, so it was unconstitutional.
weak.why: Whether a policy is wise and whether it's constitutional are different questions; Jefferson himself separated them.

aff: Which listed power does the bank carry out?
If "necessary" means useful, what wouldn't be allowed?
Could state banks do the job instead?
neg: Can Congress collect taxes without any means not listed in the Constitution?
What does "necessary" mean in ordinary speech?
If a measure helps carry out a listed power, why isn't it allowed?

items.title: Mandatory National Service
items.subtitle: policy · intermediate
items.body: Should every young American spend a year serving the country, in the military or in civilian programs like AmeriCorps?

meta.title: Mandatory National Service
meta.resolution: Resolved: The United States should require one year of national service for young adults.
meta.summary: Should every young American spend a year serving the country, in the military or in civilian programs like AmeriCorps?

background.p: The United States has had no military draft since 1973; young men must still register with the Selective Service System. Civilian service programs such as AmeriCorps and the Peace Corps are voluntary and pay modest living allowances. Several countries require military or civilian service, including Israel, South Korea, Switzerland and Norway, with very different rules.

In 2020, the congressionally created National Commission on Military, National, and Public Service released its final report, *Inspired to Serve*. It envisioned five million Americans beginning military, national or public service each year by 2031, so that service becomes "the norm, rather than the exception," and made recommendations on expanding service opportunities and on Selective Service registration.

terms.def: Full-time work for the public good, such as tutoring, conservation or disaster relief, usually for a modest stipend.
A federal agency that funds national service programs in communities.
The federal agency that keeps a list of men eligible for a military draft.
A person who refuses military service for reasons of conscience.

aff.label: Affirmative
aff.stance: A year of service would bring Americans together and meet real needs.

args.claim: Service brings together Americans from different backgrounds.
args.warrant: Working side by side with people from other regions, incomes and views builds understanding that few other experiences provide.
args.evidence: Studies of AmeriCorps and military service on civic attitudes; the National Commission's report.
args.response: The negative answers that voluntary programs already do this for those who choose, and forced participation may breed resentment.

args.claim: It meets real needs.
args.warrant: Schools, parks, disaster areas and elder care need help; a year of service from millions of young adults supplies it.
args.evidence: AmeriCorps program evaluations; reports of labor shortages in caregiving and tutoring.
args.response: The negative replies that untrained short-term workers may not fill skilled needs, and paid jobs would be displaced.

args.claim: Young people gain skills and direction.
args.warrant: A structured year teaches responsibility and job skills and gives time to choose a path before college or work.
args.evidence: Surveys of service-program alumni; gap-year research.
args.response: The negative argues that delaying college or work costs young people a year of earnings and progress.

args.claim: Citizenship includes duties as well as rights.
args.warrant: A democracy asks citizens to serve on juries and pay taxes; a year of service is a fair way to share responsibility for the common good.
args.evidence: The Commission's vision of service as a norm; comparisons with countries that require service.
args.response: The negative replies that compulsory labor is a much larger demand than jury duty.

neg.label: Negative
neg.stance: Service should be encouraged and expanded, but not required.

args.claim: Requiring a year of work intrudes on personal liberty.
args.warrant: Forcing young adults to spend a year in assigned work overrides their own choices about school, work and family.
args.evidence: Constitutional and philosophical debates about compulsory service; the history of opposition to the draft.
args.response: The affirmative answers that a wide menu of service options preserves choice within the requirement.

args.claim: The cost would be enormous.
args.warrant: Millions of young adults a year need pay, housing, training and supervision, costing far more than current programs.
args.evidence: AmeriCorps cost-per-member figures multiplied by the size of an age group.
args.response: The affirmative replies that the work produced has real value, offsetting much of the cost.

args.claim: Voluntary service works better.
args.warrant: People who choose to serve are motivated; expanding funded voluntary programs captures most of the benefits without compulsion.
args.evidence: The Commission's recommendations focused on expanding service opportunities; AmeriCorps waitlists.
args.response: The affirmative argues voluntary programs mostly attract people who are already civic-minded, missing the mixing that makes service valuable.

args.claim: It delays education and careers.
args.warrant: A required year postpones college and work, costing earnings and momentum, especially for students who are ready to start.
args.evidence: Research on delayed college entry and lifetime earnings.
args.response: The affirmative replies that many students benefit from a gap year, and service can include education benefits.

strawmen.strawman: They want to bring back the draft and send everyone to war.
strawmen.why: Most proposals include civilian options like tutoring and conservation.
strawmen.steelman: A year of military or civilian service would bring Americans together, meet real needs, and teach young people skills and citizenship.

strawmen.strawman: They think young people should only care about themselves.
strawmen.why: Many opponents support service, but voluntarily.
strawmen.steelman: Service should be expanded and encouraged, but requiring a year intrudes on liberty, costs enormously, and voluntary service captures most of the benefits.

weak.arg: Young people today are lazy and need discipline.
weak.why: An insult, not an argument, and it alienates judges.

weak.arg: It's slavery.
weak.why: An extreme comparison that minimizes real slavery and loses the judge.

aff: How much would a year of service for every young adult cost?
What happens to someone who refuses?
Would military service be required or optional?
neg: Do voluntary programs reach young people who aren't already civic-minded?
Is jury duty a fair requirement?
What did the National Commission envision for service?

items.title: Nuclear Power
items.subtitle: policy · intermediate
items.body: Nuclear plants make about a fifth of America's electricity with almost no carbon emissions, but new plants have been slow and expensive to build. Should the country build more?

meta.title: Nuclear Power
meta.resolution: Resolved: The United States should substantially expand its use of nuclear power.
meta.summary: Nuclear plants make about a fifth of America's electricity with almost no carbon emissions, but new plants have been slow and expensive to build. Should the country build more?

background.p: The United States has the world's largest commercial nuclear fleet: 94 reactors at 54 plants in 2024, with nearly 97 gigawatts of capacity, providing about 19% of the country's electricity, according to the U.S. Energy Information Administration. Natural gas provided about 43% and coal about 16% in 2023; wind, hydropower and solar together about a fifth.

Only a few new reactors have come online since 1996: Watts Bar 2 in Tennessee and two units at Plant Vogtle in Georgia (2023 and 2024). Vogtle's expansion finished years behind schedule and far over its original budget. Twelve reactors have closed since 2013, though federal programs have since supported keeping California's Diablo Canyon open and restarting Michigan's Palisades plant.

Nuclear plants emit almost no carbon dioxide while operating and run most hours of the year. Concerns include building cost and time, the long-term storage of spent fuel (the U.S. has no permanent repository), and the risk of rare but serious accidents such as Chernobyl (1986) and Fukushima (2011). Newer designs, including small modular reactors, aim to cut costs, but few have been built.

disputed.q: Will new reactors be affordable?
positions: Supporters say costs fall as builders repeat designs, as other countries have shown, and that small modular reactors can be factory-built.
Critics point to recent U.S. and European projects that ran years late and billions over budget, and note small modular reactors are largely unproven commercially.

terms.def: How much electricity a plant actually produces compared with running at full power all the time. Nuclear plants have very high capacity factors.
Electricity supplied steadily around the clock.
Used reactor fuel, which stays radioactive for a very long time and must be stored safely.
A smaller reactor design meant to be built in factories and shipped to sites.

aff.label: Affirmative
aff.stance: Nuclear power gives steady, low-carbon electricity at scale, and the country should build more.

args.claim: Nuclear provides large amounts of carbon-free electricity around the clock.
args.warrant: Unlike wind and solar, nuclear doesn't depend on weather, so it can replace fossil-fuel plants that run day and night.
args.evidence: EIA data on nuclear's share of generation and capacity factors; emissions data per unit of electricity from international assessments.
args.response: The negative answers that batteries, transmission lines and a mix of renewables can provide steady power more cheaply and sooner.

args.claim: Measured per unit of energy, nuclear's safety record is strong.
args.warrant: Air pollution from burning fossil fuels harms health continuously, while serious nuclear accidents are rare. Counted per unit of electricity, nuclear causes very few deaths.
args.evidence: Studies of deaths per terawatt-hour across energy sources; health research on air pollution from fossil fuels.
args.response: The negative replies that a single major accident can force evacuations and leave land unusable for decades, a kind of harm averages don't capture.

args.claim: Electricity demand is rising.
args.warrant: Data centers, electric vehicles and factories are increasing demand; a reliable source that runs most hours helps keep the grid stable.
args.evidence: EIA and utility forecasts of demand growth; grid operator reliability reports.
args.response: The negative argues new reactors take a decade or more, so they won't meet near-term demand.

args.claim: Building more brings costs down.
args.warrant: First-of-a-kind projects are expensive; repeating standard designs builds skilled crews and supply chains that lower later costs.
args.evidence: Cost histories of reactor programs abroad; analyses of Vogtle lessons learned; Department of Energy reports on advanced reactors.
args.response: The negative replies that the U.S. has repeatedly expected learning to cut costs, and recent projects haven't shown it.

neg.label: Negative
neg.stance: Nuclear is too slow and costly to be the right investment, and its risks are unresolved.

args.claim: New nuclear is expensive and slow.
args.warrant: Money spent on a reactor that takes ten or more years could cut more emissions sooner if spent on cheaper, faster options.
args.evidence: Vogtle 3 and 4 schedule and cost history; cost estimates comparing new nuclear with wind, solar and storage.
args.response: The affirmative answers that cheaper sources aren't steady, and storage at grid scale adds large costs of its own.

args.claim: The waste problem isn't solved.
args.warrant: Spent fuel stays dangerous for thousands of years, and the U.S. still has no permanent repository, so waste piles up at plant sites.
args.evidence: Department of Energy and Government Accountability Office reports on spent fuel storage; the history of the Yucca Mountain project.
args.response: The affirmative replies that spent fuel is small in volume, stored safely in dry casks, and that the barrier is political, not technical.

args.claim: Rare accidents can be very costly.
args.warrant: A serious accident can force evacuations, contaminate land and cost hundreds of billions, a risk that grows with more reactors.
args.evidence: Reports on Fukushima's evacuation and cleanup; Nuclear Regulatory Commission risk assessments.
args.response: The affirmative argues modern designs are safer, and that fossil-fuel pollution causes far more harm every year.

args.claim: Security and fuel risks matter.
args.warrant: More reactors mean more fuel to protect and more sites that need security, and some fuel supply has depended on imports from countries such as Russia.
args.evidence: Reports on enriched uranium imports; NRC security requirements; international nonproliferation analyses.
args.response: The affirmative replies that the U.S. can expand domestic enrichment, and plants are among the most secure civilian sites.

strawmen.strawman: Nuclear supporters don't care about accidents.
strawmen.why: Supporters argue that per unit of energy nuclear's safety record is strong compared with fossil fuels.
strawmen.steelman: Nuclear produces large amounts of steady, low-carbon power, and measured per unit of electricity its health toll is very low.

strawmen.strawman: Nuclear opponents are just afraid of anything new.
strawmen.why: Opponents point to cost, construction time and the unresolved waste question.
strawmen.steelman: New reactors take a decade and cost far more than planned, and the same money may cut emissions faster elsewhere while waste storage remains unsolved.

weak.arg: Nuclear power is completely safe.
weak.why: No energy source is completely safe; claim what the evidence supports.

weak.arg: A nuclear plant could explode like an atomic bomb.
weak.why: Reactor fuel can't explode like a nuclear weapon. Accidents are serious, but this is false and costs credibility.

aff: How long did Vogtle 3 and 4 take to build, and at what cost?
Where would the spent fuel go?
How would expansion meet demand in the next five years?
neg: What would replace nuclear plants at night when there's no sun or wind?
How many deaths per unit of energy does nuclear cause compared with coal?
Should existing plants be closed?

items.title: The Penny and Rounding
items.subtitle: policy · beginner
items.body: The U.S. Mint struck its last circulating penny in November 2025, but pennies are still legal tender. Should the country make rounding of cash totals to the nearest nickel the rule?

meta.title: The Penny and Rounding
meta.resolution: Resolved: The United States should require cash purchases to be rounded to the nearest five cents.
meta.summary: The U.S. Mint struck its last circulating penny in November 2025, but pennies are still legal tender. Should the country make rounding of cash totals to the nearest nickel the rule?

background.p: The one-cent coin had cost more to make than it was worth for years: the Mint reported a cost of 3.69 cents per penny in fiscal year 2024, and 13.78 cents per nickel. On November 12, 2025, the Mint struck the final circulating pennies in Philadelphia. The Mint said the penny remains legal tender and that businesses can still price goods in one-cent amounts. About 300 billion pennies were estimated to be in circulation.

With fewer new pennies reaching stores, some businesses have begun rounding cash totals. No federal law yet sets how rounding should work. Other countries offer examples: Canada stopped distributing pennies in 2013 and rounds cash totals (not card payments) to the nearest five cents, and the United States itself retired the half-cent coin in 1857.
Economists have studied whether rounding would cost shoppers money. Their results differ; see below.

disputed.q: Would rounding to the nearest five cents cost shoppers money?
positions: One study (Lombra, 2001) estimated rounding would cost consumers about $600 million a year, because so many prices end in 99 cents and would round up.
Another (Whaples, 2007) found that once sales tax is added, final totals are spread evenly, so rounding up and down roughly cancels out.
A study of Canadian grocery prices (Cheung, 2018) found rounding about neutral for multi-item purchases but slightly costly for one- and two-item purchases.

terms.def: Money that must be accepted for paying debts. Pennies remain legal tender even though no more are being made for circulation.
Rounding totals ending in 1, 2, 6 or 7 cents down and those ending in 3, 4, 8 or 9 up, so ups and downs can balance.
The difference between a coin's face value and its cost to make. When a coin costs more than its face value, seigniorage is negative.
Households without a bank account, who are more likely to pay in cash.

aff.label: Affirmative
aff.stance: A clear national rounding rule protects shoppers and businesses now that new pennies aren't being made.

args.claim: A national rule prevents confusion and unfair rounding.
args.warrant: Without a rule, each store decides for itself, and some may always round up. One symmetric rule, the same everywhere, tells shoppers what to expect and stops quiet overcharging.
args.evidence: Canada's 2013 rounding guidelines (symmetric, cash only, applied to the total, not to each item) and reports of U.S. stores adopting different rounding practices after the last penny was struck.
args.response: The negative answers that a federal mandate is a heavy tool for a few cents, and that states, stores or market pressure can set fair practices without Congress.

args.claim: Rounding the total is roughly neutral for consumers.
args.warrant: Sales tax and multiple items scatter final totals evenly across all the cent endings, so rounding up and rounding down balance out over many purchases.
args.evidence: Whaples (2007, Eastern Economic Journal) on rounding with sales tax; the Canadian experience since 2013.
args.response: The negative points to Cheung's 2018 finding that one- and two-item purchases do cost consumers slightly, and those small purchases are common for people who pay cash.

args.claim: It finishes the job of retiring a coin that costs more than it's worth.
args.warrant: Pennies cost several times their face value to make and slow down cash transactions. A rounding rule lets the economy stop needing pennies, so the old supply doesn't have to keep circulating.
args.evidence: U.S. Mint unit-cost figures (3.69 cents per penny in FY2024); the Mint's 2025 announcement; the precedent of retiring the half-cent in 1857.
args.response: The negative replies that production has already stopped, so the savings are already captured; rounding adds nothing to them.

args.claim: Rounding saves time at the register.
args.warrant: Counting out pennies in change takes time for cashiers and customers; across billions of cash transactions, small delays add up.
args.evidence: Research summarized by the Richmond Fed noting the time cost of handling pennies, and studies of merchants choosing convenient prices to avoid coins.
args.response: The negative argues the time saved per purchase is tiny, and cash is a shrinking share of payments, so the benefit is small.

neg.label: Negative
neg.stance: A federal rounding mandate isn't needed, and it would fall hardest on people who rely on cash.

args.claim: Rounding can cost the people who most depend on cash.
args.warrant: Low-income and unbanked households pay in cash more often, and they often make small purchases of one or two items, where rounding is less likely to balance out.
args.evidence: Lombra (2001) on rounding costs; Cheung (2018) on one- and two-item purchases; FDIC surveys of unbanked households and their use of cash.
args.response: The affirmative answers that symmetric rounding on the total keeps any cost to pennies a year, and a national rule protects those households better than store-by-store rules would.

args.claim: Pennies are still legal tender, so there's no need to force rounding.
args.warrant: About 300 billion pennies are already in circulation. Stores can keep giving exact change while that supply lasts, and customers can choose to pay exactly.
args.evidence: The U.S. Mint's November 2025 statement that the penny remains legal tender and prices may stay in one-cent increments.
args.response: The affirmative replies that the old pennies are unevenly spread, sitting in jars, so stores still run short; a rule is needed for when they do.

args.claim: Rounding raises demand for the nickel, which costs even more to make.
args.warrant: If cash totals end in 0 or 5, stores need more nickels for change. The Mint loses more on each nickel than it did on each penny.
args.evidence: U.S. Mint FY2024 cost of 13.78 cents per nickel; analyses of coin demand after penny elimination.
args.response: The affirmative argues that rounding mostly replaces pennies with fewer coins overall, and that changes to the nickel's metal content can cut its cost.

args.claim: Congress doesn't need to set a rule for every store.
args.warrant: Businesses already compete on price and fairness; states regulate pricing practices; and a federal mandate creates a one-size rule that may not fit every kind of business.
args.evidence: State consumer-protection laws on pricing; the Mint's guidance leaving pricing to businesses; examples of voluntary store rounding policies.
args.response: The affirmative answers that money is a national matter, and fifty different state rules would confuse shoppers who cross state lines.

strawmen.strawman: They just want to take money from poor people's pockets.
strawmen.why: Supporters propose symmetric rounding of the total precisely to avoid a hidden charge, and argue it is roughly neutral.
strawmen.steelman: Now that pennies aren't being made, a single fair rule (round the total, symmetrically, cash only) is the best way to protect shoppers from inconsistent store practices.

strawmen.strawman: They want to ban pennies and make everyone throw them away.
strawmen.why: The resolution is about rounding totals; existing pennies would remain legal tender.
strawmen.steelman: Rounding lets stores operate without pennies while people who have them can still spend them.

strawmen.strawman: They're just nostalgic about Lincoln's face on a coin.
strawmen.why: Opponents' main concerns are cost to cash-dependent shoppers, nickel costs, and whether a federal mandate is needed.
strawmen.steelman: Rounding can cost low-income cash users on small purchases, and with pennies still legal tender, a federal mandate may be unnecessary.

strawmen.strawman: They think the government should keep losing money on every penny forever.
strawmen.why: Penny production has already ended; opponents are arguing about rounding rules, not about restarting production.
strawmen.steelman: The savings from ending production are already won; the question is whether mandatory rounding adds benefits that outweigh its costs.

weak.arg: Nobody uses cash anymore anyway.
weak.why: Millions of Americans still use cash, and the people who do are the ones this policy affects most. Saying they don't matter weakens your own case.

weak.arg: Rounding never costs anyone a single cent.
weak.why: Rounding up does cost a few cents on some purchases; the claim is that ups and downs balance over time. Overstating it invites an easy answer.

weak.arg: Rounding will cost families hundreds of dollars a year.
weak.why: Even the study with the highest estimate works out to a few cents per person per week. Exaggerating the cost hurts your credibility.

weak.arg: Getting rid of the penny will lead to getting rid of all cash.
weak.why: That's a slippery slope with no evidence for the later steps.

aff: Does your rule round each item or the total?
What happens on a one-item purchase that ends in 9 cents?
Would card payments be rounded too?
If stores still have pennies, must they round anyway?
neg: If no rule exists, what stops a store from always rounding up?
Isn't the penny supply in stores running down now that production has stopped?
How much would rounding cost a typical cash shopper in a year?
Would fifty different state rules be easier for shoppers?

items.title: Required Personal Finance Class
items.subtitle: policy · beginner
items.body: Most states now require some personal finance instruction before graduation. Should every high school require a full, stand-alone course?

meta.title: Required Personal Finance Class
meta.resolution: Resolved: High schools should require a semester-long personal finance course for graduation.
meta.summary: Most states now require some personal finance instruction before graduation. Should every high school require a full, stand-alone course?

background.p: According to the Council for Economic Education, as reported by Education Week in June 2026, 39 states have passed laws requiring personal finance instruction for high school graduation, up from 8 in 2021. Thirteen of those states let the material be embedded in another course, such as economics, rather than taught as a stand-alone class.

Studies summarized by Education Week found that rigorous requirements in Georgia and Texas were followed by higher credit scores and fewer delinquencies among young adults, and that stand-alone courses improved credit scores through age 34, while embedded approaches showed no measurable effect. Obstacles include underfunding, shortages of trained teachers, and requirements that are delayed or watered down before taking effect.

disputed.q: Do personal finance courses change behavior?
positions: Recent studies of strong, stand-alone requirements find better credit scores and borrowing choices years later.
Older research found weak effects from financial education in general, and effects depend heavily on how a course is taught.

terms.def: A full course devoted to personal finance.
Personal finance taught as a unit inside another course, such as economics or math.
A number lenders use to judge how likely someone is to repay debt.
Falling behind on required debt payments.

aff.label: Affirmative
aff.stance: Every graduate should leave high school knowing how to budget, borrow, save and avoid costly mistakes.

args.claim: Stand-alone courses improve financial outcomes.
args.warrant: Students who learn how credit, interest and budgeting work make better choices when they get their first card, loan or paycheck.
args.evidence: Studies summarized by Education Week (2026): higher credit scores and fewer delinquencies in Georgia and Texas; credit benefits through age 34 from stand-alone courses.
args.response: The negative answers that results depend on strong teachers and funding, which many states lack.

args.claim: Young adults face big financial decisions right away.
args.warrant: Within months of graduating, many students choose student loans, sign leases or get credit cards; a mistake can follow them for years.
args.evidence: Research on student borrowing choices summarized by Education Week; data on young adults' debt.
args.response: The negative replies that families, colleges and banks also teach these skills at the moment they're needed.

args.claim: A required course reaches students whose families can't teach it.
args.warrant: Students from families with financial experience learn at home; a requirement gives everyone the same start.
args.evidence: Surveys of financial knowledge by family income; Education Week on equity arguments.
args.response: The negative argues that a weak course doesn't close gaps, and resources would be better spent on strong optional courses.

args.claim: Embedded units don't work as well.
args.warrant: When finance is squeezed into another course, it often gets little time; only a stand-alone course guarantees real instruction.
args.evidence: Findings that only 39% of students in embedded states receive any personal finance instruction, and that embedded approaches show no measurable effect.
args.response: The negative answers that better embedded units, not a new requirement, could fix this.

neg.label: Negative
neg.stance: A new semester requirement crowds a full schedule and depends on resources many schools lack.

args.claim: Schedules are already full.
args.warrant: Every new graduation requirement displaces something else, such as electives, arts, career courses or advanced classes.
args.evidence: State graduation requirements and course-load data; school counselors' reports on scheduling.
args.response: The affirmative answers that few subjects are as directly useful to every student.

args.claim: Many schools lack trained teachers and funding.
args.warrant: A required course taught by an untrained teacher with no materials may do little, as weak programs have shown.
args.evidence: Education Week on underfunded mandates and teacher shortages.
args.response: The affirmative replies that funding and training should come with the requirement, as in the states with strong results.

args.claim: Effects depend on quality, not the mandate.
args.warrant: The good results come from rigorous, well-supported programs; mandating a course without those conditions may not repeat them.
args.evidence: Research distinguishing rigorous requirements from weak ones; older studies finding small effects of financial education.
args.response: The affirmative argues the mandate is what creates the course, and quality can follow.

args.claim: Some topics are best learned when needed.
args.warrant: Lessons on mortgages or retirement accounts may be forgotten by the time students use them; timely help works better.
args.evidence: Research on "just-in-time" financial education; findings that knowledge fades without use.
args.response: The affirmative replies that many key decisions (loans, credit cards) come right after high school.

strawmen.strawman: They think one class will make every teenager rich.
strawmen.why: Supporters argue for better credit and borrowing outcomes, which studies have measured.
strawmen.steelman: Stand-alone personal finance courses lead to better credit and borrowing decisions, reaching students whose families can't teach these skills.

strawmen.strawman: They don't think money skills matter.
strawmen.why: Opponents agree the skills matter but question a mandate without resources.
strawmen.steelman: A semester requirement crowds full schedules, and without trained teachers and funding it won't deliver the results strong programs show.

weak.arg: Nobody learns about money anywhere else.
weak.why: Families, jobs and banks teach many skills; overstatement invites easy answers.

weak.arg: Kids can just watch videos online.
weak.why: Online quality varies widely, and research on structured courses shows real effects.

aff: What would students drop to make room?
Who would teach it, and with what training?
Do embedded units ever work?
neg: What did studies find about stand-alone courses and credit scores?
When do students make their first big financial decisions?
How should students without family help learn these skills?

items.title: Phones in School
items.subtitle: policy · beginner
items.body: Most states now require schools to ban or restrict student phones. Should the ban cover the whole day, "bell to bell," including lunch and passing periods?

meta.title: Phones in School
meta.resolution: Resolved: Schools should ban student cell phones for the entire school day.
meta.summary: Most states now require schools to ban or restrict student phones. Should the ban cover the whole day, "bell to bell," including lunch and passing periods?

background.p: As of spring 2026, at least 37 states and the District of Columbia required school districts to ban or restrict student phone use, according to reporting by the Associated Press and The 74. Policies range from "off and away" during class to bell-to-bell bans in which phones are locked in pouches or lockers all day.

A large study published by the National Bureau of Economic Research in 2026, co-led by Stanford economist Thomas Dee and using data from about 4,600 schools that used lockable pouches, found average effects on test scores close to zero over the first three years. Suspensions rose about 16% in the first year and returned to normal by the third. Student well-being dipped in the first year and was above its starting level by the third. Teachers reported personal phone use in class falling from 61% to 13% under bell-to-bell bans.

disputed.q: Do phone bans raise achievement?
positions: The largest U.S. study to date found average test-score effects close to zero in the first three years, with some newer schools seeing gains.
Supporters point to studies from other countries and to large drops in classroom phone use, and argue benefits may take time to appear.

terms.def: Phones are put away for the whole school day, including lunch and passing periods.
Phones must be silent and out of sight during class but may be used at other times.
A locking pouch students keep with them; it is unlocked at the end of the day.

aff.label: Affirmative
aff.stance: A full-day ban gives students hours of focus and face-to-face time that a class-only rule can't.

args.claim: A full-day ban cuts phone use far more than class-only rules.
args.warrant: When phones are allowed at lunch and between classes, students keep checking them, and notifications pull attention back into class. Locking them away removes the temptation.
args.evidence: The 2026 NBER study's teacher surveys (phone use in class fell from 61% to 13% under bell-to-bell bans); device-ping data dropping by about 30% by year three.
args.response: The negative answers that less phone use hasn't yet shown up as higher test scores, so the benefit is unproven.

args.claim: Students' well-being improves over time.
args.warrant: Without the constant pull of social media during the day, students talk to each other more and face less online conflict at school.
args.evidence: The same study's finding that well-being dipped in year one but rose above baseline by year three; surveys of students and teachers in ban schools.
args.response: The negative points out that the first-year dip and rise in suspensions are real costs, and later gains may reflect other changes.

args.claim: Clear, simple rules are easier to enforce.
args.warrant: A class-only rule means teachers argue with students all day about whether a phone is out. One rule for the whole day removes the gray areas.
args.evidence: Teacher surveys and union statements supporting full-day policies; district reports on enforcement time.
args.response: The negative replies that the 2026 study found suspensions rose in the first year, so strict rules can also create more conflict.

args.claim: Schools can meet safety and family needs another way.
args.warrant: Parents can reach students through the school office, and students with medical needs can be given exceptions, so a full ban need not cut off emergencies.
args.evidence: State laws with exceptions for medical devices and emergencies; school emergency-communication plans.
args.response: The negative argues that in an emergency, parents want direct contact, and office lines can be overwhelmed.

neg.label: Negative
neg.stance: Phones should be put away in class, but a full-day ban costs too much for too little proven gain.

args.claim: The evidence for full-day bans is not yet strong.
args.warrant: A rule affecting millions of students should show clear results. The largest U.S. study found test-score effects close to zero in the first three years.
args.evidence: The 2026 NBER study of about 4,600 schools (Dee and colleagues), as reported by AP and The 74.
args.response: The affirmative answers that the same study found big drops in phone use and later gains in well-being, and achievement effects may take longer.

args.claim: Families want to reach their children.
args.warrant: Parents use phones to coordinate rides, changes in plans and emergencies. Locking phones away all day removes that link.
args.evidence: Parent surveys on school phone policies; reports from districts debating emergency communication.
args.response: The affirmative replies that the school office and exceptions handle real needs, and that phones can distract students during an emergency.

args.claim: Teens need to learn to manage phones, not just be separated from them.
args.warrant: Adults must manage devices at work and home. Allowing phones at lunch while banning them in class teaches self-control that a total ban skips.
args.evidence: Digital-citizenship curricula; arguments from educators favoring class-only policies.
args.response: The affirmative answers that self-control is easier to learn with fewer temptations, and teens still have phones before and after school.

args.claim: Strict bans can raise discipline problems at first.
args.warrant: Enforcement creates confrontations, and suspensions take students out of class, which hurts learning.
args.evidence: The 2026 study's finding of a roughly 16% rise in suspensions in the first year.
args.response: The affirmative points out that the same study found the increase disappeared by the third year.

strawmen.strawman: Ban supporters think phones are evil and want to take them away from teenagers.
strawmen.why: Supporters focus on the school day, not on teens' phone use at home.
strawmen.steelman: During school hours, a simple full-day ban sharply cuts phone use and, over time, appears to improve student well-being.

strawmen.strawman: Opponents want kids scrolling social media during math class.
strawmen.why: Most opponents support putting phones away in class; they object to full-day bans.
strawmen.steelman: Class-time rules capture most of the benefit; a full-day ban adds costs for families and discipline without proven gains in learning.

weak.arg: Phone bans will raise test scores right away.
weak.why: The largest study found no average test-score effect in the first years. Claim what the evidence supports.

weak.arg: Students need phones to learn.
weak.why: Schools provide laptops or tablets for schoolwork; personal phones aren't required for learning.

aff: What did the largest study find about test scores?
How would a parent reach a child in an emergency?
Would your ban cover lunch? Why?
neg: Should phones be put away during class?
What did the study find about phone use in class under full-day bans?
How would teachers enforce a class-only rule?
