items.title: Plastic Bag Bans
items.subtitle: policy · beginner
items.body: Many states and cities ban thin plastic shopping bags. Research shows bans cut plastic bag litter but can increase paper and trash-bag use. Is a ban the best policy?

meta.title: Plastic Bag Bans
meta.resolution: Resolved: States should ban single-use plastic shopping bags.
meta.summary: Many states and cities ban thin plastic shopping bags. Research shows bans cut plastic bag litter but can increase paper and trash-bag use. Is a ban the best policy?

background.p: California banned single-use plastic grocery bags statewide in late 2016, after 139 of its cities and counties had passed local bans, and many other states and cities have followed with bans or fees. Economist Rebecca Taylor (University of Sydney) and colleagues studied California's local bans and found they cut about 40 million pounds of plastic bag trash a year. But shoppers bought more small trash bags (sales of 4-gallon bags rose 120%), so about 30% of the plastic saved came back as thicker garbage bags, and paper bag use rose by about 80 million pounds a year.

Life-cycle studies complicate the picture. A 2011 U.K. government study found a cotton tote must be reused 131 times to beat a plastic grocery bag on climate impact, and a Danish government study counting more kinds of environmental harm put the figure for an organic cotton bag far higher. Taylor's research also found that a small fee on bags encouraged reusable bags about as effectively as a ban.

disputed.q: Are bans better for the environment overall?
positions: Bans clearly reduce plastic bag litter, which harms wildlife and waterways and doesn't biodegrade.
When shoppers switch to paper or buy more trash bags, total greenhouse gas emissions can rise; the answer depends on what you measure.

terms.def: A thin bag meant to be used once, usually given out at checkout.
A study of a product's environmental effects from production to disposal.
A small charge for each bag, meant to encourage reusable bags.
When banning one product shifts use to a substitute, such as thicker trash bags.

aff.label: Affirmative
aff.stance: Thin plastic bags cause lasting litter and harm; a ban removes them effectively.

args.claim: Bans sharply cut plastic bag waste.
args.warrant: When stores can't give out thin bags, shoppers bring their own or use fewer, removing millions of pounds of plastic each year.
args.evidence: Taylor's research: about 40 million pounds a year less plastic bag trash in California cities with bans.
args.response: The negative answers that about 30% of that came back as trash bags, and paper use rose sharply.

args.claim: Plastic bags are an especially harmful kind of litter.
args.warrant: Light bags blow into waterways and oceans, tangle wildlife, clog drains and break into small pieces that last for many years.
args.evidence: Litter surveys and studies of plastic debris; Taylor's point that bans reduce nonbiodegradable litter.
args.response: The negative replies that better litter control and recycling target the problem without banning a useful product.

args.claim: A clear rule is simple for stores and shoppers.
args.warrant: One statewide rule avoids a patchwork of city laws and quickly changes habits.
args.evidence: California's move from 139 local bans to a statewide law.
args.response: The negative argues that a fee is just as simple and leaves more choice.

args.claim: Habits change, and reusable bags become normal.
args.warrant: Once people get used to bringing bags, the change sticks, reducing all kinds of disposable bags over time.
args.evidence: Studies of reusable bag use after bans and fees.
args.response: The negative replies that cotton totes must be reused many times to beat plastic, and many aren't.

neg.label: Negative
neg.stance: Bans shift waste to paper and trash bags; fees or other policies work as well with fewer side effects.

args.claim: Substitutes cancel much of the benefit.
args.warrant: Shoppers who used grocery bags for trash or pet waste buy thicker plastic bags instead, and many switch to paper.
args.evidence: Taylor: small trash-bag sales up 120%, about 30% of plastic savings offset, and about 80 million pounds more paper waste per year.
args.response: The affirmative answers that total plastic still falls, and paper breaks down instead of persisting as litter.

args.claim: Alternatives can be worse for the climate.
args.warrant: Paper and cotton bags take more energy and resources to make; unless reused many times, they can cause more emissions.
args.evidence: The 2011 U.K. study (131 uses for a cotton tote); the Danish government study.
args.response: The affirmative replies that sturdy plastic reusable bags beat thin bags after a modest number of uses.

args.claim: Fees work about as well as bans.
args.warrant: A small charge nudges most shoppers to bring bags while letting those who need one buy it, avoiding the trash-bag shift.
args.evidence: Taylor's research finding a small fee as effective as a ban in encouraging reusable bags.
args.response: The affirmative argues fees can be paid without thought by some shoppers, so bans cut use more reliably.

args.claim: Bans can burden low-income shoppers.
args.warrant: Paying for reusable bags or paper bag fees adds costs for families on tight budgets.
args.evidence: Analyses of bag-policy costs by income; programs giving free reusable bags.
args.response: The affirmative replies that the costs are small and programs can provide free bags.

strawmen.strawman: Ban supporters think banning bags will save the oceans.
strawmen.why: Supporters argue that bans cut a particularly harmful form of litter, not that they solve ocean plastic alone.
strawmen.steelman: Bans remove millions of pounds of plastic bag waste and a persistent, harmful kind of litter, and quickly change habits.

strawmen.strawman: Opponents don't care about pollution.
strawmen.why: Opponents point to evidence that bans shift waste and that fees work as well.
strawmen.steelman: Bans shift waste to paper and trash bags and can raise emissions; a fee achieves similar results with fewer side effects.

weak.arg: Paper bags are always better for the environment.
weak.why: Life-cycle studies find paper often has higher climate impact unless reused.

weak.arg: Reusable bags spread disease, so bans are dangerous.
weak.why: Washing bags addresses hygiene; this isn't a strong argument against bag policy.

aff: What happened to trash-bag sales after bans?
How many times must a cotton tote be reused to beat a plastic bag?
Would a fee work as well?
neg: How much plastic bag trash did California's bans eliminate?
Does paper break down in the environment faster than plastic?
Would you support a fee on both paper and plastic bags?

items.title: Ranked-Choice Voting
items.subtitle: policy · advanced
items.body: Voters rank candidates in order; if no one wins a majority, last-place candidates are eliminated and their votes move to the next choice. Maine and Alaska use it statewide. Should more states?

meta.title: Ranked-Choice Voting
meta.resolution: Resolved: States should adopt ranked-choice voting for statewide elections.
meta.summary: Voters rank candidates in order; if no one wins a majority, last-place candidates are eliminated and their votes move to the next choice. Maine and Alaska use it statewide. Should more states?

background.p: In **ranked-choice voting** (RCV, or instant-runoff voting) voters rank candidates. If no one gets a majority of first choices, the last-place candidate is eliminated and those ballots count for their next choice, repeating until someone has a majority. Maine adopted it in 2018 for many state and federal races; Alaska also uses it. Most U.S. use is in nonpartisan city elections. In Maine's 2018 Second District race, the first-round leader lost after the second round, and court challenges to the system failed.

Research summarized by political scientists David Kimball and Joseph Anthony in 2026 found RCV lets voters express fuller preferences, can attract more candidates and is associated with less negative campaigning in cities, but adds complexity, with some evidence of voter confusion (especially in disadvantaged communities), and generally little change in turnout. Several states have banned RCV, and repeal efforts have appeared where it is used.

disputed.q: Does RCV make campaigns more civil?
positions: Surveys in cities using RCV report less negative campaigning, since candidates seek second-choice votes.
Negative campaigning has increased in Maine since adoption, and effects may differ for partisan statewide races.

terms.def: Voters rank candidates; the weakest are eliminated round by round until one has a majority.
The candidate with the most votes wins, even without a majority.
A candidate who draws votes from a similar candidate, helping a third candidate win.
When all of a voter's ranked candidates are eliminated, so the ballot no longer counts in later rounds.

aff.label: Affirmative
aff.stance: Ranked-choice voting gives voters more choice and ensures winners have majority support.

args.claim: Winners need majority support.
args.warrant: Under plurality voting, a candidate can win with far less than half when votes split; RCV continues counting until someone has a majority of remaining ballots.
args.evidence: Examples of plurality winners with minority support; Maine's 2018 results.
args.response: The negative answers that with exhausted ballots, the "majority" is only of ballots still counting, not of all voters.

args.claim: It ends the spoiler problem.
args.warrant: Voters can rank a third-party favorite first without fear of helping their least-favorite candidate win.
args.evidence: Research finding increased support for third-party candidates under RCV.
args.response: The negative replies that spoiler effects can still occur in some RCV elections, and third parties rarely win.

args.claim: Campaigns can become more positive.
args.warrant: Candidates want to be voters' second choice, so attacking rivals' supporters is risky.
args.evidence: Studies of cities using RCV reporting less negativity and more satisfaction.
args.response: The negative points out that negativity increased in Maine's partisan races, so city results may not carry over.

args.claim: It saves the cost of separate runoff elections.
args.warrant: States that require majorities otherwise hold second elections, which cost money and often have low turnout.
args.evidence: Costs and turnout of runoff elections in states that use them.
args.response: The negative replies that RCV has its own costs for equipment, counting and voter education.

neg.label: Negative
neg.stance: Ranked-choice voting adds complexity and confusion without clear improvements.

args.claim: It's more complex for voters and officials.
args.warrant: Ranking many candidates and following multi-round counts is harder; confused voters rank fewer candidates and trust the results less.
args.evidence: Studies of voter confusion under RCV, especially in disadvantaged communities, summarized by Kimball and Anthony.
args.response: The affirmative answers that most voters report understanding RCV, and education reduces confusion.

args.claim: Results take longer and can seem less transparent.
args.warrant: Ballots must be collected centrally for later rounds, delaying results, and come-from-behind wins can make losers' supporters distrust the outcome.
args.evidence: Tabulation timelines in RCV jurisdictions; repeal efforts after unexpected outcomes.
args.response: The affirmative replies that delays are short and the rules are public before the election.

args.claim: Exhausted ballots can leave voters out of the final count.
args.warrant: Voters who don't rank all candidates may have no say in the final round, so the winner's "majority" may not be a majority of all voters.
args.evidence: Studies of ballot exhaustion in RCV elections.
args.response: The affirmative argues that voters in a separate runoff can also sit out, and exhaustion reflects voters' own choices.

args.claim: Turnout and outcomes change little.
args.warrant: If RCV doesn't raise turnout or change who wins much, its costs and complexity aren't justified.
args.evidence: Research finding little turnout change after adoption.
args.response: The affirmative replies that the benefits are in voter choice and majority support, not turnout.

strawmen.strawman: They want to rig elections for their side.
strawmen.why: Supporters argue for majority winners and ending spoilers, which can help any party.
strawmen.steelman: RCV ensures winners have majority support among ballots counted, lets voters back third-party favorites without spoiling, and can reduce negative campaigning.

strawmen.strawman: They think voters are too dumb to count to three.
strawmen.why: Opponents cite measured confusion, delays and exhausted ballots, not voters' intelligence.
strawmen.steelman: RCV adds complexity that confuses some voters, delays results and can exclude exhausted ballots, without clearly improving turnout or outcomes.

weak.arg: RCV will end polarization.
weak.why: Evidence on polarization is limited; Maine has seen more negativity, not less.

weak.arg: RCV is unconstitutional because it violates one person, one vote.
weak.why: Courts, including in Maine, have rejected this argument.

aff: What happens to a ballot whose ranked candidates are all eliminated?
Has negative campaigning gone down in Maine?
How long do RCV counts take?
neg: What happens under plurality when two similar candidates split the vote?
How much do separate runoff elections cost?
Did courts uphold Maine's system?

items.title: Federalists vs Anti-Federalists, 1787–88
items.subtitle: policy · advanced
items.body: After the Constitutional Convention, Americans argued for months in newspapers and state conventions about whether to adopt the new Constitution. The Federalists won, but the Anti-Federalists won the Bill of Rights.

meta.title: Federalists vs Anti-Federalists, 1787–88
meta.resolution: Historical question (1787–88): Should the states ratify the proposed Constitution?
meta.summary: After the Constitutional Convention, Americans argued for months in newspapers and state conventions about whether to adopt the new Constitution. The Federalists won, but the Anti-Federalists won the Bill of Rights.

background.p: In September 1787 the Constitutional Convention in Philadelphia proposed a new Constitution to replace the Articles of Confederation, under which the national government could not tax, regulate trade between states, or enforce its decisions well. The Constitution would take effect once nine state conventions ratified it.

Supporters, called **Federalists**, made their case in essays such as *The Federalist*, written by Alexander Hamilton, James Madison and John Jay under the name Publius. Opponents, the **Anti-Federalists**, wrote under names like Brutus, Cato and the Federal Farmer, warning that the new government would be too powerful and too distant from the people, and that the Constitution lacked a bill of rights. New Hampshire became the ninth state to ratify in June 1788. Several states ratified while recommending amendments, and the First Congress proposed the Bill of Rights in 1789; it was ratified in 1791.

terms.def: The first U.S. constitution (in effect from 1781), which created a weak national government.
Formal approval; here, by state conventions.
Madison's argument in Federalist No. 10 that a large republic can better control factions.
The Constitution's rule that federal law is the supreme law of the land.
The first ten amendments, ratified in 1791.

aff.label: Federalists (ratify)
aff.stance: The Articles had failed; the Constitution creates an effective government with safeguards against abuse.

args.claim: The Articles of Confederation had failed.
args.warrant: Without power to tax or regulate commerce, Congress couldn't pay its debts, defend the country or stop states from fighting over trade.
args.evidence: Unpaid war debts, trade disputes among states, and Shays' Rebellion (1786–87) as described in The Federalist.
args.response: Anti-Federalists answered that the Articles could be amended to fix specific problems without creating a powerful new government.

args.claim: Separated powers and checks prevent tyranny.
args.warrant: Dividing power among three branches, each able to check the others, keeps any one from becoming dangerous.
args.evidence: The Federalist, especially Madison's essays on checks and balances.
args.response: Anti-Federalists replied that the Senate and presidency could combine into an aristocracy, and that checks among officials don't protect against all of them together.

args.claim: A large republic controls faction better.
args.warrant: In a large country, many interests make it hard for any one faction to form an oppressive majority.
args.evidence: Madison, Federalist No. 10.
args.response: Brutus argued that free republics had historically been small, and a distant government couldn't truly represent so many people.

args.claim: The federal government's powers are listed and limited.
args.warrant: The Constitution grants specific powers; what isn't granted isn't given, so a bill of rights isn't needed and could even suggest the government had powers it lacked.
args.evidence: Hamilton's arguments in The Federalist (No. 84) against adding a bill of rights.
args.response: Anti-Federalists pointed to the Necessary and Proper and Supremacy Clauses, which they said could expand federal power without limit.

neg.label: Anti-Federalists (oppose or amend first)
neg.stance: The Constitution concentrates too much power far from the people and lacks a bill of rights.

args.claim: The new government would swallow the states.
args.warrant: Broad clauses like Necessary and Proper and the Supremacy Clause, plus federal power to tax, could let the national government override the states and grow without limit.
args.evidence: Brutus I (October 1787) and other Anti-Federalist essays.
args.response: Federalists answered that the federal government had only listed powers, and the states kept all others.

args.claim: A government over a huge country can't represent the people.
args.warrant: With few representatives for many people, Congress would be dominated by the wealthy and distant from ordinary citizens.
args.evidence: Brutus and the Federal Farmer on representation in a large republic.
args.response: Madison replied in Federalist No. 10 that a larger republic would choose better representatives and resist factions.

args.claim: Liberty needs a written bill of rights.
args.warrant: Without explicit protections for speech, religion, jury trial and against unreasonable searches, a powerful government could violate them.
args.evidence: State conventions' recommended amendments; Anti-Federalist essays.
args.response: Federalists replied that listing some rights might imply others weren't protected, though Madison later led the effort to add the Bill of Rights.

args.claim: Standing armies and federal taxing power threaten freedom.
args.warrant: A national government able to raise armies in peacetime and tax directly could enforce its will against the people.
args.evidence: Anti-Federalist writings on armies and taxation.
args.response: Federalists argued that a nation needs the power to defend itself and pay its debts, and that elected representatives control both.

strawmen.strawman: The Federalists wanted a king.
strawmen.why: Federalists argued for an elected, limited government with separated powers.
strawmen.steelman: The Articles had failed; the Constitution creates an effective but limited government whose separated powers and extended republic guard against tyranny.

strawmen.strawman: The Anti-Federalists wanted no national government at all.
strawmen.why: Most wanted a stronger union than the Articles provided, but with more limits and a bill of rights.
strawmen.steelman: Broad clauses and distant representation threatened the states and the people's liberty; a bill of rights and narrower powers were needed before ratifying.

weak.arg: Everyone important supported the Constitution, so it must be right.
weak.why: An appeal to authority; prominent figures such as Patrick Henry and George Mason opposed it.

weak.arg: The Constitution was illegal, so it should be ignored.
weak.why: A procedural complaint (the Convention exceeded its instructions) that doesn't answer the arguments about the government's design.

aff: What stops Congress from using the Necessary and Proper Clause to expand its powers?
Why not add a bill of rights now?
How many people will each representative represent?
neg: How would you pay the war debts under the Articles?
Can the Articles be amended without every state agreeing?
What does Federalist No. 10 say about large republics?

items.title: Taking Away Recess
items.subtitle: policy · beginner
items.body: Health guidance says students shouldn't lose recess for misbehavior or unfinished work, but many teachers use it as a consequence. Should schools stop?

meta.title: Taking Away Recess
meta.resolution: Resolved: Elementary schools should not take away recess as a punishment.
meta.summary: Health guidance says students shouldn't lose recess for misbehavior or unfinished work, but many teachers use it as a consequence. Should schools stop?

background.p: Guidance from the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention and SHAPE America (2017) recommends at least 20 minutes of recess a day for all K–12 students, and recommends that schools not exclude students from recess for discipline or academic reasons, nor use physical activity as punishment. Only a minority of states require daily recess, and data compiled for these materials found that about half of elementary schools prohibit or discourage withholding recess.

Illinois passed a law in 2021 requiring 30 minutes of daily unstructured recess in kindergarten through fifth grade and banning withholding it as discipline; other states and districts limit the practice. One survey reported by NBC News found 86% of U.S. teachers had reduced or taken away recess as a consequence. Teachers who use it say it is quick and effective, since recess is the time children want most, and some ask what else they can do about misbehavior. Both sides generally agree recess is valuable; the question is whether taking it away is an acceptable consequence.

terms.def: Keeping a student inside during part or all of recess, as a consequence or to finish work.
Responding to misbehavior by having students repair the harm and talk it through.

aff.label: Affirmative
aff.stance: Recess is part of a child's school day, not a reward, and taking it away backfires.

args.claim: Children need recess to learn well.
args.warrant: Breaks for play restore attention, so students return to class more focused. Removing the break makes the afternoon harder for the child and the class.
args.evidence: CDC and SHAPE America recess guidance (2017) summarizing links between recess and attention, behavior and achievement.
args.response: The negative answers that losing a few minutes now and then is very different from removing recess, and the research is about recess overall.

args.claim: The students most often kept in are often the ones who most need to move.
args.warrant: Restless or impulsive children are kept in more often, yet physical activity is part of what helps them manage behavior. The punishment can make the problem worse.
args.evidence: Teacher and pediatric reports; research on physical activity and attention in children.
args.response: The negative replies that teachers can choose other consequences for those students while still having the option for others.

args.claim: Recess teaches social skills that a classroom can't.
args.warrant: Playing, sharing equipment and settling disputes on the playground build cooperation and problem-solving.
args.evidence: CDC/SHAPE America materials citing social and emotional benefits; research on play and social development.
args.response: The negative argues that a child who just hurt someone may need time away from peers, and one missed recess doesn't erase these benefits.

args.claim: Better consequences exist.
args.warrant: Losing a classroom privilege, a talk with the teacher, a call home, or repairing the harm can teach the lesson without taking away exercise.
args.evidence: Districts and states that have banned withholding recess and use other consequences; guidance on restorative practices.
args.response: The negative answers that many alternatives are weaker or slower, and teachers need a consequence children feel right away.

neg.label: Negative
neg.stance: Teachers need simple, mild consequences, and a few minutes of lost recess is one of the gentlest.

args.claim: Teachers need consequences that work right away.
args.warrant: Young children connect a consequence to an action best when it comes soon. A few minutes off recess is immediate and easy to understand.
args.evidence: Teacher surveys on classroom management; research on the timing of consequences for young children.
args.response: The affirmative answers that other immediate consequences exist that don't take away exercise.

args.claim: Losing some recess is milder than many alternatives.
args.warrant: Detention, suspension or removal from class cost more learning time. Missing part of recess keeps the child in class.
args.evidence: Research on the harms of exclusionary discipline such as suspension; school discipline data.
args.response: The affirmative replies that the choice isn't only recess or suspension; many mild consequences don't cost activity.

args.claim: Sometimes recess is when the problem happens.
args.warrant: If a child hurt someone on the playground, a short break from the playground protects others and fits the behavior.
args.evidence: Playground incident reports; school safety guidance.
args.response: The affirmative answers that supervised alternatives (a different area, a walk with an adult) keep the child active while protecting others.

args.claim: Schools should decide, not a blanket rule.
args.warrant: Teachers know their students. A strict ban removes judgment in cases where a short loss of recess is the best response.
args.evidence: Teacher and principal associations' positions on local discretion; state laws that discourage but allow exceptions.
args.response: The affirmative replies that health guidance applies to all children, and judgment can be exercised among the many other consequences.

strawmen.strawman: They think kids should never face consequences.
strawmen.why: The affirmative supports consequences, just not ones that remove physical activity.
strawmen.steelman: Recess restores attention and builds social skills, and the children most often kept in need it most, so schools should use other consequences.

strawmen.strawman: They think recess doesn't matter.
strawmen.why: Most on the negative value recess; they defend a short loss as a mild consequence.
strawmen.steelman: A few minutes off recess is immediate, mild and keeps children in class, so teachers should keep it as an option.

weak.arg: Taking away recess is child abuse.
weak.why: Wildly overstated; it loses the judge at once.

weak.arg: Kids who misbehave don't deserve recess.
weak.why: Recess isn't a reward, and this ignores evidence about why children need it.

aff: What consequence would you use instead for a child who hit someone at recess?
Is losing five minutes of recess the same as losing all of it?
Should a child ever stay in to finish work?
neg: Do the children most often kept in tend to be the most restless?
What does CDC guidance say about withholding recess?
Could a teacher use a consequence that doesn't remove exercise?

items.title: Rent Control
items.subtitle: policy · intermediate
items.body: Rent control limits how fast landlords can raise rents. It protects tenants now, but many economists worry it reduces housing over time. Should cities use it?

meta.title: Rent Control
meta.resolution: Resolved: Cities should adopt rent control to address high housing costs.
meta.summary: Rent control limits how fast landlords can raise rents. It protects tenants now, but many economists worry it reduces housing over time. Should cities use it?

background.p: **Rent control** (or rent stabilization) limits rent increases for existing tenants, often to a set percentage a year. Most modern versions are milder than the strict rent freezes of the mid-1900s: they usually allow yearly increases tied to inflation and let rents reset when a tenant moves out. Several states, including California and Oregon, have statewide caps on rent increases, while many states forbid cities from adopting rent control.

A widely cited study of San Francisco's 1994 expansion of rent control (Diamond, McQuade and Qian, American Economic Review, 2019) found it did what it promised for covered tenants, who were about 20% more likely to stay in their homes and less likely to be displaced from the city. But landlords of covered buildings reduced rental housing supply by about 15%, mainly by selling to owner-occupants or redeveloping, which likely pushed up market rents for everyone else in the long run.

disputed.q: Do modern rent stabilization laws reduce housing supply?
positions: Studies of San Francisco and other places find landlords convert or sell units, shrinking the rental supply.
Supporters argue milder modern laws, with exemptions for new construction, avoid most of these effects, and that tenant stability is worth some cost.

terms.def: A milder form of rent control that allows regular, limited increases.
Letting a unit's rent reset to market rate when a tenant leaves.
Tenants being forced to move, often out of their neighborhood, by rising rents.
How much the amount of housing changes when prices change.

aff.label: Affirmative
aff.stance: Rent control keeps families in their homes and communities while longer-term fixes take hold.

args.claim: Rent control prevents displacement.
args.warrant: When rents jump suddenly, tenants must move, sometimes far from jobs, schools and family. Limiting increases lets them stay.
args.evidence: Diamond, McQuade and Qian (2019): covered tenants about 20% more likely to stay at their address.
args.response: The negative answers that the same study found a 15% drop in rental supply, raising rents for everyone not covered.

args.claim: Stable housing has wide benefits.
args.warrant: Children do better when they don't change schools often, and long-time residents keep neighborhood ties, local businesses and community groups going.
args.evidence: Research on residential stability and children's outcomes; studies of displacement's effects on health.
args.response: The negative replies that these benefits go only to current tenants, while newcomers and young families face higher rents.

args.claim: Modern rent stabilization avoids old mistakes.
args.warrant: Caps tied to inflation, exemptions for new buildings and rent resets between tenants protect landlords' returns and keep building going.
args.evidence: Design of state laws such as California's and Oregon's caps; analyses of exemptions for new construction.
args.response: The negative argues landlords still respond by converting or selling units, as the San Francisco study found even with exemptions.

args.claim: Building new housing takes years; tenants need help now.
args.warrant: Even if more construction is the long-term answer, people facing large increases this year can't wait a decade.
args.evidence: Data on permitting and construction timelines; local rent-increase data.
args.response: The negative replies that targeted rent assistance helps those in need now without discouraging supply.

neg.label: Negative
neg.stance: Rent control helps some current tenants but shrinks and worsens the housing supply, raising costs for others.

args.claim: Rent control reduces the supply of rental housing.
args.warrant: When rents are capped, owners have reasons to convert units to condos, sell to owner-occupants or redevelop, removing rentals from the market.
args.evidence: Diamond, McQuade and Qian (2019): about a 15% reduction in rental supply among covered buildings.
args.response: The affirmative answers that well-designed laws can restrict conversions and exempt new construction.

args.claim: It can raise rents for everyone else.
args.warrant: Fewer rentals on the market means more competition for the units that remain, pushing up rents for newcomers and young people.
args.evidence: The San Francisco study's conclusion that reduced supply likely raised market rents; economists' surveys on rent control.
args.response: The affirmative replies that rents were rising fast anyway, and the main cause is too little construction, which rent control doesn't prevent.

args.claim: It's poorly targeted.
args.warrant: Rent control helps whoever already holds a covered unit, regardless of income, while low-income newcomers get nothing.
args.evidence: Studies of who lives in rent-controlled units by income.
args.response: The affirmative replies that many covered tenants are lower-income long-time residents, and means tests could be added.

args.claim: Better tools address high costs.
args.warrant: Allowing more homes to be built and giving rent assistance to those in need lower costs without discouraging supply.
args.evidence: Research on zoning and housing costs; evaluations of housing vouchers.
args.response: The affirmative answers that zoning reform is slow and vouchers are underfunded, so tenants need protection now.

strawmen.strawman: Rent control supporters think landlords shouldn't make any money.
strawmen.why: Modern proposals allow regular increases and exempt new construction.
strawmen.steelman: Limiting sudden rent increases keeps families in their homes and communities, and modern designs protect landlords' returns while long-term fixes take hold.

strawmen.strawman: Opponents don't care if families get evicted.
strawmen.why: Many opponents favor rent assistance and building more housing.
strawmen.steelman: Rent control shrinks the rental supply and raises rents for everyone not covered; building more and targeted assistance help more people.

weak.arg: Rent control will make housing affordable for everyone.
weak.why: It limits increases for covered tenants; it doesn't lower rents generally.

weak.arg: Rent control destroys cities, like bombing.
weak.why: An exaggerated old quip; argue from the studies instead.

aff: What did the San Francisco study find about rental supply?
Would new buildings be exempt?
How would your plan help someone moving to the city?
neg: What did the same study find about covered tenants staying in their homes?
What should a family facing a 30% increase do this year?
How long does it take to build enough new housing?

items.title: School Uniforms
items.subtitle: policy · beginner
items.body: About one in five U.S. public schools requires uniforms. Do they improve learning and school life enough to justify the rule?

meta.title: School Uniforms
meta.resolution: Resolved: Public schools should require students to wear uniforms.
meta.summary: About one in five U.S. public schools requires uniforms. Do they improve learning and school life enough to justify the rule?

background.p: The share of U.S. public schools requiring uniforms grew from about 12% in 1999–2000 to about 22% in 2015–16, according to federal survey data reported by The Journalist's Resource. Uniforms are more common in elementary schools, in cities, and in schools serving low-income families. Many other schools have dress codes that limit certain clothing without requiring a uniform.

Research on uniforms is mixed. A study of a large urban district in the Southwest (Gentile and Imberman, 2012) found that adopting uniforms slightly improved attendance in the secondary grades and was linked to teachers staying longer in elementary schools, with no detectable effect on achievement or discipline. A 2021 Ohio State study of a national sample of elementary students (Ansari) found no consistent effect on behavior or social skills, and fifth graders in uniform schools reported a slightly weaker sense of belonging. Older national studies disagree about achievement, and researchers dispute how some of those data should be read.

disputed.q: Do uniforms improve achievement or behavior?
positions: Some studies find modest benefits, such as better attendance in the upper grades or teachers reporting a calmer climate.
Others, using large national data sets, find no effect on achievement or behavior, and researchers disagree about how to read some of the data.

terms.def: Required clothing of set colors and styles, such as a navy polo and khaki pants.
Rules that forbid some clothing (for example, clothing with offensive words) without prescribing what to wear.
A rule letting families decline the uniform, sometimes with a reason such as religion or cost.

aff.label: Affirmative
aff.stance: Uniforms help schools focus on learning and ease pressures on students and families.

args.claim: Uniforms reduce visible differences in wealth.
args.warrant: When everyone wears the same clothes, students can't be ranked by brand names, and families feel less pressure to keep up with expensive fashion.
args.evidence: Surveys of parents and teachers at uniform schools; school district reports; studies of student perceptions such as Sanchez, Yoxsimer and Hill (2012).
args.response: The negative answers that students still see differences in shoes, phones, bags and hairstyles, so the pressure moves rather than disappears.

args.claim: Uniforms can improve attendance and school climate.
args.warrant: A shared look signals that school is a place for work, and simpler morning routines remove one reason to be late or stay home.
args.evidence: Gentile and Imberman (2012) on attendance gains in secondary grades and teacher retention after uniforms were adopted in a large urban district.
args.response: The negative replies that the same study found no effect on achievement or discipline, and a national study (Ansari, 2021) found no consistent behavior benefits.

args.claim: Uniforms make schools safer and easier to supervise.
args.warrant: Staff can spot visitors who don't belong on campus, and uniforms remove clothing that signals gang membership or causes conflict.
args.evidence: School safety guidance and principal reports; teacher surveys such as Wade and Stafford (2003) finding teachers at uniform schools perceived less gang presence.
args.response: The negative argues that safety depends on supervision and building security, and that a dress code can ban gang-related clothing without requiring a uniform.

args.claim: Uniforms can save families money and time.
args.warrant: A few sets of uniform clothes can replace a larger school wardrobe, and children spend less time deciding what to wear.
args.evidence: Price comparisons of uniform sets versus typical back-to-school clothing; district uniform-assistance programs.
args.response: The negative cites research (Norum, Weagley and Norton, 1998) finding households didn't buy less regular clothing, so uniforms became an added cost.

neg.label: Negative
neg.stance: Uniform rules restrict students without delivering reliable benefits.

args.claim: The evidence for uniforms is weak.
args.warrant: If a rule restricts every student every day, it should have clear benefits. Large studies using national data find no consistent effect on achievement or behavior.
args.evidence: Ansari (2021, Early Childhood Research Quarterly) using a national sample of elementary students; Gentile and Imberman (2012) finding no effect on achievement or discipline; reviews noting that schools adopting uniforms often change other things at the same time.
args.response: The affirmative replies that national data can't tell good uniform policies from poor ones, and that careful district studies (like Gentile and Imberman) do find benefits.

args.claim: Uniforms limit students' self-expression.
args.warrant: Clothing is one of the main ways young people show who they are and practice making choices; schools should teach responsible choices, not remove them.
args.evidence: Student surveys at uniform schools (for example, Sanchez, Yoxsimer and Hill, 2012, where most students disliked uniforms); Ansari (2021) finding a weaker sense of belonging among fifth graders in uniform schools; Tinker v. Des Moines (1969) on student expression.
args.response: The affirmative answers that students keep many ways to express themselves (words, art, activities, accessories), and Tinker concerned a political message, not everyday fashion.

args.claim: Uniforms can add costs for families.
args.warrant: Families must buy uniforms on top of the clothes children wear outside school, and growing children need new sizes often.
args.evidence: Norum, Weagley and Norton (1998) on household clothing spending; district uniform price lists.
args.response: The affirmative replies that schools can supply uniforms to families who need help, and that a few uniform sets cost less than a full school wardrobe.

args.claim: Enforcing uniforms takes time away from learning.
args.warrant: When uniforms are required, staff must check them and discipline violations, and students can miss class for something unrelated to learning.
args.evidence: School discipline records on dress-code violations; research on time lost to discipline; student reports of detentions for uniform violations.
args.response: The affirmative argues enforcement is mostly simple once a uniform is routine, and a clear uniform is easier to enforce than a vague dress code.

strawmen.strawman: Uniform supporters want every kid to look like a robot.
strawmen.why: Supporters aim to reduce clothing pressures and distractions, not to erase personality.
strawmen.steelman: Uniforms reduce visible wealth differences and morning hassles, and some careful studies find better attendance, so they can help schools focus on learning.

strawmen.strawman: Uniform opponents just want kids to wear whatever they want, even offensive clothes.
strawmen.why: Most opponents support dress codes that forbid offensive or unsafe clothing; they object to requiring one outfit.
strawmen.steelman: A dress code can handle real problems; requiring uniforms adds cost and restrictions without consistent evidence of benefits.

weak.arg: Uniforms will end bullying.
weak.why: Bullying has many causes besides clothing. Claiming too much makes the real benefits look doubtful.

weak.arg: Uniforms violate the First Amendment.
weak.why: Courts have generally upheld school uniform policies; the free-expression argument is stronger as a matter of values than of law.

aff: Which studies show uniforms raise achievement, and how large is the effect?
Would your policy include help for families who can't afford uniforms?
Can students still show visible wealth through shoes, bags or phones?
neg: Do you support a dress code? How is it different from a uniform?
Can you name a study showing uniforms hurt learning?
If a school's parents vote for uniforms, should the school adopt them?

items.title: Self-Driving Cars
items.subtitle: policy · intermediate
items.body: Driverless taxis already carry passengers in several U.S. cities under state rules. Should national rules open roads everywhere to them?

meta.title: Self-Driving Cars
meta.resolution: Resolved: The federal government should allow fully driverless vehicles on public roads nationwide.
meta.summary: Driverless taxis already carry passengers in several U.S. cities under state rules. Should national rules open roads everywhere to them?

background.p: Companies such as Waymo operate fully driverless ride services in several U.S. cities, under a patchwork of state and local rules. Waymo's peer-reviewed analysis of about 7.1 million driverless miles in Phoenix, San Francisco and Los Angeles through October 2023 found about 85% fewer injury-reported crashes than a human-driver benchmark, while noting the benchmarks are imprecise and some comparisons were not statistically significant.

Setbacks have shaped the debate: in October 2023, California suspended Cruise's driverless permit after one of its cars dragged a pedestrian who had been struck by another vehicle, and the company later ended its robotaxi business. A frequently quoted claim that "94% of serious crashes are due to human error" comes from a 2015 federal memo that assigned the last event before a crash to the driver; the head of the National Transportation Safety Board called the statistic misleading in 2022, and the agency said it would reword it.

disputed.q: Are driverless cars safer than human drivers?
positions: Company data from millions of miles show far fewer injury crashes than human benchmarks in the cities studied.
Critics note the data come mostly from the companies, cover limited cities and conditions, and compare against imprecise human baselines.

terms.def: A vehicle that can drive itself in some or all conditions.
A vehicle that drives itself with no human needed, but only within certain areas or conditions.
The specific places and conditions where a self-driving system is designed to work.
When federal law overrides state or local law on the same subject.

aff.label: Affirmative
aff.stance: Driverless vehicles can save lives and widen mobility, and one national framework is better than a patchwork.

args.claim: Driverless cars may be safer than human drivers.
args.warrant: Automated systems don't drink, text, get tired or speed on purpose, which are major factors in serious crashes.
args.evidence: Waymo's peer-reviewed comparison (85% fewer injury-reported crashes over 7.1 million miles); NHTSA crash data on impairment and distraction.
args.response: The negative answers that the data come mostly from the company, from a few cities with good weather, and the benchmarks are imprecise.

args.claim: They can give mobility to people who can't drive.
args.warrant: Older adults, people with disabilities and people without cars could travel independently.
args.evidence: Census and transportation data on non-drivers; disability-advocacy reports on driverless service.
args.response: The negative replies that most driverless service is in dense cities, so rural non-drivers may not benefit for years.

args.claim: A national framework beats a patchwork.
args.warrant: When rules differ by state and city, companies can't scale, and safety standards vary. One federal standard can be stricter and clearer.
args.evidence: Comparisons of state AV laws; federal motor vehicle safety standards as a model.
args.response: The negative argues states and cities know their roads, and federal preemption could block local safety rules.

args.claim: Waiting has a cost in lives.
args.warrant: If a safer technology is held back, people continue to die in crashes it might have prevented.
args.evidence: NHTSA annual traffic death counts; safety analyses of AV performance.
args.response: The negative replies that rushing an unproven technology everywhere risks new kinds of crashes and public backlash.

neg.label: Negative
neg.stance: Driverless cars should expand step by step under local oversight until safety is proven across conditions.

args.claim: Safety isn't yet proven everywhere.
args.warrant: Results in sunny cities don't show how the cars handle snow, rural roads or unusual events, so national approval is premature.
args.evidence: Waymo's own note that benchmarks are imprecise and results limited to certain cities; reports on AV performance in rare situations.
args.response: The affirmative answers that the resolution can include conditions; federal approval can still require testing for each area.

args.claim: Failures can be new and serious.
args.warrant: Automated systems can fail in ways no human would, and accountability is unclear when no one is driving.
args.evidence: California's 2023 suspension of Cruise's permit after a pedestrian was dragged; NHTSA investigations of AV incidents.
args.response: The affirmative replies that regulators acted quickly, showing oversight works, and that human crashes are far more common.

args.claim: Local governments need control over their streets.
args.warrant: Cities manage traffic, emergency response and street use; nationwide permission could stop them from setting limits that fit local conditions.
args.evidence: City officials' complaints about AVs blocking emergency vehicles; state and city regulatory disputes.
args.response: The affirmative argues national safety rules can leave room for local traffic management.

args.claim: Jobs for millions of drivers are at stake.
args.warrant: Truck, taxi and delivery drivers could lose work quickly if driverless vehicles spread nationwide before workers can adjust.
args.evidence: Bureau of Labor Statistics data on driving occupations; labor union statements.
args.response: The affirmative replies that adoption will take years, and new jobs in maintenance and operations will appear.

strawmen.strawman: They want to let robots drive kids to school with no testing.
strawmen.why: Supporters favor national safety standards and point to millions of tested miles.
strawmen.steelman: Driverless cars appear far safer than human drivers where they operate, can help people who can't drive, and need one clear national framework.

strawmen.strawman: They're just afraid of new technology.
strawmen.why: Opponents point to limited data, real failures and the need for local control.
strawmen.steelman: Safety hasn't been shown across all conditions, failures can be new and serious, and cities need control, so expansion should be gradual and local.

weak.arg: 94% of crashes are caused by human error, so driverless cars will prevent 94% of crashes.
weak.why: The NTSB called that statistic misleading, and it doesn't follow that machines would avoid all those crashes.

weak.arg: Self-driving cars will be hacked and used as weapons.
weak.why: A speculative worst case without evidence; cybersecurity is a fair point, but argue it with evidence.

What happened with Cruise in 2023?
Would cities keep any say?
neg: What did Waymo's peer-reviewed study find about injury crashes?
How many people die on U.S. roads each year?
What evidence would convince you to allow driverless cars more widely?

items.title: Social Media Age Limits
items.subtitle: policy · intermediate
items.body: Australia now bans social media accounts for children under 16. Should the United States do the same?

meta.title: Social Media Age Limits
meta.resolution: Resolved: The United States should prohibit social media accounts for people under 16.
meta.summary: Australia now bans social media accounts for children under 16. Should the United States do the same?

background.p: In 2023, the U.S. Surgeon General issued an advisory on social media and youth mental health. It reported that up to 95% of teens use social media, that teens average about 3.5 hours a day, and that those spending more than three hours a day faced double the risk of poor mental health outcomes such as depression and anxiety symptoms. It said "we do not yet have enough evidence to determine if social media use is sufficiently safe" for young people, while also noting benefits such as connection for isolated youth.

In late November 2024, Australia passed a law making platforms such as TikTok, Instagram, Snapchat, Facebook, Reddit and X liable for fines of up to A$50 million if they systematically fail to keep children under 16 off their services, with the rule taking effect about a year later. The law relies on "age assurance" methods rather than requiring uploaded IDs. In the U.S., several states have passed age-related social media laws, and courts have blocked some of them, including Utah's 2023 law, after challenges from the tech industry group NetChoice.

disputed.q: Does social media cause poorer mental health in teens?
positions: Many studies find links between heavy use and depression and anxiety, and some experiments in which people cut back show improvements.
Other researchers say most studies show correlation, not cause, the average effects are small, and some teens benefit from online communities.

terms.def: Ways of checking or estimating a user's age, from ID uploads to estimates based on behavior or face scans.
Rules allowing minors to use a service only with a parent's permission.
The constitutional protection of speech, which courts have applied to online platforms and users, including minors.

aff.label: Affirmative
aff.stance: Young teens should not have social media accounts until they're older, just as other risky products have age limits.

args.claim: Heavy social media use is linked to poorer mental health in teens.
args.warrant: Early adolescence is a sensitive time for brain development and self-image. Platforms designed to maximize time and attention hit young teens especially hard.
args.evidence: The 2023 Surgeon General's advisory (double the risk of poor mental health above three hours a day); studies of social media use and depression and anxiety.
args.response: The negative answers that most of this evidence is correlational, the average effects are small, and some teens benefit.

args.claim: Individual families can't solve it alone.
args.warrant: When every classmate is on an app, one family's rule leaves a child left out. A law changes the norm for everyone, which no family can do.
args.evidence: Parent groups' pledges to delay smartphones; surveys of parents who feel pressure to allow accounts.
args.response: The negative replies that parental tools and community pledges can shift norms without government bans.

args.claim: Platforms should carry responsibility.
args.warrant: Companies have the technical ability to estimate ages. Putting the duty and the fines on platforms makes them design for it.
args.evidence: Australia's law placing fines on platforms rather than families; reports on platforms' age-estimation tools.
args.response: The negative argues that age checks threaten everyone's privacy, adults included.

args.claim: Other age limits show society accepts this kind of rule.
args.warrant: The law sets minimum ages for driving, tobacco and alcohol because some risks are too high for children; social media can be treated the same way.
args.evidence: Existing age laws; the Surgeon General's call for stronger safety standards and age minimums.
args.response: The negative replies that speech differs from products like tobacco; it is protected by the First Amendment.

neg.label: Negative
neg.stance: A ban is the wrong tool: it threatens privacy and free expression, is easy to evade, and cuts off benefits.

args.claim: Age checks threaten everyone's privacy.
args.warrant: To keep under-16s off, platforms must check the age of every user, which means collecting IDs or face scans from adults too and creating data that can leak.
args.evidence: Cato Institute analysis of age-verification systems quoted in PBS reporting; data breach records.
args.response: The affirmative answers that age-estimation methods can work without storing IDs, as Australia's law encourages.

args.claim: A ban raises serious free-speech problems.
args.warrant: Teens have speech rights too. Blocking access to major platforms cuts them off from news, art and political discussion.
args.evidence: Court rulings blocking state laws (for example, Utah's 2023 law) after NetChoice's challenges; First Amendment scholarship.
args.response: The affirmative replies that the law limits accounts, not viewing public information, and that a narrowly written law can pass review.

args.claim: Some teens depend on online communities.
args.warrant: Isolated teens, including those with disabilities or rare interests, find support and friends online that they can't find locally.
args.evidence: The Surgeon General's advisory noting benefits for marginalized youth; studies of online support communities.
args.response: The affirmative argues these teens can still use messaging and other supervised spaces, and are also among those most harmed.

args.claim: Bans are easy to get around and may push teens to riskier spaces.
args.warrant: Teens can lie about their age or use other apps and sites with fewer protections, so a ban may move use out of sight.
args.evidence: Reporting on enforcement questions about Australia's law; history of age-limit evasion online.
args.response: The affirmative replies that a rule doesn't have to be perfect to work; age limits on alcohol aren't perfect either, but they reduce use.

strawmen.strawman: They think the internet is evil and want to keep teens offline.
strawmen.why: Supporters target social media accounts for under-16s, not the internet as a whole.
strawmen.steelman: Heavy social media use is linked to poorer teen mental health, families can't change the norm alone, and a platform-enforced age limit makes the change for everyone.

strawmen.strawman: They don't care about teens' mental health; they just defend tech companies.
strawmen.why: Opponents raise privacy, free speech and the needs of isolated teens.
strawmen.steelman: Age checks would expose everyone's data, a ban raises free-speech problems, and it cuts isolated teens off from support while being easy to evade.

weak.arg: Social media is the only cause of teen depression.
weak.why: Mental health has many causes; claim what the evidence supports.

weak.arg: Teens will just get around it, so there's no point.
weak.why: Imperfect enforcement isn't a full answer; many age laws reduce harm despite evasion.

aff: How would a platform know a user's age without collecting IDs?
What happens to a 15-year-old who relies on an online support group?
Have courts upheld state laws like this?
neg: What does the Surgeon General's advisory say about teens who use social media more than three hours a day?
Can one family's rule work when every classmate has an account?
Should there be any age limit? If so, what?

items.title: Funding Space Exploration
items.subtitle: policy · intermediate
items.body: NASA's budget is about a third of one percent of federal spending, far below its Apollo-era peak. Should the country spend more on exploring space?

meta.title: Funding Space Exploration
meta.resolution: Resolved: The United States federal government should substantially increase funding for space exploration.
meta.summary: NASA's budget is about a third of one percent of federal spending, far below its Apollo-era peak. Should the country spend more on exploring space?

background.p: NASA's budget was about $24.9 billion in fiscal years 2024 and 2025 and about $24.4 billion in 2026, roughly 0.33 to 0.36% of all federal spending. At the height of the Apollo program in 1966, NASA's share peaked at about 4.4%.

NASA's work includes human spaceflight (the Artemis program to return astronauts to the Moon), robotic science missions, Earth-observing satellites and aeronautics research. Private companies now launch many cargo and crew missions under NASA contracts, which changes what public money buys. Supporters point to scientific discoveries, technology spinoffs, jobs and national leadership; critics point to cost overruns and to needs on Earth.

disputed.q: How large are the economic returns from space spending?
positions: Supporters cite studies of jobs, spinoff technologies and commercial space industries that grew from NASA programs.
Skeptics say returns are hard to measure and that the same money spent on research or programs on Earth might return as much or more.

terms.def: NASA's program to return astronauts to the Moon and prepare for Mars.
A technology developed for space that finds uses on Earth.
What else the same money could have bought.
The part of the federal budget Congress sets each year, as opposed to programs like Social Security that run automatically.

aff.label: Affirmative
aff.stance: Space exploration returns science, technology and leadership far beyond its small share of the budget.

args.claim: Space science answers big questions and helps life on Earth.
args.warrant: Satellites and probes study climate, weather, asteroids and the origins of the solar system; much of that knowledge can be gained no other way.
args.evidence: NASA Earth science missions and weather data; planetary defense tests; the Planetary Society's analyses of NASA science.
args.response: The negative answers that Earth-observing satellites and science can be funded without increasing human exploration, and the resolution asks for more overall.

args.claim: Space programs drive technology and industry.
args.warrant: Hard engineering problems push advances in materials, computing and medicine, and NASA contracts helped create a commercial launch industry.
args.evidence: NASA Spinoff publications; the growth of commercial launch companies under NASA contracts.
args.response: The negative replies that many spinoffs would likely have been invented anyway, and direct research funding is a more efficient way to get technology.

args.claim: Funding is small, so a meaningful increase is affordable.
args.warrant: At about a third of one percent of federal spending, even a large percentage increase is a small part of the budget.
args.evidence: NASA budget history (Wikipedia, Planetary Society); federal spending totals.
args.response: The negative argues that every program says it is small, and with large deficits, new spending must clear a high bar.

args.claim: Leadership in space matters for security and inspiration.
args.warrant: Other nations are expanding space programs; leading in space affects satellites, alliances and the rules for using the Moon, and it inspires students to study science.
args.evidence: Reports on international lunar programs; surveys of students and STEM interest; Defense Department reliance on space systems.
args.response: The negative replies that military and commercial space are funded separately, and inspiration is hard to measure.

neg.label: Negative
neg.stance: Space is valuable, but a substantial increase isn't the best use of limited public money right now.

args.claim: Urgent needs on Earth come first.
args.warrant: Money spent on rockets isn't spent on medical research, infrastructure or reducing the deficit, which may help more people sooner.
args.evidence: Federal budget data and deficit projections from the Congressional Budget Office; comparisons of returns on other research spending.
args.response: The affirmative answers that this is a false choice; NASA is a tiny share of spending, and cutting it would barely change other budgets.

args.claim: Big NASA programs often run over budget.
args.warrant: When programs repeatedly cost more and take longer than planned, more money may simply fund delays.
args.evidence: Government Accountability Office reports on NASA major projects and the Space Launch System; NASA Inspector General audits.
args.response: The affirmative replies that fixed-price commercial contracts are lowering costs, and more stable funding reduces delays.

args.claim: Private companies can do more of the work.
args.warrant: Commercial firms now launch cargo and crews and invest their own money, so public spending can focus on science while private money builds transportation.
args.evidence: NASA's commercial crew and cargo programs; private investment in launch companies.
args.response: The affirmative argues companies depend on NASA contracts, so cutting public money would shrink the commercial industry too.

args.claim: Robotic missions give more science per dollar.
args.warrant: Probes and telescopes can explore far more cheaply than human missions, which need life support and safety systems.
args.evidence: Cost comparisons of robotic and crewed missions; Planetary Society analyses of science budgets.
args.response: The affirmative replies that the resolution covers both, and human exploration achieves things robots can't, such as flexible fieldwork.

strawmen.strawman: They want to spend billions on rockets while people go hungry.
strawmen.why: Supporters argue space science helps people on Earth and costs a small share of the budget.
strawmen.steelman: At a third of one percent of federal spending, space exploration returns science, technology, industry and leadership that justify a larger investment.

strawmen.strawman: They think space exploration is a waste of time.
strawmen.why: Many on the negative support space science; they question a substantial increase now.
strawmen.steelman: With large deficits, cost overruns and growing private investment, a big increase in public space spending isn't the best use of limited funds.

weak.arg: We need to colonize Mars because Earth is doomed.
weak.why: Speculative and easy to answer; focus on near-term benefits.

weak.arg: NASA's budget could end world hunger.
weak.why: The numbers don't support it, and it's a false dilemma.

What do GAO audits say about NASA cost overruns?
Could private companies do some of this work?
neg: How much would cutting NASA's budget add to other programs?
Do weather forecasts rely on satellites?
Would you increase funding for NASA science while cutting human spaceflight?

items.title: Public Money for Stadiums
items.subtitle: policy · intermediate
items.body: Cities often help pay for stadiums to keep or attract teams. Most economists say the local economic payoff is small. Are there other reasons the spending is worth it?

meta.title: Public Money for Stadiums
meta.resolution: Resolved: Cities should not use public funds to build professional sports stadiums.
meta.summary: Cities often help pay for stadiums to keep or attract teams. Most economists say the local economic payoff is small. Are there other reasons the spending is worth it?

background.p: State and local governments have spent billions of dollars helping build stadiums and arenas for professional teams, through direct spending, bonds, tax breaks and infrastructure. Teams often seek new venues when leases end, and cities compete to keep or attract them.

Economists have studied these deals for decades and largely agree that the local economic benefits are small compared with the public cost: in a 2005 survey of American Economic Association members, 85% agreed governments should eliminate subsidies to professional sports, and in a 2017 University of Chicago panel of economists, 80% agreed stadium subsidies likely cost taxpayers more than the local economic benefits. Supporters respond that teams bring civic pride and quality-of-life benefits that economic studies don't fully capture, and that a stadium can anchor redevelopment of a neighborhood.

disputed.q: How much are a team's non-economic benefits worth to residents?
positions: Supporters cite civic pride, shared identity and studies showing residents value having a team.
Critics say these benefits are real but usually far smaller than the subsidies, and stadiums also bring traffic and other costs.

terms.def: Public money or tax breaks given to support a private business.
Spending at a stadium often replaces other local entertainment spending rather than adding new spending.
Something many people can enjoy at once, like civic pride, that markets may underprovide.
Money a government borrows and repays with interest over time.

aff.label: Affirmative
aff.stance: Stadium subsidies cost taxpayers far more than they return; private owners should pay.

args.claim: Studies find little local economic growth from stadiums.
args.warrant: Families have limited entertainment budgets; money spent at games is mostly money not spent at local restaurants, movies or bowling alleys, so total spending barely changes.
args.evidence: Decades of studies reviewed by economists such as John Charles Bradbury and Brad Humphreys; the 2017 University of Chicago economists' panel.
args.response: The negative answers that economic studies miss civic and quality-of-life benefits residents clearly value.

args.claim: The money has better uses.
args.warrant: Public dollars spent on a stadium could fund schools, roads, parks or lower taxes, which benefit more residents.
args.evidence: City budget comparisons; the size of recent stadium deals.
args.response: The negative replies that some stadium funding comes from visitor taxes and wouldn't otherwise be available for schools.

args.claim: Teams use the threat of moving to extract money.
args.warrant: Leagues limit the number of teams, so cities bid against each other, and team owners capture the public money.
args.evidence: Histories of team relocations and threats; economists' analyses of league structure.
args.response: The negative argues that a city that refuses may actually lose its team, and with it real civic value.

args.claim: Owners can pay for their own buildings.
args.warrant: Teams and leagues earn large revenues from media, tickets and sponsorships; privately financed stadiums show it can be done.
args.evidence: Examples of privately financed stadiums; team valuation data.
args.response: The negative replies that private financing is rare, and some cities have negotiated public returns such as revenue sharing.

neg.label: Negative
neg.stance: Cities can reasonably invest in stadiums for the civic value teams bring and for redevelopment.

args.claim: Teams bring civic value that money studies miss.
args.warrant: A team gives a city shared identity, pride and something to celebrate together; residents who never attend still enjoy following it.
args.evidence: Contingent-valuation studies of residents' willingness to pay for teams; surveys of civic pride.
args.response: The affirmative answers that economists who study this find these values are usually much smaller than the subsidies.

args.claim: A stadium can anchor redevelopment.
args.warrant: Well-planned districts with housing, shops and transit around a venue can revive underused areas that private investment alone wouldn't.
args.evidence: Case studies of mixed-use stadium districts; city development reports.
args.response: The affirmative replies that the record of such districts is mixed, and the same money could fund redevelopment directly.

args.claim: Visitors pay part of the cost.
args.warrant: Hotel and rental-car taxes collect money mostly from out-of-towners, so residents bear less of the cost.
args.evidence: Financing structures of recent stadium deals.
args.response: The affirmative answers that those taxes could fund other public needs, so they still have an opportunity cost.

args.claim: Cities can bargain for a fair deal.
args.warrant: Instead of refusing outright, cities can demand revenue sharing, community benefits and ownership of the building, getting real returns.
args.evidence: Stadium agreements with public revenue sharing or community benefit agreements.
args.response: The affirmative argues that with leagues limiting teams, cities rarely have the bargaining power to get fair terms.

strawmen.strawman: They hate sports and want teams to leave.
strawmen.why: Supporters of the resolution can love their teams and still want owners to pay for stadiums.
strawmen.steelman: Economists find stadiums return little local growth for their cost; public money has better uses, and owners can finance their own buildings.

strawmen.strawman: They want to hand billionaires free money.
strawmen.why: Defenders point to civic value, redevelopment and deals that share returns with the public.
strawmen.steelman: Teams bring civic value residents care about, stadiums can anchor redevelopment, visitors pay part of the cost, and cities can negotiate fair returns.

weak.arg: Stadiums never bring any benefit.
weak.why: Too absolute; the strongest argument is that benefits are small relative to cost.

weak.arg: A new stadium will create thousands of permanent jobs.
weak.why: Most stadium jobs are seasonal and part-time; economists' studies contradict large job claims.

aff: If your city refuses, and the team leaves, what does the city lose?
Do residents value a team even if they never attend?
What about stadiums funded by tourist taxes?
neg: What do surveys of economists say about stadium subsidies?
Why doesn't stadium spending add much to the local economy?
Would the team really leave? Where would it go?
