items.title: Standardized Tests in College Admissions
items.subtitle: policy · intermediate
items.body: Many colleges went test-optional during the pandemic; some, like Dartmouth and MIT, have brought requirements back. Should selective colleges require scores?

meta.title: Standardized Tests in College Admissions
meta.resolution: Resolved: Selective colleges should require applicants to submit SAT or ACT scores.
meta.summary: Many colleges went test-optional during the pandemic; some, like Dartmouth and MIT, have brought requirements back. Should selective colleges require scores?

background.p: During the COVID-19 pandemic, most selective colleges stopped requiring SAT or ACT scores. Since then, some have reinstated requirements. Dartmouth announced in February 2024 that it would require scores again, citing its own study that scores predicted academic success at Dartmouth better than high school grades and that test-optional policies had led some disadvantaged applicants with strong scores not to submit them. MIT had already reinstated its requirement.

Research disagrees about what predicts college success best. Opportunity Insights at Harvard found test scores predicted college performance at highly selective colleges better than high school grades, while also finding that wealthier students were far more likely to have very high scores. A 2020 study of about 55,000 Chicago Public Schools graduates (Allensworth and Clark) found high school GPA predicted college graduation about five times better than ACT scores, and that the ACT's predictive power varied from school to school.

disputed.q: Which predicts college success better, grades or test scores?
positions: Studies at highly selective colleges (Dartmouth, Opportunity Insights) find test scores add predictive power beyond grades, especially as grade inflation grows.
Studies across broader groups of colleges (such as Allensworth and Clark's Chicago study) find GPA predicts graduation better, and scores vary in meaning by high school.

terms.def: Applicants may choose whether to submit scores.
All applicants must submit scores (sometimes with exceptions).
The college doesn't consider scores even if submitted.
How well a measure forecasts later outcomes, such as college grades or graduation.
A rise in average grades without a matching rise in learning, which makes grades less informative.

aff.label: Affirmative
aff.stance: A common, objective measure helps selective colleges find talented students, including those from less advantaged backgrounds.

args.claim: Test scores add information grades can't.
args.warrant: High schools grade differently, and grade inflation compresses many students at the top. A common test lets colleges compare applicants on the same scale.
args.evidence: Dartmouth's 2024 internal study; Opportunity Insights research on selective colleges; College Board and ACT validity studies.
args.response: The negative replies that broader studies (Allensworth and Clark) find GPA predicts graduation better, and test scores vary in meaning by school.

args.claim: Requiring scores can help disadvantaged applicants.
args.warrant: Under test-optional rules, some students from under-resourced schools with good scores don't submit them, not knowing their scores would stand out in context.
args.evidence: Dartmouth's finding that many applicants who would have benefited didn't submit, and that under-resourced applicants with a 1400 were twice as likely to be admitted as others with the same score.
args.response: The negative answers that colleges can encourage submission without requiring it, and that requirements still deter students who can't access test prep.

args.claim: Without tests, other factors favor the wealthy even more.
args.warrant: If scores aren't used, colleges lean more on essays, recommendations and activities, which wealthier families can polish with paid help.
args.evidence: Dartmouth's argument that test-optional policies shift weight to counselor recommendations; research on extracurricular advantages of high-income students.
args.response: The negative replies that test scores themselves track family income closely, so tests don't remove the advantage.

args.claim: Tests help colleges place and support students.
args.warrant: Knowing a student's math and reading level helps advisers place them in the right courses and offer help early.
args.evidence: College placement research; university reports on using scores for advising.
args.response: The negative argues placement tests after admission do this better, without affecting who gets in.

neg.label: Negative
neg.stance: Colleges should be free to judge applicants without required tests, which reflect advantage as much as ability.

args.claim: High school grades predict college graduation better.
args.warrant: Grades reflect years of effort, persistence and study habits, which matter for finishing college, while one test day captures a narrower set of skills.
args.evidence: Allensworth and Clark (2020), Educational Researcher: GPA predicted graduation about five times better than ACT scores among Chicago graduates.
args.response: The affirmative answers that this study covered a broad group of colleges; at highly selective colleges, scores add power beyond grades.

args.claim: Scores reflect family advantages.
args.warrant: Wealthier students can pay for prep courses and retake tests, so scores partly measure opportunity rather than talent.
args.evidence: Opportunity Insights finding the wealthiest applicants far more likely to score 1500 or higher; College Board data on scores by family income.
args.response: The affirmative replies that the same research found low-income students with the same scores did just as well in college, so scores still identify talent.

args.claim: Requirements can discourage good applicants.
args.warrant: Students who test poorly or can't afford tests may not apply at all, shrinking the pool before admissions officers see them.
args.evidence: Application increases at colleges after going test-optional; surveys of students on why they apply where they do.
args.response: The affirmative answers that more applications don't mean more good admits, and Dartmouth found test-optional didn't increase low-income enrollment.

args.claim: Colleges should choose their own policies.
args.warrant: Colleges differ in mission and students. A blanket requirement prevents each from using the evidence that fits its own applicants.
args.evidence: The range of policies among selective colleges (required, optional, blind) and their stated reasons.
args.response: The affirmative replies that the resolution says what selective colleges *should* do, not that it must be imposed by law.

strawmen.strawman: Supporters think a single test score tells you everything about a person.
strawmen.why: Supporters argue scores add information alongside grades, essays and context, not replace them.
strawmen.steelman: With grades inflated and schools uneven, a common test adds useful information, and requiring it can help disadvantaged students with strong scores stand out.

strawmen.strawman: Opponents just want to make college easier to get into.
strawmen.why: Opponents argue grades predict graduation better and that tests reflect family advantage.
strawmen.steelman: Grades capture persistence and predict graduation well; required tests add a barrier that tracks family income, so colleges should be free to go without them.

weak.arg: Tests are the only fair way to compare students.
weak.why: Overstates the case and ignores income gaps in scores; the stronger claim is that tests add information.

weak.arg: Tests are biased, so they're useless.
weak.why: Research shows scores do predict college performance; the argument should be about how much and compared to what.

aff: What do studies outside highly selective colleges find?
How would students who can't afford test prep be helped?
Should colleges consider scores in the context of a student's school?
neg: How should colleges compare grades from very different high schools?
What did Dartmouth find about disadvantaged applicants under test-optional?
If grades are inflated, how should colleges tell top students apart?

items.title: Later School Start Times
items.subtitle: policy · beginner
items.body: Pediatricians recommend later starts for teenagers, and California made them law. But buses, sports and family schedules all depend on the bell. Should schools start later?

meta.title: Later School Start Times
meta.resolution: Resolved: Middle and high schools should start no earlier than 8:30 a.m.
meta.summary: Pediatricians recommend later starts for teenagers, and California made them law. But buses, sports and family schedules all depend on the bell. Should schools start later?

background.p: The American Academy of Pediatrics recommends that middle and high schools start no earlier than 8:30 a.m., because teenagers' internal clocks shift later during puberty and they need about 8.5 to 9.5 hours of sleep. In 2011–12, the CDC found the average U.S. public middle and high school started at 8:03 a.m., and about 82% started before 8:30.

California passed a law in 2019 requiring most high schools to start no earlier than 8:30 a.m. and middle schools no earlier than 8:00 a.m., with exceptions for some rural districts and a few years to comply. A 2017 RAND study estimated that later start times nationwide could produce economic gains (from better academic results and fewer car crashes) of about $9 billion a year, outweighing costs within a few years. Critics point to transportation costs, conflicts with sports and jobs, and research suggesting the extra sleep may be modest.

disputed.q: How much extra sleep and learning do later starts bring?
positions: Studies of districts that changed often find students sleep more and are less sleepy in class; some find better attendance and grades.
Others find the extra sleep is modest (15 to 30 minutes in some studies) and academic gains are unsettled.

terms.def: The body's internal daily clock, which shifts later in adolescence.
Using the same buses for several schools by staggering their start times.
An optional class before the regular start of the school day.

aff.label: Affirmative
aff.stance: School should start when teenagers' bodies are ready to learn.

args.claim: Teenagers need more sleep than early schedules allow.
args.warrant: Puberty shifts teens' sleep later, so most can't fall asleep early. A 7:30 start means many are short on sleep every school day.
args.evidence: CDC MMWR (2015) and AAP recommendations; sleep studies of adolescents.
args.response: The negative replies that the extra sleep found in some studies is modest, because some teens simply stay up later.

args.claim: Better sleep supports health and safety.
args.warrant: Sleep-deprived teens face more risk of drowsy driving, mood problems and illness. More sleep reduces these risks.
args.evidence: RAND (2017) on fewer car crashes; studies of districts that delayed start times and crash or health data.
args.response: The negative answers that these effects vary by study and district, and other changes (screen-time limits, sleep education) can help too.

args.claim: The economic benefits outweigh the costs.
args.warrant: Gains from better academic performance and fewer crashes add up over years, while costs like new bus schedules are mostly one-time.
args.evidence: RAND (2017): about $9.3 billion a year in national gains, with benefits exceeding costs within about two to three years.
args.response: The negative replies that the gains are estimates far in the future, while bus and staffing costs hit district budgets now.

args.claim: Students learn better when they're awake.
args.warrant: First-period classes full of sleepy students teach less. Moving the start time puts learning in hours when teens are more alert.
args.evidence: Studies of attendance, tardiness and grades in districts that changed; teacher reports.
args.response: The negative argues the academic evidence is unsettled, as Education Week reported.

neg.label: Negative
neg.stance: Start times should be set locally, because a later bell shifts real costs onto families and schools.

args.claim: Transportation costs can be large.
args.warrant: Many districts run the same buses for high schools, middle schools and elementary schools in tiers. Moving high schools later can mean more buses and drivers, or earlier starts for young children.
args.evidence: District transportation studies; Brookings estimate of about $150 per student cited by RAND; Education Week's discussion of bus costs.
args.response: The affirmative answers that this is mostly a one-time scheduling problem, and RAND finds benefits outweigh costs within a few years.

args.claim: Later dismissal squeezes afternoons.
args.warrant: Sports, jobs, family care duties and homework all move later, so students may lose sleep at the other end of the day or give up activities.
args.evidence: Athletic association schedules; surveys of working students; Education Week's reporting on activity conflicts.
args.response: The affirmative replies that districts that changed have adjusted schedules, and sleep in the morning matters more for teens' biology.

args.claim: Family schedules don't all move.
args.warrant: Parents who start work early may not be able to drive later, and older siblings who watch younger ones after school may get home later.
args.evidence: Parent surveys in districts considering changes; Education Week on family scheduling.
args.response: The affirmative answers that a later start also means parents are more likely to be home when students get out, reducing unsupervised time.

args.claim: The extra sleep and learning may be small.
args.warrant: If students go to bed later when school starts later, the net sleep gain shrinks, and so do the benefits.
args.evidence: Studies finding gains of 15 to 30 minutes of sleep; research finding unsettled academic effects.
args.response: The affirmative replies that even 30 more minutes a night adds up to hours a week for chronically short-sleeping teens.

strawmen.strawman: Supporters think teens are lazy and should be allowed to sleep in.
strawmen.why: The argument rests on adolescent biology and health recommendations, not on laziness.
strawmen.steelman: Puberty shifts teens' sleep later, so early bells cause chronic sleep loss with health and safety costs; starting at 8:30 fits their biology, and the benefits outweigh the costs.

strawmen.strawman: Opponents don't care about kids' health.
strawmen.why: Opponents point to costs, family logistics and modest measured gains.
strawmen.steelman: Later starts can require more buses, squeeze sports and jobs, and burden families, while the measured sleep gains may be modest; districts should decide for themselves.

weak.arg: Starting later will fix teen mental health.
weak.why: Sleep is one factor among many; overstating it hurts credibility.

weak.arg: Kids should just go to bed earlier.
weak.why: This ignores the research on adolescent sleep cycles, the strongest part of the other side's case.

aff: How much extra sleep did students actually get in the districts that changed?
How would your plan handle elementary bus schedules?
Who pays for new buses?
neg: What do pediatricians recommend, and why?
Do teenagers' sleep cycles shift during puberty?
Would you support later starts if a district could do it without new buses?

items.title: Tariffs to Protect Manufacturing
items.subtitle: policy · advanced
items.body: Tariffs are taxes on imports. Supporters see them as a tool to rebuild factories and secure supply chains; critics see higher prices and retaliation. Which is right?

meta.title: Tariffs to Protect Manufacturing
meta.resolution: Resolved: The United States should use broad tariffs to protect domestic manufacturing.
meta.summary: Tariffs are taxes on imports. Supporters see them as a tool to rebuild factories and secure supply chains; critics see higher prices and retaliation. Which is right?

background.p: A **tariff** is a tax on imported goods, paid when the goods enter the country. Tariffs make imports more expensive, which can help domestic producers compete but raises costs for buyers, including American factories that use imported parts. Tariffs are as old as the country. Until the Civil War, customs duties supplied most of the federal government's money, and they stayed its largest single source until the income tax began in 1913. Alexander Hamilton's Report on Manufactures (1791) listed "protecting duties" among the ways to build American industry and make the country "independent on foreign nations, for military and other essential supplies."

Tariffs have also divided the country. The Tariff of 1828, which critics called the "Tariff of Abominations," raised duties to protect Northern manufacturers but raised costs for Southern states that exported cotton and bought imported goods. South Carolina declared the tariffs void in 1832, and the Nullification Crisis ended only with the Compromise Tariff of 1833, which lowered rates over several years. The Smoot-Hawley Tariff Act of 1930 raised duties on more than 20,000 imported goods. More than 1,000 economists urged a veto, and trading partners such as Canada answered with tariffs of their own. U.S. trade fell sharply in the years that followed. Most economists see Smoot-Hawley as worsening the Great Depression, not causing it. From 1934 on, the country moved toward trade agreements that lowered tariffs on both sides.

More recent cases give researchers numbers to study. In 2002 the United States placed tariffs of up to 30% on many steel imports for three years; they were lifted in December 2003, after a World Trade Organization ruling against them. The U.S. International Trade Commission estimated that steel producers gained, steel-using industries lost sales, and the net effect on the whole economy was a small loss. Studies of the 2018–2019 tariffs found that their cost passed almost fully into U.S. prices (Amiti, Redding and Weinstein) and that, for manufacturing as a whole, higher input costs and other countries' retaliation outweighed the gains from protection (Flaaen and Pierce, Federal Reserve). Tariffs remain a live question in U.S. trade policy.

disputed.q: Do tariffs bring back manufacturing jobs?
positions: Supporters point to industries such as steel that gained output under protection, and to the growth of American industry behind high tariffs in the 1800s.
Studies of the 2002 steel tariffs and the 2018–2019 tariffs found that gains in protected industries were offset by losses in industries that use their products and in exports hit by retaliation.

disputed.q: Did high tariffs build American industry in the 1800s?
positions: Some historians credit protective tariffs, from Hamilton's plan to the high Civil War-era rates, with giving young American industries room to grow.
Other economic historians argue that a large market, abundant resources, immigration and new technology explain most of that growth, and the country might have grown as fast with lower tariffs.

terms.def: A tax on imported goods.
Tariffs another country places on our exports in response.
The network of suppliers that provide parts and materials for a product.
The idea that countries gain by specializing in what they produce at the lowest relative cost and trading.
Government action to build up particular industries.

aff.label: Affirmative
aff.stance: Tariffs can rebuild American industry, protect national security and strengthen workers' bargaining power.

args.claim: Some industries matter for national security.
args.warrant: A country that can't make its own steel, chips, ships or medicines depends on others in a crisis. Tariffs help keep those industries at home.
args.evidence: Hamilton's Report on Manufactures (1791) on making the country independent for "military and other essential supplies"; Section 232 of the Trade Expansion Act of 1962, which allows import limits for national security; reports on supply shortages during the pandemic.
args.response: The negative answers that targeted support for critical industries works better than broad tariffs on everything.

args.claim: Tariffs counter unfair trade practices.
args.warrant: When other governments subsidize their industries or keep our goods out, free trade isn't a level field; tariffs give leverage to change those practices.
args.evidence: U.S. Trade Representative reports on foreign subsidies; the Reciprocal Trade Agreements Act of 1934, which used tariff levels as bargaining chips to win lower foreign tariffs.
args.response: The negative replies that retaliation hurts American exporters, especially farmers, and other tools (trade cases, alliances) can address unfair practices.

args.claim: Manufacturing supports communities and good jobs.
args.warrant: Factory closures hit some towns hard, and service jobs haven't replaced the wages or stability. Protecting manufacturing protects those communities.
args.evidence: Research on the "China shock" (Autor, Dorn and Hanson) and job losses in manufacturing regions; steel producers' gains in output under the 2002 tariffs, as estimated by the U.S. International Trade Commission.
args.response: The negative answers that automation explains much of the job decline, and tariffs raise costs for manufacturers who use imported parts.

args.claim: Tariffs raise revenue.
args.warrant: Import taxes bring in money that can reduce other taxes or deficits.
args.evidence: Customs duties supplied most federal revenue until the Civil War and stayed the largest source until 1913; the U.S. International Trade Commission's estimate of about $650 million in added tariff revenue from the 2002 steel tariffs.
args.response: The negative points out that the revenue comes largely from American buyers through higher prices, and the 2002 study found it was offset by lower wages and profits elsewhere.

neg.label: Negative
neg.stance: Broad tariffs raise prices, invite retaliation and cost more jobs than they save.

args.claim: Tariffs raise prices for American families and businesses.
args.warrant: Importers pass much of the tax on to buyers, and domestic competitors can raise their prices too.
args.evidence: Amiti, Redding and Weinstein (Journal of Economic Perspectives, 2019): the 2018 tariffs passed almost fully into the prices Americans paid for imports; the 1828 tariff's higher costs for Southern buyers.
args.response: The affirmative replies that the price effect is modest and is a fair cost for security and good jobs.

args.claim: Net manufacturing jobs can fall.
args.warrant: Many American factories use imported parts; making those parts more expensive hurts them, and retaliation closes export markets.
args.evidence: Flaaen and Pierce (Federal Reserve, 2019) on the 2018–2019 tariffs; the U.S. International Trade Commission's finding that steel-using industries lost sales under the 2002 tariffs.
args.response: The affirmative argues that short-term costs give way as supply chains move home, which takes years to show up.

args.claim: Retaliation hurts exporters, especially farmers.
args.warrant: When other countries respond with tariffs on American goods, exporters lose sales; the government has had to send aid to farmers to offset losses.
args.evidence: Canada's and Europe's retaliation against Smoot-Hawley (1930) and the fall in U.S. exports; USDA data on farm exports and trade-aid payments after 2018.
args.response: The affirmative replies that retaliation is temporary and leverage produces better trade deals in the end.

args.claim: Targeted tools work better than broad tariffs.
args.warrant: Subsidies for specific critical industries, trade cases against specific unfair practices, and working with allies protect security without taxing every import.
args.evidence: Analyses of the CHIPS Act and other targeted programs; World Trade Organization dispute cases.
args.response: The affirmative answers that subsidies cost taxpayers directly, while tariffs raise money, and allies don't always cooperate.

strawmen.strawman: Tariff supporters don't understand that tariffs are paid by Americans.
strawmen.why: Many supporters accept some price effects as a cost worth paying for security and jobs.
strawmen.steelman: Tariffs protect industries vital to national security, give leverage against unfair trade, and help rebuild manufacturing communities, which is worth modest price increases.

strawmen.strawman: Free traders don't care about factory workers.
strawmen.why: Opponents argue tariffs cost more manufacturing jobs than they save, and favor targeted help.
strawmen.steelman: Broad tariffs raise prices, invite retaliation and, as studies of 2018–2019 show, can cost more manufacturing jobs than they protect; targeted tools work better.

weak.arg: Foreign countries pay the tariffs.
weak.why: Tariffs are paid by importers when goods enter the country; studies find much of the cost passes to U.S. buyers.

weak.arg: Tariffs caused the Great Depression.
weak.why: Historians and economists see the Smoot-Hawley tariff as worsening, not causing, the Depression. Overstating it costs credibility.

aff: Who pays a tariff when goods arrive at a U.S. port?
What did the Federal Reserve study find about the 2018–2019 tariffs?
Which industries would you exempt for parts that aren't made here?
neg: Should the U.S. be able to make its own steel and computer chips?
What would you do about foreign subsidies?
Why have manufacturing towns struggled?

items.title: Term Limits for Congress
items.subtitle: policy · intermediate
items.body: Presidents are limited to two terms, but members of Congress can serve as long as voters reelect them. Most Americans say they favor term limits. Would they make Congress better?

meta.title: Term Limits for Congress
meta.resolution: Resolved: The United States should adopt term limits for members of Congress.
meta.summary: Presidents are limited to two terms, but members of Congress can serve as long as voters reelect them. Most Americans say they favor term limits. Would they make Congress better?

background.p: Members of Congress have no term limits. In U.S. Term Limits, Inc. v. Thornton (1995), the Supreme Court held that states cannot impose term limits on their members of Congress; a constitutional amendment would be needed. Proposed amendments in recent Congresses would cap House service at three or six terms and Senate service at two, usually not counting terms already served.

Support for term limits is broad and bipartisan in polls; a 2013 Gallup survey found 75% would vote for them. Fifteen states limit the terms of their own state legislators, generally to between 6 and 12 years, which gives researchers evidence on how limits work in practice. The Congressional Research Service summarizes the main arguments: supporters say turnover makes Congress more responsive; opponents say elections already let voters remove members and that experience keeps power with elected officials rather than staff and lobbyists.

disputed.q: How have state legislative term limits worked?
positions: Supporters point to more turnover and new kinds of candidates.
Several studies find that limits shift influence toward governors, staff and lobbyists because members leave before gaining expertise.

terms.def: A cap on how many terms a person may serve in an office.
The edge sitting officeholders have in elections, from name recognition, fundraising and staff.
The part of the Constitution describing how it can be amended.
Understanding of how an organization works, built over time.

aff.label: Affirmative
aff.stance: Limits would bring fresh people and ideas into Congress and loosen the grip of long-serving incumbents.

args.claim: Incumbents are very hard to defeat.
args.warrant: Name recognition, fundraising networks and district lines give sitting members large advantages, so elections alone rarely produce turnover.
args.evidence: Reelection rates for House incumbents; research on the incumbency advantage.
args.response: The negative answers that voters reelect members they like, and that high reelection rates reflect choice, not failure.

args.claim: Turnover makes Congress more responsive.
args.warrant: Members who know they'll return to private life are more likely to think like their constituents and less like career politicians.
args.evidence: CRS summary of arguments for limits; surveys on public trust in Congress.
args.response: The negative replies that members facing a fixed exit may look ahead to lobbying jobs, which can make them less responsive.

args.claim: It would reduce the concentration of power in long-serving members.
args.warrant: Seniority helps decide committee chairs; limits spread leadership among more members and regions.
args.evidence: Histories of seniority and committee power; party rules that already limit chair terms.
args.response: The negative argues that parties already limit chair terms, which addresses this without limiting voters' choices.

args.claim: Most Americans want it.
args.warrant: When large, bipartisan majorities support a reform for decades, Congress's refusal looks like self-interest.
args.evidence: Gallup (2013) and other polls cited by CRS.
args.response: The negative replies that popularity doesn't show a reform will work, and voters can impose limits themselves by voting members out.

neg.label: Negative
neg.stance: Term limits take choices away from voters and drain Congress of the expertise it needs.

args.claim: Elections are already term limits.
args.warrant: Voters can remove any member at the next election; term limits take away their right to keep a representative they want.
args.evidence: CRS summary of arguments against; the Supreme Court's reasoning in Thornton about voters' choices.
args.response: The affirmative answers that incumbency advantages make elections an imperfect check.

args.claim: Limits shift power to staff, lobbyists and the executive branch.
args.warrant: Lawmaking is complex; members who leave just as they master it leave more of the work to unelected staff, lobbyists and agencies.
args.evidence: Studies of state legislative term limits; the CRS summary.
args.response: The affirmative replies that state results vary and Congress could strengthen its own staff and research offices.

args.claim: Experience matters for good laws.
args.warrant: Knowledge of budgets, defense, health policy and the rules of Congress takes years to build; limits throw it away.
args.evidence: Examples of long-serving legislators' work on complex legislation; studies of legislative effectiveness and experience.
args.response: The affirmative answers that a limit of twelve years still allows real expertise to develop.

args.claim: Lame-duck members may be less accountable.
args.warrant: A member in a final term doesn't face voters again, so the electoral check disappears for that term.
args.evidence: Research on behavior of term-limited officials in their last term.
args.response: The affirmative replies that the same is true of second-term presidents, and the benefits outweigh this.

strawmen.strawman: They think everyone in Congress is corrupt.
strawmen.why: Supporters argue about incentives and incumbency advantages, not about every member's character.
strawmen.steelman: Incumbents' advantages make elections a weak check; limits bring turnover and fresh perspectives and reduce concentrated power, as most Americans want.

strawmen.strawman: They want politicians to stay in office forever.
strawmen.why: Opponents trust voters to decide and worry about expertise and lobbyists.
strawmen.steelman: Elections already let voters remove members; limits take away voters' choice and shift power to staff, lobbyists and agencies.

weak.arg: Term limits will end corruption.
weak.why: Overclaiming; argue about turnover and incentives.

weak.arg: Term limits are unconstitutional.
weak.why: A constitutional amendment would make them constitutional; Thornton only stops states from imposing them alone.

Why can't voters simply vote out members they don't like?

items.title: Tipping at Restaurants
items.subtitle: policy · beginner
items.body: In most American restaurants, a large part of a server's pay comes from tips. Some restaurants have tried raising menu prices and ending tips instead. Which way is better for workers and diners?

meta.title: Tipping at Restaurants
meta.resolution: Resolved: Restaurants in the United States should replace tipping with service-included prices.
meta.summary: In most American restaurants, a large part of a server's pay comes from tips. Some restaurants have tried raising menu prices and ending tips instead. Which way is better for workers and diners?

background.p: Under federal law, an employer may pay a tipped worker a cash wage as low as $2.13 an hour, as long as tips bring the worker up to the federal minimum wage of $7.25; if they don't, the employer must make up the difference. States set their own rules. As of July 2026, the U.S. Department of Labor lists seven states (Alaska, California, Minnesota, Montana, Nevada, Oregon and Washington) that require the full state minimum wage before tips.

Cornell professor Michael Lynn, who has studied tipping for decades, found that tip percentages are only weakly related to how customers rate the service. In 2015, Union Square Hospitality Group, a well-known New York restaurant company, ended tipping and raised menu prices, partly so kitchen workers could share in the money. It brought tipping back in 2020, when the pandemic cut restaurant sales. Lynn's research found that some restaurants that dropped tipping saw their online service ratings fall, more so when they added a service charge than when they raised menu prices.

disputed.q: Would servers earn more or less without tips?
positions: At busy full-service restaurants, servers often earn more from tips than most restaurants could pay in wages, so many would earn less.

Supporters reply that tips swing from shift to shift and restaurant to restaurant, and that servers at slower restaurants, and kitchen workers who get few or no tips, could earn more and more steadily.

terms.def: The part of the minimum wage that an employer may count from tips instead of paying in cash wages. Under federal law, up to $5.12 an hour.
Menu prices that already include the cost of service, so no tip is expected. Sometimes called "hospitality included."
A set percentage added to the bill by the restaurant. Unlike a tip, it isn't voluntary and belongs to the restaurant, which decides how to pay it out.

terms.term: Front of house / back of house
terms.def: Restaurant workers who serve guests (servers, bartenders, hosts) and those who work out of sight (cooks, dishwashers).

aff.label: Affirmative
aff.stance: Service-included prices give workers steady pay, share it more fairly, and show diners the real price.

args.claim: Workers deserve steady, predictable pay.
args.warrant: Tips rise and fall with the weather, the shift and the mood of each table. A wage built into prices lets workers plan rent and bills.
args.evidence: Studies of earnings volatility among tipped workers; the Economic Policy Institute's comparison of poverty rates for tipped workers in states with different tipped wages (2014).
args.response: The negative answers that steady pay can also be lower pay; many servers would trade higher average earnings for steadiness only if the total were the same.

args.claim: Tips don't measure service well.
args.warrant: If tips barely track how good the service was, they don't reward good work. They mostly reflect things the server doesn't control, like the size of the bill and the customer's habits.
args.evidence: Michael Lynn's research at Cornell finding tip percentages are only weakly related to customers' ratings of service.
args.response: The negative replies that even a weak link is some link, and servers still have a reason to be attentive, which a flat wage doesn't give.

args.claim: Kitchen workers are left out.
args.warrant: Cooks and dishwashers help make every meal but usually share little of the tips. Building service into prices lets the restaurant pay the whole team.
args.evidence: Union Square Hospitality Group's stated reason for its 2015 policy: back-of-house workers couldn't share in guests' generosity.
args.response: The negative points out that the same company brought tipping back in 2020, and that tip pools already let restaurants share tips more widely in many states.

args.claim: Diners should see the real price.
args.warrant: A menu that lists $15 when the meal costs about $18 after the tip makes prices harder to compare. Most countries print the full price.
args.evidence: Consumer surveys on frustration with tipping requests; restaurant pricing practices in countries without tipping.
args.response: The negative replies that American diners are used to tipping and know to add it, and that higher menu prices can drive them to competitors who still list lower prices.

neg.label: Negative
neg.stance: Tipping lets diners reward service, lets skilled servers earn well, and keeps menu prices low.

args.claim: Many servers earn more with tips.
args.warrant: At busy restaurants, tips can add up to more per hour than a restaurant could afford in wages. Ending tips would cut pay for the workers the policy aims to help.
args.evidence: Lynn's 2018 interview giving New York server earnings of about $25 to $30 an hour, well above cooks' pay; surveys of servers' views on tipping.
args.response: The affirmative answers that those figures describe busy city restaurants; across the country, tipped workers in states with low cash wages have higher poverty rates.

args.claim: Higher menu prices hurt restaurants.
args.warrant: When one restaurant raises its menu prices 20 percent and the place next door doesn't, diners see the first as more expensive, even if the total bill is the same.
args.evidence: Lynn's research on restaurants that ended tipping, including falling online service ratings; restaurants that tried and dropped no-tipping policies.
args.response: The affirmative replies that the problem fades if all restaurants change together, which is what the resolution asks.

args.claim: Diners like having a say.
args.warrant: Tipping lets a customer reward a server who went out of the way and hold back for poor service. A fixed price takes that choice away.
args.evidence: Consumer surveys on tipping, such as those summarized by Lynn and Withiam, including a 1998 reader survey in which most preferred to choose their own tip over an automatic charge.
args.response: The affirmative answers that the same research found a majority favored guaranteed server wages, and that a choice that barely tracks service isn't much of a reward.

args.claim: Tips keep labor costs flexible for small restaurants.
args.warrant: Restaurants run on thin margins. When pay rises and falls with sales, a slow month doesn't sink the business, which protects jobs.
args.evidence: Industry data on restaurant profit margins; reports from restaurant owners about the cost of moving to higher wages.
args.response: The affirmative replies that this shifts business risk onto workers, who then carry the slow months instead of the owner.

strawmen.strawman: They want to take money away from servers.
strawmen.why: Supporters want pay to be steadier and shared more fairly, and many expect wages to make up for lost tips.
strawmen.steelman: Tips barely track service, swing from shift to shift and leave kitchen workers out; building service into prices gives the whole staff steady pay and shows diners the real price.

strawmen.strawman: They just want restaurants to pay workers less.
strawmen.why: Defenders of tipping often argue that tips let skilled servers earn more than wages would.
strawmen.steelman: At many restaurants tips pay servers more than wages could, keep menu prices competitive and let diners reward good service.

weak.arg: Tipping is un-American.
weak.why: Tipping has been common in the United States for more than a century; argue about pay and prices, not labels.

weak.arg: If servers wanted more money, they'd get another job.
weak.why: It dodges the question of which pay system works better, and the same could be said of any job.

What happens to a server who earns more from tips today than the new wage?
Why did some restaurants that tried this go back to tipping?
neg: How should a cook or dishwasher share in a good night?
If tips barely track service, what are they rewarding?
What happens to a server's rent payment after a slow week?

items.title: Universal Basic Income
items.subtitle: policy · advanced
items.body: A universal basic income would give every adult a regular cash payment with no conditions. Pilot programs have tested smaller versions. Would a national program be wise?

meta.title: Universal Basic Income
meta.resolution: Resolved: The United States federal government should provide a universal basic income.
meta.summary: A universal basic income would give every adult a regular cash payment with no conditions. Pilot programs have tested smaller versions. Would a national program be wise?

background.p: A **universal basic income** (UBI) is a regular cash payment to every adult, regardless of income or work, with no rules on how it's spent. Most U.S. experiments have tested **guaranteed income**: payments to selected low- or moderate-income people, which is narrower than a true UBI.

In Stockton, California, 125 residents received $500 a month for two years (2019–2021). Recipients moved from part-time to full-time work at more than twice the rate of a comparison group and reported better well-being. A larger randomized study run by OpenResearch gave $1,000 a month for three years; recipients worked about 1.3 fewer hours a week than the comparison group, spent the money mostly on basic needs, and early gains in stress and mental health faded. The researchers called the results mixed.

Cost is a central question. Because a UBI goes to everyone, even a modest payment adds up to trillions of dollars a year, unless it replaces other programs or is paid for by large tax changes. Supporters and critics disagree about which programs it should replace.

disputed.q: Does unconditional cash reduce work?
positions: Some pilots (such as Stockton) found no drop, or even more full-time work, among recipients.
The larger OpenResearch study found a modest drop of about 1.3 hours a week, and critics argue a permanent national program could have larger effects.

terms.def: Regular cash for everyone, with no conditions.
Cash payments to people below an income level, often in pilot programs.
Available only to people with incomes below a set limit.
A plan in which people below an income level receive money from the tax system instead of paying.

aff.label: Affirmative
aff.stance: A basic income would give everyone a secure floor, simply and with dignity.

args.claim: Cash gives people security and freedom to improve their lives.
args.warrant: A steady floor lets people handle emergencies, look for better jobs, train for new careers or care for family without falling into crisis.
args.evidence: Stockton SEED results (more full-time work, more people able to cover a $400 emergency); guaranteed-income pilot reports.
args.response: The negative answers that Stockton was small, and the larger OpenResearch study found mixed results, including slightly less work.

args.claim: A universal program is simpler and less stigmatizing.
args.warrant: Means-tested programs require paperwork, and many eligible people never receive benefits. Giving everyone the same payment removes red tape and shame.
args.evidence: Research on take-up rates in existing programs; administrative costs of means-tested aid.
args.response: The negative replies that sending money to the wealthy is wasteful; it raises the cost enormously for little gain.

args.claim: It removes traps in current programs.
args.warrant: When benefits shrink as earnings rise, some people lose almost as much aid as they gain in pay. A universal payment doesn't shrink when you work more.
args.evidence: Analyses of effective marginal tax rates for low-income families; economists' work on the negative income tax.
args.response: The negative argues those traps can be fixed by phasing benefits out more slowly, at far less cost.

args.claim: Recipients use cash responsibly.
args.warrant: People know their own needs best; studies show they spend cash mostly on necessities rather than on harmful things.
args.evidence: OpenResearch study findings on spending (food, housing, transportation); Stockton spending data.
args.response: The negative answers that responsible spending doesn't settle whether a national program is affordable or the best use of the money.

neg.label: Negative
neg.stance: A universal basic income would cost too much, could reduce work, and spreads money too thinly.

args.claim: The cost is enormous.
args.warrant: Paying even a modest amount to every adult costs trillions each year, requiring large tax increases or cuts to programs people rely on.
args.evidence: Budget arithmetic using Census population counts; analyses of UBI proposals by budget groups.
args.response: The affirmative answers that the net cost is smaller once taxes recover payments from higher earners and some programs are replaced.

args.claim: It may reduce work over time.
args.warrant: When people receive income regardless of work, some will work less; across a whole economy, that lowers output and tax revenue.
args.evidence: OpenResearch results (about 1.3 fewer hours a week); earlier U.S. negative income tax experiments in the 1970s.
args.response: The affirmative replies that the drop was modest and some time went to caregiving, education or job searching.

args.claim: Targeted programs help the poor more per dollar.
args.warrant: Money given to everyone is money not concentrated on those in greatest need; targeted aid can give poor families much more for the same budget.
args.evidence: Comparisons of targeted versus universal transfer costs; research on the EITC and child tax credits.
args.response: The affirmative argues targeting misses many eligible people, and universal programs build broad public support.

args.claim: The evidence doesn't yet support a national program.
args.warrant: Pilots are small, temporary and local; a permanent national program could change prices, work and behavior in ways pilots can't show.
args.evidence: The researchers' own description of the OpenResearch results as mixed; the small size of Stockton's study.
args.response: The affirmative answers that the evidence so far shows few harms, and a national program can be phased in and studied.

strawmen.strawman: UBI supporters want people to get paid to sit on the couch.
strawmen.why: Supporters argue cash gives security to work, train or care for family, and pilots found little drop in work.
strawmen.steelman: A universal floor gives everyone security and freedom, avoids the red tape and work traps of current programs, and pilots show people spend it on necessities.

strawmen.strawman: UBI opponents don't care about poor people.
strawmen.why: Many opponents favor targeted aid that gives the poor more per dollar.
strawmen.steelman: A universal payment would cost trillions, may reduce work, and spreads money to everyone instead of concentrating it on those in need; pilots don't show a national program would work.

weak.arg: UBI pays for itself.
weak.why: No credible estimate supports this; argue about net cost and value instead.

weak.arg: People will spend it all on drugs and gambling.
weak.why: Studies found spending mostly on basic needs; the claim is contradicted by evidence.

aff: How much would you pay each adult, and what would it cost in a year?
Which existing programs would it replace?
What did the OpenResearch study find about hours worked?
neg: What did recipients in Stockton and the OpenResearch study spend money on?
What share of eligible people actually receive means-tested benefits?
Would you support a smaller guaranteed income for low-income families?

items.title: Video Games and Young People
items.subtitle: value · beginner
items.body: Most American teens play video games. Research finds both benefits and risks, and much of it can't show cause and effect. On balance, do games help young people more than they hurt?

meta.title: Video Games and Young People
meta.resolution: Resolved: Video games do more good than harm for young people.
meta.summary: Most American teens play video games. Research finds both benefits and risks, and much of it can't show cause and effect. On balance, do games help young people more than they hurt?

background.p: In a fall 2023 Pew Research Center survey, 85 percent of U.S. teens ages 13 to 17 said they play video games, including 97 percent of boys and about three-quarters of girls. Among teens who play, 56 percent said games have helped their problem-solving skills and 47 percent said they have made a friend online through a game. At the same time, 41 percent said gaming has hurt their sleep, 14 percent of all teens said they spend too much time gaming, and 43 percent of players said they have been harassed or bullied while gaming.

In 2020, the American Psychological Association said there is "insufficient scientific evidence" of a causal link between violent video games and violent behavior, while noting a small, reliable link with milder aggression such as yelling and pushing. The World Health Organization lists "gaming disorder" in its disease classification, ICD-11: a pattern of impaired control over gaming that continues despite harm, usually for at least 12 months. WHO says it affects only a small share of people who play.

Other studies point in different directions, and most have limits. A 2022 study of nearly 2,000 children ages 9 and 10, announced by the National Institutes of Health, found that children who played three or more hours a day did better on tests of impulse control and working memory than children who didn't play, but it couldn't show that gaming caused the difference. A 2022 Oxford study using real play data from about 39,000 adult players found little evidence that time spent playing affected well-being; it studied adults, not children.

disputed.q: Do violent video games make young people more aggressive?
positions: Many studies, summarized by the APA, find a small but reliable link between violent games and aggressive behavior such as yelling and pushing.
Other researchers argue that the link is smaller still or disappears when studies control for other factors, and that it doesn't extend to real violence, as the APA also says.

disputed.q: Is gaming addiction common?
positions: Some researchers and clinicians see problem gaming as a growing concern, which is why WHO added gaming disorder to ICD-11.
Others argue that the label risks treating heavy but healthy play as illness, and WHO itself says the disorder affects only a small share of players.

terms.def: Two things happening together (correlation) doesn't prove one causes the other (causation). Many gaming studies show only correlation.
A condition in WHO's ICD-11 marked by impaired control over gaming, gaming taking priority over other activities, and continuing despite harm.
A purchase in a game that gives a random reward. Some governments and regulators have examined whether loot boxes work like gambling.
Time spent on any screen. Researchers increasingly study what people do on screens, not only how long.

aff.label: Affirmative
aff.stance: For most young people, games build skills, friendships and joy, and the harms fall on a small share who can be helped without losing the benefits for everyone else.

args.claim: Games build thinking skills.
args.warrant: Many games require planning, quick decisions, trial and error and memory. Practicing these skills for fun can carry over to schoolwork and life.
args.evidence: The 2022 NIH-announced study finding better impulse control and working memory in children who game; Pew's finding that 56 percent of teen players say games helped their problem solving.
args.response: The negative answers that the NIH study can't show games caused the difference, since children with stronger skills may simply choose to play more.

args.claim: Games build friendships.
args.warrant: Playing together, in the same room or online, gives young people shared goals, teamwork and a way to keep in touch. For shy children it can be an easier way to connect.
args.evidence: Pew (2024): 47 percent of teen players have made a friend online through a game, and 47 percent say games have helped their friendships.
args.response: The negative replies that the same survey found 43 percent of players have been harassed or bullied while gaming, so online play brings risks too.

args.claim: Fears about violence aren't supported.
args.warrant: Games have often been blamed for youth violence, but if the evidence doesn't show games cause violence, that worry shouldn't weigh heavily.
args.evidence: The APA's 2020 statement that evidence doesn't support a causal link between violent games and violent behavior; the NIH-announced study finding no link to increased violence.
args.response: The negative answers that the APA also found a small, reliable link with aggressive behavior, which matters even if it isn't violence.

args.claim: Harms come from too much, not from games.
args.warrant: Lost sleep and problem gaming happen mostly when play crowds out other things. Families can set limits, so the problem is balance, not games.
args.evidence: WHO's statement that gaming disorder affects a small share of players; Pew's finding that most teens say they play the right amount.
args.response: The negative replies that games are designed to keep players playing, so limits are harder to keep than this suggests.

neg.label: Negative
neg.stance: For many young people, games cost sleep, time and money, expose them to harassment, and are built to be hard to put down; the claimed benefits are uncertain.

args.claim: Games cut into sleep and other activities.
args.warrant: Young people need sleep, exercise, reading and time with family. Hours spent gaming come out of these, and many teens say so themselves.
args.evidence: Pew (2024): 41 percent of teen players say gaming has hurt their sleep, rising to about two-thirds of those who say they play too much; pediatric guidance on sleep.
args.response: The affirmative answers that this is an argument for limits, not against games, and many teens report no sleep problem.

args.claim: Many games are designed to keep players hooked.
args.warrant: Rewards, streaks, random prizes and in-game purchases are built to keep people playing and spending. Young people are less able to resist these designs.
args.evidence: WHO's inclusion of gaming disorder in ICD-11; Federal Trade Commission actions over loot boxes and in-game spending marketed to children, such as a 2025 settlement with a game maker.
args.response: The affirmative replies that many games have no such features, and parents and rules can address the ones that do without condemning all games.

args.claim: Online gaming exposes young people to harassment.
args.warrant: Playing with strangers online means insults, threats and unwanted contact from strangers. These harms can follow children well beyond the game.
args.evidence: Pew (2024): 43 percent of teen players have been harassed or bullied while gaming, 12 percent physically threatened, and 80 percent of teens say harassment over games is a problem for people their age.
args.response: The affirmative answers that this is a problem with online chat, not with games, and that privacy settings and playing with friends reduce it.

args.claim: The benefits are uncertain.
args.warrant: Studies showing benefits are mostly correlations, often small, and some study adults. A case for "more good than harm" needs stronger evidence than that.
args.evidence: The limits noted in the NIH-announced study (it can't show cause) and the Oxford study (adult players only, seven games, six weeks).
args.response: The affirmative replies that the evidence for harm has the same limits, so the question comes down to what young people themselves report, which is mostly positive.

strawmen.strawman: They think kids should play games all day.
strawmen.why: Supporters usually favor limits; they argue that games played in balance do more good than harm.
strawmen.steelman: Most young people who play gain thinking skills, friendships and enjoyment, fears about violence aren't supported, and the harms come mostly from excess, which families can manage.

strawmen.strawman: They think video games turn kids into violent criminals.
strawmen.why: Most opponents today argue about sleep, time, design that keeps players hooked, harassment and spending, not violence.
strawmen.steelman: Games often cost young people sleep and time, are designed to be hard to stop, and bring harassment and spending risks, while the claimed benefits rest on weak evidence.

weak.arg: Games are fun, so they must be good.
weak.why: Fun is a real benefit, but it doesn't answer the evidence on sleep, harassment and spending.

weak.arg: Games rot your brain.
weak.why: It's a slogan, not evidence, and it ignores studies that find no harm or even some benefits to thinking skills.

neg: Is the harm from games themselves, or from playing too much?
Why did the APA say violence can't be blamed on games?
Do your harms apply to a child who plays an hour of a puzzle game with family?

items.title: Lowering the Voting Age to 16
items.subtitle: policy · beginner
items.body: A few U.S. cities and several countries let 16-year-olds vote. Should the whole country?

meta.title: Lowering the Voting Age to 16
meta.resolution: Resolved: The voting age in the United States should be lowered to 16.
meta.summary: A few U.S. cities and several countries let 16-year-olds vote. Should the whole country?

background.p: The 26th Amendment, ratified in 1971 in about three months, lowered the voting age in all U.S. elections from 21 to 18. Changing it for federal elections again would take another constitutional amendment, but cities can set rules for their own local elections. About a dozen cities in California, Maryland, New Jersey and Vermont let 16- and 17-year-olds vote in some local elections; Takoma Park, Maryland, was the first. Austria lowered its voting age to 16 in 2007. Brazil and Argentina let 16-year-olds vote in national elections, and Scotland has let them vote in its own parliament and local elections since 2016.

Supporters cite studies finding that 16-year-olds score similarly to adults on civic knowledge and skills, that youth turnout in Takoma Park was about double that of older voters, and that voting early can build a lifelong habit. Opponents point to the law's other age limits, low civics scores on national tests, and polls showing most Americans oppose the change.

disputed.q: Are 16-year-olds ready to vote?
positions: Studies such as Hart and Atkins (2011) find 16-year-olds similar to adults on civic knowledge and skills, and an Austrian study found their vote choices of similar quality.
Others point to brain development in the teen years and to national civics test scores as reasons for caution.

terms.def: The 1971 amendment that set the voting age at 18 for all U.S. elections.
The idea that people who vote in their first eligible election are more likely to keep voting.
An election for city, county or school board offices, which cities can sometimes open to younger voters.

aff.label: Affirmative
aff.stance: Sixteen-year-olds are ready to vote, and starting earlier builds lifelong voters.

args.claim: Sixteen-year-olds can make informed choices.
args.warrant: The skills voting requires (gathering information and weighing options calmly) are in place by 16, unlike quick decisions under pressure.
args.evidence: Hart and Atkins (2011) on civic knowledge and skills; Wagner and colleagues on vote quality in Austria.
args.response: The negative answers that national civics test scores are low, and many young voters may copy their parents.

args.claim: Voting at 16 builds a lifelong habit.
args.warrant: At 16, most young people live at home and attend school, where teachers and families can help them vote for the first time; at 18, many are moving and miss their first election.
args.evidence: Takoma Park turnout among 16- and 17-year-olds (about double that of older voters); research on habit formation in voting.
args.response: The negative replies that Takoma Park is a small, unusual city, and results there may not carry over.

args.claim: Young people have a stake in decisions.
args.warrant: Sixteen-year-olds work, pay taxes, drive and live with the long-term results of today's choices on schools, debt and the environment.
args.evidence: Labor data on teen employment and taxes; examples of policies with long-term effects.
args.response: The negative argues that many rights and duties begin at 18, and voting fits with them.

args.claim: Other democracies have done it without harm.
args.warrant: When countries like Austria lowered the voting age, they didn't see worse elections, suggesting the fears are overstated.
args.evidence: Austria (2007), Scotland (since 2016), Brazil and Argentina; studies of Austrian young voters.
args.response: The negative replies that a few countries' experience is limited, and U.S. civic education differs.

neg.label: Negative
neg.stance: Eighteen is the right line: it matches adulthood in law and gives time for civic learning.

args.claim: The law treats 18 as adulthood for good reasons.
args.warrant: We don't let 16-year-olds sign contracts, serve on juries or enlist without permission; voting, which decides laws for everyone, belongs with those adult responsibilities.
args.evidence: Ages set in federal and state law; Britannica's summary of the opposing case.
args.response: The affirmative answers that many ages already differ (driving at 16, drinking at 21), so there's no single age of adulthood.

args.claim: Many teens haven't finished their civic education.
args.warrant: Students often take government classes late in high school; letting them vote first puts the ballot ahead of the lesson.
args.evidence: NAEP civics results (2022: 20% of eighth-graders proficient); state civics course requirements.
args.response: The affirmative replies that many adults also score poorly on civics tests, and we don't test adults before voting.

args.claim: Teens may be more influenced by parents and teachers.
args.warrant: Most 16-year-olds live at home and spend their days at school, so their votes may echo the adults around them rather than independent judgment.
args.evidence: Research on political socialization in families; Britannica's summary of the opposing case.
args.response: The affirmative answers that adults are also influenced by family and friends, and teens often disagree with their parents.

args.claim: The public doesn't support it.
args.warrant: Changing who votes is a basic change to democracy and should have broad agreement, which this lacks.
args.evidence: Polls showing large majorities opposed, such as a 2019 Hill-HarrisX poll (84% opposed).
args.response: The affirmative replies that lowering the age to 18 was once unpopular too, and rights shouldn't depend on polls.

strawmen.strawman: They want children voting.
strawmen.why: The proposal concerns 16- and 17-year-olds, not young children.
strawmen.steelman: Sixteen-year-olds have the civic skills to vote, and starting while they're at home and in school builds lifelong voting habits, as Takoma Park and Austria suggest.

strawmen.strawman: They think teenagers are stupid.
strawmen.why: Opponents argue about legal adulthood, civic education and independence, not intelligence.
strawmen.steelman: Eighteen matches the other responsibilities of adulthood, gives time for civic education, and the change lacks broad public support.

weak.arg: If you can drive, you can vote.
weak.why: Driving and voting require different things; this analogy is easy to attack.

weak.arg: Next they'll want 10-year-olds voting.
weak.why: A slippery slope with no evidence of the later steps.

aff: How would the change happen for federal elections?
How big is Takoma Park, and how many young people voted?
Should 16-year-olds serve on juries?
neg: What did studies find about 16-year-olds' civic knowledge compared with adults?
Do we test adults' civics knowledge before they vote?
What happened in Austria after 2007?

items.title: Year-Round School
items.subtitle: policy · beginner
items.body: Year-round schools usually keep the same number of school days but trade the long summer for shorter breaks spread through the year. Is that a better calendar?

meta.title: Year-Round School
meta.resolution: Resolved: Public schools in the United States should adopt a year-round calendar.
meta.summary: Year-round schools usually keep the same number of school days but trade the long summer for shorter breaks spread through the year. Is that a better calendar?

background.p: Most year-round schools don't add days; they rearrange them. A **single-track** calendar shortens summer and adds breaks ("intersessions") through the year, in patterns like 45 days of school and 15 days off. A **multi-track** calendar splits students into groups on staggered schedules so a building can serve more students. About 3,700 public schools (4.1%) used a year-round calendar in 2011–12, according to the Congressional Research Service.

Studies of achievement are mixed and often weak in design. The CRS summarized a general consensus of no effect or a small positive effect, with some evidence of benefits for students from low-income families. Research on "summer learning loss" (for example, a review by Cooper and colleagues) found students lose ground over long summers, especially lower-income students in reading, though newer studies debate how large the loss is.

disputed.q: How large is summer learning loss?
positions: Older studies found students lose about a month of learning over the summer, more for low-income students in reading.
Some newer analyses find smaller or more varied losses and question the measurement in older studies.

terms.def: All students follow the same year-round schedule.
Students are split into groups with staggered schedules, so part of the school is always on break.
A break of a few weeks during the school year, sometimes used for extra help or enrichment.
The drop in skills some students show after a long summer break.

aff.label: Affirmative
aff.stance: Shorter, more frequent breaks help students keep what they learn and give schools more ways to help.

args.claim: Shorter breaks reduce summer learning loss.
args.warrant: Skills fade without practice. A three-week break gives less time to forget than a ten-week break, so less time is spent reviewing in the fall.
args.evidence: Reviews of summer learning loss (Cooper and colleagues); district comparisons of fall review time.
args.response: The negative replies that the total time off is the same, so forgetting may simply spread across more breaks, and studies of achievement find little effect.

args.claim: It can help students from low-income families most.
args.warrant: Families with fewer resources can't always afford summer camps, trips or tutors, so long summers widen gaps. Spreading breaks and using intersessions for extra help narrows them.
args.evidence: CRS summary noting some evidence of benefits for economically disadvantaged students; research on summer reading gaps.
args.response: The negative answers that free summer programs could target those students directly without changing every family's calendar.

args.claim: Intersessions give timely extra help.
args.warrant: A student who falls behind in October can get catch-up help in the November intersession instead of waiting for summer school.
args.evidence: Descriptions of intersession programs in year-round districts; district reports on remediation.
args.response: The negative argues intersession programs cost money and many districts can't staff them, so the benefit depends on extra funding.

args.claim: Multi-track calendars can ease crowding.
args.warrant: When a quarter of students are always on break, a building can serve more students, saving the cost of new schools.
args.evidence: CRS summary of multi-track savings, including a Clark County, Nevada study.
args.response: The negative points out that multi-track schedules put siblings on different calendars and are hard on families and staff.

neg.label: Negative
neg.stance: Year-round calendars disrupt families and communities without clear academic gains.

args.claim: The academic evidence is weak.
args.warrant: A disruptive change should show clear benefits. Most studies find no effect or a small one, and many have design problems.
args.evidence: CRS (2014) summary of the research, including Cooper and colleagues' note that a credible study had yet to be done, and a California study finding no effect on test scores.
args.response: The affirmative replies that small gains concentrated among low-income students still matter, and weak studies mean we should try and measure, not refuse.

args.claim: It complicates family life.
args.warrant: Parents must find child care for several breaks a year instead of one summer, and families with children in different schools may face different calendars.
args.evidence: CRS discussion of family scheduling problems; parent surveys in districts that tried and dropped year-round calendars.
args.response: The affirmative answers that communities adapt with intersession programs and camps, and some parents prefer breaks in other seasons.

args.claim: Summer has value of its own.
args.warrant: Summer jobs, camps, family farms and businesses, and long stretches of free time teach responsibility and independence that school can't.
args.evidence: CRS note on lost summer jobs for older students and effects on summer businesses; research on youth summer employment.
args.response: The affirmative replies that a shorter summer still leaves several weeks, and breaks in other seasons offer their own opportunities.

args.claim: Costs and operations can rise.
args.warrant: Buildings used all year need air conditioning and year-round maintenance, and staff on different schedules are harder to train and coordinate.
args.evidence: CRS discussion of higher operating costs and staff burnout concerns.
args.response: The affirmative answers that multi-track savings on buildings often outweigh operating costs, as the CRS also notes.

strawmen.strawman: They want kids in school all year with no summer at all.
strawmen.why: Most year-round calendars keep about 180 school days and a shorter summer.
strawmen.steelman: Rearranging the same number of days into shorter, more frequent breaks may reduce forgetting and allow timely extra help, especially for students from low-income families.

strawmen.strawman: They just want a long vacation.
strawmen.why: Opponents point to weak evidence, family scheduling, summer jobs and costs.
strawmen.steelman: Without clear academic gains, the costs to families, older students' summer work and school operations aren't worth the change.

weak.arg: Students in year-round school go to school more days.
weak.why: Usually false; most year-round calendars have the same number of days. The other side will catch it at once.

weak.arg: Kids will be miserable without summer.
weak.why: Students still get breaks, including a shorter summer; this overstates the change.

aff: Does your calendar add school days or rearrange them?
What evidence shows achievement gains, and how large?
Who pays for intersession programs?
neg: Is summer learning loss real for low-income students?
Would you support a year-round calendar if a district chose it?
How do families in year-round districts handle child care?

items.title: Zoos
items.subtitle: value · beginner
items.body: Zoos say they protect endangered species and teach visitors to care about wildlife. Critics say captivity harms many animals and the benefits are overstated. Which weighs more?

meta.title: Zoos
meta.resolution: Resolved: Zoos do more good than harm.
meta.summary: Zoos say they protect endangered species and teach visitors to care about wildlife. Critics say captivity harms many animals and the benefits are overstated. Which weighs more?

background.p: Modern accredited zoos describe their missions as conservation, education, research and animal welfare. Many take part in cooperative breeding programs for threatened species and fund field conservation. Some species, such as the California condor and the Arabian oryx, survived in part because of breeding in zoos and similar facilities, and were later returned to the wild.

Evidence on zoos' effects on visitors is mixed. A 2019 review in *Frontiers in Psychology* (Godinez and Fernandez) found that interactive programs and naturalistic exhibits improve learning and attitudes, and that visitors take more conservation actions on site, but that few studies compare zoo visitors with non-visitors, so the effect on behavior after leaving is largely unknown. Visitors who see animals pacing or showing other repetitive behaviors rate the animals' welfare and their own visit lower.
Standards vary widely: accredited zoos follow detailed welfare rules, while some roadside attractions do not. The resolution asks about zoos in general, so debaters should say which zoos they mean.

disputed.q: Do zoo visits change how people treat wildlife?
positions: Studies find visitors learn and take conservation actions at the zoo, especially through interactive programs.
Reviews note few studies follow visitors afterward or compare them with non-visitors, so lasting effects are uncertain.

terms.def: A zoo that meets an association's standards for animal care, safety and conservation.
A cooperative breeding program among zoos to keep a healthy captive population of a threatened species.
Repetitive behavior with no clear purpose, such as pacing, often seen as a sign of poor welfare.
Releasing animals bred in captivity back into the wild.

aff.label: Affirmative
aff.stance: Good zoos save species, fund conservation and help people care about wildlife.

args.claim: Zoos help save endangered species.
args.warrant: When wild populations collapse, a carefully managed captive population can keep a species alive and supply animals for reintroduction.
args.evidence: Recoveries of the California condor and Arabian oryx; cooperative breeding program records.
args.response: The negative answers that only a small share of zoo animals belong to threatened species in such programs.

args.claim: Zoos fund and support conservation in the wild.
args.warrant: Ticket sales and donations pay for field researchers, habitat protection and anti-poaching work that wouldn't otherwise be funded.
args.evidence: Zoo association reports on field conservation spending; partnerships with wildlife agencies.
args.response: The negative replies that the same money could go straight to habitat protection without keeping animals in captivity.

args.claim: Zoos teach people to value wildlife.
args.warrant: Seeing a living animal creates a connection that a screen can't, especially for children who will never see one in the wild.
args.evidence: Godinez and Fernandez (2019) on learning from interactive programs and naturalistic exhibits.
args.response: The negative answers that the same review found little evidence of lasting behavior change after visitors leave.

args.claim: Zoos advance science that helps wild animals.
args.warrant: Research on animal health, reproduction and behavior in zoos helps veterinarians and field biologists protect wild populations.
args.evidence: Studies published by zoo researchers; veterinary advances from zoo medicine.
args.response: The negative argues that animals in captivity may behave differently, limiting what research shows about the wild.

neg.label: Negative
neg.stance: Captivity harms many animals, and the benefits zoos claim are smaller than they appear.

args.claim: Captivity can harm animal welfare, especially for some species.
args.warrant: Wide-ranging, intelligent or social animals such as elephants, great apes and large carnivores may suffer in limited spaces, shown by pacing and other stereotypic behaviors.
args.evidence: Welfare research on elephants and carnivores in captivity; Godinez and Fernandez on visitor reactions to stereotypic behavior.
args.response: The affirmative answers that modern accredited zoos have redesigned habitats and some have stopped keeping species that do poorly.

args.claim: Most zoo animals aren't part of conservation programs.
args.warrant: If the main justification is saving species, keeping many animals that aren't endangered or ever released is hard to justify.
args.evidence: Inventories of zoo collections compared with threatened-species lists.
args.response: The affirmative replies that non-endangered animals still serve education and fundraising that support conservation.

args.claim: Education claims are weakly supported.
args.warrant: If visits don't change behavior after people leave, a key benefit is overstated.
args.evidence: The 2019 review's finding that the zoo's effect beyond its walls is largely unknown.
args.response: The affirmative argues that the absence of long-term studies isn't evidence of no effect.

args.claim: Protecting habitats does more good.
args.warrant: Species survive long-term only if their habitats survive; money and attention spent on captive collections may be better spent protecting wild places.
args.evidence: Conservation research on habitat loss as a leading threat to species.
args.response: The affirmative replies that zoos already fund habitat work, and captive populations are insurance when habitats fail.

strawmen.strawman: Zoo supporters think animals exist for our entertainment.
strawmen.why: Supporters emphasize conservation, research and education, and accredited zoos follow welfare standards.
strawmen.steelman: Good zoos keep endangered species alive, fund field conservation and help people, especially children, care about wildlife.

strawmen.strawman: Zoo critics want every animal set free in the wild tomorrow.
strawmen.why: Many critics favor sanctuaries, phasing out certain species and funding habitats, not sudden release.
strawmen.steelman: Captivity harms many animals, most zoo animals aren't in conservation programs, and the education benefits are poorly supported; habitat protection does more good.

weak.arg: Animals in zoos are happier because they get free food.
weak.why: Welfare research shows needs beyond food; this is easy to refute.

weak.arg: Zoos are just prisons for animals.
weak.why: A slogan; it skips the conservation evidence your opponent will raise.

aff: What share of zoo animals belong to endangered-species programs?
Which species do poorly in captivity?
What does research show about visitors' behavior after they leave?
neg: How did the California condor survive?
Should accredited zoos and roadside attractions be judged the same way?
Where would the animals in zoos go?
